units.la: EX non paucorum fratrum aliorumque virorum graviuum[?] et magnorum relatu atque indiciis intellexi; esse quosdam, qui res novas molian-tur in Ecclesiâ & introducere doctrinam Pontificiam conentur de Potestate Magistratus in rebus Ecclesiasticis. Atque ut eo suo fine potiri queant, adornare eos jam libellum in Hollandiâ brevi committendum prelo, & me hinc inde acerbe tradu-
units.tr: I have learned, from the report and information of not a few brothers and other weighty and distinguished men, that there are certain people who are stirring up new things in the Church and trying to introduce the Papist doctrine concerning the power of the magistrate in ecclesiastical affairs. And so that they may attain their end, they are preparing a little book, soon to be committed to the press in Holland, and from every side they bitterly traduce me.

units.la: PRÆFATIO.
units.tr: PREFACE.

units.la: cere ob doctrinam Ecclesiarum Reformatarum propositam sub initium anni trigesimi octavi in Disputatione impressâ Daventriæ. Quare auctores mihi erant, ut eam Disputationem, quia in nullius ferè manibus e-rat, publico darem;idq; ob duas causas. Primò enim ex illius lectione multos cognituros, quæ sit doctrina Ecclesiarum Reformatarum de ea materia, adeoq; molimina illa minus successus habitura. Deinde retusum iri eo modo calumnias istorum, ut-pote quæ solâ Disputationis il-lius lectione evidentissimè coar-guantur. guantur. Res hæc me non pa-rum suspensum & dubium tenuit. Nam ex una parte quòminus ipsorum consilio locus dandus videretur, invidiæ & malignitatis metus obstabat, quam haud dubiè magis, quàm antehac incursurus essem apud novandi & turbandi cu-pidos, ideò, quod tàm pulchris & heroicis scilicet ipsorum ausibus impedimento essem. Ex altera parte atrocitas ipsa moliminis me avocabat, quæ alios ad resistendum animare solet. Cogitabam enim, cùm res non solum Religionis, sed etiam
units.tr: I was reviled for the doctrine of the Reformed Churches set forth at the beginning of the year 1638 in a printed disputation at Deventer. For this reason, several men advised me to make that disputation public, since hardly anyone had it in their hands. They gave two reasons. First, from reading it, many would come to know what the doctrine of the Reformed Churches on this matter is, and so those schemes would have less success. Second, the slanders of those men would be blunted in this way, since they are most plainly refuted by reading that disputation alone. This matter has kept me not a little anxious and undecided. On the one hand, the fear of envy and malice stood in the way of giving place to their plan, and I would undoubtedly meet this more than before from those who desire innovation and disturbance, because I would stand in the way of their so fine and heroic undertakings. On the other hand, the very atrocity of the scheme drew me away, since such things usually rouse others to resist. For I was thinking that, since the matter concerns not only religion but also

units.la: PRÆFATIO.
units.tr: PREFACE.

units.la: Reipublicæ agatur, Magistratus omnes cordatos, non solum virium, sed etiam animi satis habituros ad jus potestatemque suam etiam me tacente defendendam. Satis quippe eos nosse' agi hîc de summa rerum suarum, dum & melior ac nobilior pars potestatis ipsis eripitur, & hac erepta altera pars, quæ circa res civiles occupatur, nequaquam in tuto esse potest. Habet enim, secundum doctrinam Ecclesiarum Reformatarum omnium, Magistratus sceptrum duos veluti apices, potestatem nimirum Ecclesiasticam externam, non
units.tr: ...the commonwealth is at stake. Every prudent magistrate will have enough, not only of strength but also of spirit, to defend his right and power even if I say nothing. For they well know that what is at issue here is the whole of their position: the better and nobler part of their power is being snatched away, and once that is taken, the other part, which concerns civil affairs, cannot possibly be safe. For, according to the teaching of all the Reformed Churches, the magistrate holds the sceptre with two points, as it were, namely external ecclesiastical power, not

units.la: PRÆFATIO.
units.tr: PREFACE.

units.la: non quidvis pro lubitu faciendi, sed secundùm verbū Dei externè gubernandi Ecclesiam; quam potestatem Constantinus Magnus egregiè expressit distinctam à potestate formali interna & ministeriali Pastorum, dicendo: Vos estis Episcopi intra Ecclesiam, ego Episcopus extra Ecclesiam à Deo constitutus. Hic unus apex est. Alter est potestas civilis. Ita ut si Magistratui eripiatur potestas Ecclesiastica, non integer amplius Magistratus, sed ex parte tantum sit; quandoquidem ei ademta erit pars una po-
units.tr: not to do whatever it pleases, but to govern the Church externally according to the Word of God. Constantine the Great expressed this power admirably, distinguishing it from the formal, internal and ministerial power of the pastors, when he said: "You are bishops within the Church; I am a bishop appointed by God outside the Church." This is one point of the sceptre. The other is civil power. So that if ecclesiastical power is taken away from the magistrate, he is no longer whole, but only in part; for one part of his power has been taken from him.

units.la: PRÆFATIO.
units.tr: PREFACE.

units.la: testatis ipsius & quidem præcipua ac potissima ; utpote que tantò nobilior est civili, quantò anima corpore, salus & fælicitas æterna prosperitate temporali præstantior est. Et ea parte nobiliore erepta , periclitatur & altera , quemadmodum experientia Papatus docet maximè in Regno florentissimo Angliæ. Cum enim eripi sibi sivissent Reges & Principes potestatem Ecclesiasticam ab Episcopis & Sacerdotibus, illi ulterius progressi sunt, & arripuerunt sibi etiam potestatem temporalem, Regna tributaria sibi fecerunt,
units.tr: of that power, and indeed its chief and most important part; for it is as much nobler than the civil power as the soul is more excellent than the body, and eternal salvation and happiness are more excellent than temporal prosperity. And when this nobler part has been snatched away, the other is also put in peril, as the experience of the Papacy teaches most of all in the most flourishing kingdom of England. For when kings and princes had allowed the ecclesiastical power to be wrested from them by bishops and priests, those men went further and seized for themselves temporal power as well, and made kingdoms tributary to themselves,

units.la: PRÆFATIO.
units.tr: PREFACE.

units.la: imo etiam Monarchiam tem-poralem supra omnes Reges ac Principes sibi vindicârunt, & quidem (quod probè notandum) ex eo ipso fundamento, quod potestatem Ecclesiasticam omnem ad se transtulissent. Unde inferebant, multò magis temporalem potestatem ad se pertinere, quemadmodum apud Bellarminum lib. s.[?] de Pontif. Rom. capp. s.[?] 6. &c. videre est: qui cum suis Theologis longè astutius Papæ potestatem temporalem astruit, dum eam ex Spirituali seu Ecclesiasticâ derivat, quàm Canonistæ, qui illam directè juris divini esse contendunt. Unde insignis ille servus Dei Daniel Chamierius lib. 15. de Oecumenico Pontif. c. 1. ait, Pontificem Romanum sibi arrogare potestatem temporalem in statum Politicum, tanquam APPENDICEM potestatis Spiritualis. Ex quo per se sequitur eos, qui potestatibus supereminentibus eripiunt potestatem circa res Ecclesiasticas, spolium committere gravissimum, rebellionis, adeoque laesae majestatis sese reos constituere, quemadmodum Theologi Reformati multis
units.tr: Indeed they also claimed for themselves a temporal monarchy above all kings and princes, and that (which should be carefully noted) on the very ground that they had transferred to themselves all ecclesiastical power. From this they inferred that temporal power pertains to them all the more, as can be seen in Bellarmine, book s.[?] on the Roman Pontiff, chapters s.[?] 6, etc., who, together with his theologians, asserts the temporal power of the Pope far more cunningly than the canonists do, since he derives it from the spiritual or ecclesiastical power, whereas the canonists contend that it is directly of divine right. Hence that notable servant of God, Daniel Chamier, in book 15 on the Oecumenical Pontiff, chapter 1, says, that the Roman Pontiff arrogates to himself temporal power over the political state, as an APPENDIX of spiritual power. From this it follows of itself that those who snatch from supreme powers the power over ecclesiastical matters commit a most grievous robbery, and thereby make themselves guilty of rebellion and so of high treason, as the Reformed theologians in many places

units.la: PRÆFATIO.
units.tr: PREFACE.

units.la: multis in scriptis hactenus pronunciarunt. Ex tali rebelli doctrina non possunt non etiam gravissimæ seditiones, tumultus & bella civilia oriri. Nam quando populorum animis & auribus instillatur illa doctrina; improbare discunt & taxare actiones ac decreta sancta Magistratuum circa res Ecclesiasticas, & judicant ea illicita esse, adeoque se non teneri illis obedire. Unde præceps ad arma furor errantium populorum sequitur, cum nihil sit, quòd æquè populum adversus Reges & Magistratus commoveat, quam si in
units.tr: have hitherto declared in many writings. From such a rebellious doctrine there cannot fail to arise the gravest seditions, tumults and civil wars. For when that doctrine is instilled into the minds and ears of the peoples, they learn to disapprove and censure the actions and holy decrees of magistrates concerning ecclesiastical affairs, and they judge them to be unlawful, and so consider themselves not bound to obey them. Hence there follows the headlong fury of the misguided peoples taking up arms, since there is nothing that stirs the people against kings and magistrates so effectively as when, in

units.la: PRÆFATIO.
units.tr: PREFACE.

units.la: rebus Ecclesiæ ac Religionis præ-varicari videantur. Hinc sanguinis effusiones oriuntur & omnia sursum ac deorsum vertuntur. Hæc igitur cum mecum animo reputarem, existimabam satius fore, ut Reip. proceribus cura omnis isthæc relinqueretur, atque ego tacitum fabulæ spectatorem agerem. Sed ex altera parte me movit me Christiana charitas erga eos, quamvis de mepessimè meritos. Cui enim bono, cogitabam, sinere ipsos ruere in justissimam indignationem superemi-nentium potestatum? cui bono permittere, quantum in te est,
units.tr: they seem to transgress in matters of the Church and of religion. From this come bloodshed and everything turned upside down. When I considered these things in my own mind, I thought it better that all this concern be left to the leading men of the state, and that I should play the silent spectator of the drama. But on the other hand, Christian love for them moved me, though they have deserved very badly of me. For I kept thinking: what good is it to let them rush headlong into the most just indignation of the supreme powers? What good is it to allow, as far as lies in you,

units.la: PRÆFATIO.
units.tr: PREFACE.

units.la: ut Ecclesiam[?] cum Republicâ turbent, atque omnia sursum deorsum vertant? An non præstabit revocare eos maturè à molimine, impedire quominus impingant, adeoque à lapsu gravis-simo eos præservare? Id quod melius fieri non poterit, quàm ubi viderint, verâ doctrinâ jam benè imbutos esse animos à cujus cognitione omnibus modis tum per calumnias, tum per alias artes homines prohibere conantur. Accedit quod lege non solùm naturæ, sed etiam verbi divini famam meam ho-nestam non paucis laboribus per
units.tr: that they throw the Church and the commonwealth into confusion and turn everything upside down? Would it not be better to call them back in good time from their undertaking, to stop them from rushing headlong, and so to preserve them from a most grievous fall? This could not be done better than when they see that minds are already well steeped in true doctrine, the knowledge of which men try in every way to keep from them, both by slanders and by other devices. Add to this that by the law not only of nature but also of the divine word, my honest reputation, won by no small labours through

units.la: PRÆFATIO.
units.tr: PREFACE.

units.la: Dei gratiam pro veritate divinâ & ministerio verbi contra adversarios ad extremam invidiam usque suscepti (qua in re nihil mihi, sed omnem laudem Deo adscribo) apud Ecclesias Dei partam asserere teneor. Condescendo igitur in aliorum judicium & sententiam, ac publico do Dissertatione hanc de Episcopatu Constantini M. seu doctrinam de Potestate Magistratus in rebus Ecclesiasticis. Quæ quidem doctrina non mea est privata; sed totius Ecclesiæ Reformatæ ad annum saltem usque trigesimum octavum, quo primum
units.tr: I am bound to affirm before the Churches of God that the grace of God has secured for me the reputation I have gained, having taken up the divine truth and the ministry of the Word against adversaries, even to the point of extreme hatred (in which matter I ascribe nothing to myself, but all praise to God). I therefore yield to the judgment and opinion of others and publish this dissertation on the episcopate of Constantine the Great, or the doctrine of the power of the magistrate in ecclesiastical affairs. This doctrine is not my private opinion, but that of the whole Reformed Church, at least up to the year 1638, when first

units.la: PRÆFATIO.
units.tr: PREFACE.

units.la: mùm impressa fuit Disputatio illa. Ut adeo nemo doctrinæ illi vel novitatis, vel injuriæ in Episcopos & pastores, vel adulationis erga Reges, Principes, Ordines & quoscunque Magistratus, vel turbarum, vel erroris, vel alterius criminis alicujus dicam scribere possit, nisi ejusdem totam Ecclesiam Reformatam arguere; adeoque se oppido impudentem, turbulentum & male feriatum hominem re ipsâ ostendere velit. Hoc cùm ita sit, hortor & rogo omnes & singulos Orthodoxos, maximè autem pios servos Dei
units.tr: Since that Disputation was first printed, no one can say that I am writing anything new in doctrine, unjust to bishops and ministers, flattering to kings, princes, orders and any magistrates whatever, or causing troubles, error or any other crime, unless he means to accuse the whole Reformed Church of the same things; and so he would show himself in fact to be a shamelessly impudent, turbulent and idle fellow. This being so, I urge and beg all and each of the orthodox, and especially the pious servants of God

units.la: PRÆFATIO.
units.tr: PREFACE.

units.la: Ecclesiarumque ministros, ut hanc modestam & veram doctrinam fidis animis custodiant; & caveant sibi à fermento ac supercilio Pontificio, atque à Novitatibus. Potuissem autem materiam hanc latissimè deducere; sed volui Disputationem illam repetere & quidem sine ulla mutatione, additione, detractione, ne quis calumniari posset me ante hac aliter docuisse et scripsisse, quàm nunc; quamvis si in melius proficere potuissem, nemo nisi perfrictæ frontis homo id mihi objicere posset. Sed firma stat doc-trina
units.tr: and the ministers of the churches, that they may keep this modest and true doctrine with faithful hearts, and beware of the leaven and the haughtiness of the Papists, and of novelties. I could indeed have developed this matter at great length; but I preferred to repeat that Disputation, and indeed without any change, addition or omission, so that no one could slander me by saying that I had previously taught and written otherwise than I do now; although, if I had been able to make progress for the better, no one but a man of brazen forehead could object this to me. But the sound doctrine stands firm

units.la: PRÆFATIO.
units.tr: PREFACE.

units.la: [?]Ætrina Reform. Ecclesiæ etiam in hac parte, ita ut ea illustrari quidem possit, sed in melius aut verius mutari nequeat. Accedit quòd malui me continere intra angustios istos limites ob duas causas. Primò enim Theologi plurimi eam rem tractarunt abundè, qui argumenta adversæ partis omnia & proposuêre & refutavêre: ita ut ego nihil in eam rem contulerim, nisi quòd in certum ordinem & capita perspicuè & distinctè congesserim, quæ ab aliis sparsim dictasunt. Deinde malim laborare circa alias materias (si quid
units.tr: The doctrine of the Reformed Church on this point too, so that it may indeed be illustrated but cannot be changed for the better or made more true. Moreover, I preferred to keep myself within these narrow limits for two reasons. First, very many theologians have treated this matter at length, and have both set out and refuted all the arguments of the opposing side; so that I have contributed nothing to the matter except to arrange, in a certain order and under clear and distinct headings, what others have said scattered about. Second, I would rather labour on other subjects (if anything

units.la: PRÆFATIO.
units.tr: PREFACE.

units.la: forté præcedentibus meis Deus adjicere velit) & speciatim in eruendo ex antiquitate Ecclesiasticâ thesauro prudentiæ veteris Ecclesiæ; quàm circa hanc. Satis enim malitiam sæculi, satis malignas illius machinationes atque insultus, ut alia graviora etiam non dicam expertus sum; adeo ut me tantùm non pigeat ordinariis laboribus aliquid adjicere in futurum. Et de hac materia, quandoquidem puto me in ea quoque parte puritati Religionis et paci Ecclesiæ, quorum utrumque meus semper scopus fuit, satis ex officio & conscientia
units.tr: perhaps, if God wills to add to my earlier works God and especially in drawing from the treasury of ancient Church antiquity the wisdom of the early Church, rather than on this subject. For I have had enough of the malice of this age and its malicious schemes and assaults, and of other, even graver, trials I will not mention; so much so that I am scarcely reluctant to add, in future, something to my ordinary labours. And concerning this matter, since I think I have served the purity of Religion and the peace of the Church, both of which have always been my aim, sufficiently from duty and conscience

units.la: PRÆFATIO.
units.tr: PREFACE.

units.la: sciētia fecisse,cum nemine contēdere desidero. Suffecerit mihi, si res in meo relinquatur arbitrio, quod huic Disputationi addidi Respon. meam ad interrogata quę ante ānos fere quatuor non solum ad me missa fuerunt, sed etiam hinc inde sparsa dicuntur; quæ hîc bonâ fide totidem literis & syllabis tibi exhibeo, una cum illa responsione mea quâ tunc è vestigio defunctus fui. Ex eâ non pauca circa hanc materiam clariora fient: adeò ut existimem bonis omnibus, pacis, veritatis ac modestię amantibus, quantum necesse est, satisfecisse. Si quid tamen dubii superfit alicujus animo, & absit calumniandi studium, ei satisfacere semper paratus ero per Dei gratiam, quandoquidem de doctrinæ hujus veritate firmiter persuasus sum. Quod si autem quis vel ipse, vel (uti Simoniæ sunt quorundam artes) aliorum operâ, per meum latus doctrinam hanc oppugnare vel suspectam reddere ausus fuerit, adeoque larvam sibi egregiè detractam velit; sciat nihil esse tàm absconditum aut in obscuro factū quod non sol sit aspecturus cum rubore & confusione eorum, qui malè
units.tr: I have done so in good conscience, and I have no wish to contend with anyone. It will be enough for me, if the matter is left to my own judgment, that I have added to this Disputation my Response to the questions which were sent to me about four years ago and which are said to be circulating here and there. I present them here in good faith, word for word and syllable for syllable, together with that reply of mine which I then gave on the spot. From it not a few things about this subject will become clearer, so that I think I have satisfied, as far as necessary, all good men who love peace, truth and moderation. If, however, any doubt remains in someone's mind, and there is no desire to calumniate, I shall always be ready to satisfy him, by the grace of God, since I am firmly persuaded of the truth of this doctrine. But if anyone, either himself or (as is the trick of some Simonists) through the work of others, has dared to attack this doctrine or make it suspect by coming at me from the side, and wishes to have his mask thoroughly torn off, let him know that nothing is so hidden or done in obscurity that it will not come to light, to the blushing and confusion of those who act wickedly

units.la: PRÆFATIO .
units.tr: PREFACE.

units.la: malè agunt. Et in eo necessita-tis & coactionis casu protestor me non permissurum per Dei gratiam quantum in me erit, ut quis ita licentiosè Ecclesiæ pacem turbare ac veritatem eâ in parte violare ausit. Satis enim experientia Papatus per tot secula nos innumeris & inenarrabilibus modis docuit, quæ mala in Ecclesia & Rep. Euangelicâ expectanda essent, si contraria & nefaria illa doctrina Pontificia tanquam postliminio reduceretur. Et sint nobis in exemplum atque cautelam ea, quæ nunc in Angliâ & Scotiâ conti-gerunt
units.tr: act wickedly. And in that case of necessity and compulsion I declare that, by the grace of God, I will not permit, so far as lies in me, anyone to dare so licentiously to disturb the peace of the Church and to violate the truth in that respect. For the experience of Papacy over so many centuries has taught us in countless and inexpressible ways what evils were to be expected in the Church and the Evangelical commonwealth, if that contrary and wicked Papist doctrine were brought back as if by right of postliminy. Let these things that now happen in England and Scotland be for us an example and a warning.

units.la: PRÆFATIO.
units.tr: PREFACE.

units.la: gerunt & quotidie contingunt.
units.tr: happen and occur daily.

units.la: Quæ res etiam eos, qui novarum rerum cupidi sunt à pruritu suo revocare debet. Et oro omnes ac singulos, ut considerent, si quæ sit materia Theologica, quæ prudentiam magnam requirat, certè eam in doctrina de Gubernatio-ne Ecclesiæ oppidò necessariam esse. Quem in finem pro mei judicii mediocritate ex doctrina Ecclesiæ has quatuor maximas observandas esse existimo. Primò, ut prætextu libertatis Ecclesiæ, h. e. ministrorum tuendæ non nimium ipsis, Magistratui autem nimis parum tribuatur:
units.tr: This matter ought also to call back from their itch those who are eager for novelties. And I beg all and each to consider whether there is any theological subject that requires great prudence; certainly in the doctrine of the government of the Church this is most necessary. To this end, according to the modest measure of my judgment, I think these four greatest points must be observed from the doctrine of the Church. First, that under the pretext of the freedom of the Church, that is, of protecting the ministers, too much should not be granted to them, and too little to the magistrate;

units.la: PRÆFATIO.
units.tr: PREFACE.

units.la: vicissim ne prætextu potestatis Magistratus asserendæ, huic ni-mium, ministris autem nimis parum tribuatur. Utriusq; & defectus & excessus character est, si res in Papatum abeat vel Hierarchicum vel Politicum. Hierarchicus Papatus est, quando ministerium in dominium convertitur ἀνυπεύθυνον[?] & ei non solum gubernatio interna, ut par est, attribuitur, sed etiam e-xterna, & Magistratus sub mi-nisterium ita deprimitur, ut vel Magistratus potestas circa Ecclesiastica dependere statuatur à ministris, vel id quod Magi-
units.tr: Conversely, the claim of the magistrate's power must not be used to give the magistrate too much and the ministers too little. Both the defect and the excess are marked: a matter becomes papal, whether hierarchical or political. The hierarchical papacy exists when the ministry is turned into a lordship [ἀνυπεύθυνον, unaccountable], and it is given not only internal government, as is right, but also external government. The magistrate is so pushed down under the ministry that either the magistrate's power in ecclesiastical matters is held to depend on the ministers, or that which the Magi-

units.la: PRÆFATIO.
units.tr: PREFACE.

units.la: statui proprium est, iis attri-buatur, vel denique id, quod Magistratui pariter & ministris certo respectu competit, in solos ministros conferatur. Politicus Papatus est, quando Magistratui potestas absoluta in rebus Ecclesiasticis defertur, & ei non solum gubernatio externa, sed & interna adscribitur, ministeriumq; ita sub eum deprimitur, ut vel illud immedi-atè non à Christo, sed à Magistratu fluere statuatur, sive quoad substantiam ab eo depen-dere; vel ut Magistratui tribuantur actiones, quæ propriæ sunt
units.tr: ...belongs to the state, be attributed to them; or finally, that which belongs equally to the magistrate and the ministers in a certain respect be conferred on the ministers alone. Political Papacy is when absolute power in ecclesiastical matters is handed over to the magistrate, and to him is ascribed not only external government but also internal, and the ministry is so far subordinated to him that either its very existence is held to flow not immediately from Christ but from the magistrate, or at least its substance is held to depend on him; or that actions which are proper to the ministry are attributed to the magistrate

units.la: PRÆFATIO:
units.tr: PREFACE:

units.la: sunt ministerii, vel ut, quod Magistratui & ministris suo modo ac diverso respectu com-mune est, soli Magistratui as-scribatur. Hoc unum est. Se-cundò observandum in Gubernatione Ecclesiæ esse quedam di-vini juris, & in verbo Dei determinata; alia autem in verbo Dei non contineri, sed indifferentia esse, adeoque in libertate Ecclesiæ cujus nutricius est Magistratus, & juris humani positivi esse. Illa sunt ἀκίνητα seu immutabilia; ac à nullo homi-num variari possunt. Hæc au-tem κινητὰ[?] sunt seu mutabilia;
units.tr: are of the ministry, or what is common to the magistrate and the ministers, in their own and different respects, is ascribed to the magistrate alone. This is the first point. Secondly, it must be observed that in the government of the Church some things are of divine right and determined in the Word of God, while others are not contained in the Word of God but are indifferent, and so belong to the liberty of the Church, of which the magistrate is the nurse, and to positive human law. The former are unmovable [ἀκίνητα], that is, immutable, and can be varied by no man. The latter are movable [κινητά], that is, mutable;

units.la: PRÆFATIO.
units.tr: PREFACE.

units.la: sed quę non nisi bono ordine, hoc est, consensu atque auctoritate Ecclesiæ & Magistratus[?] Orthodoxi mutari possunt. Illa ubivis locorum & quicunque sit status Reip. in qua Ecclesia est, obtinere debent; hæc pro locorum, Rerump. & ingeniorum quoque indole diversa sunt. Neque enim simpliciter verum est, quod Pontificii volunt, regimen Ecclesiasticum regimini Politico attemperandum esse. Nam id de iis, quæ ἀκίνητα[?] sunt in gubernatione Ecclesiæ, salsissimum est. Quâ de re breviter, sed nervosè[?] disserit egregigius quisquis ille est (nam nomen illius nobis temporum ini-quitas invidet) & eruditissimus scriptor, qui Historiam motuum regni Scotiæ hoc ipso anno nobis dedit p. 245. Tertiò observan-dum, in statu perturbato Ecclesiæ, & quando Magistra-tus supremus officium non face-re vult, Ecclesiam aut saniorem illius partem in extremo periculo religionis constitutam, plus potestatis conjunctâ cum proceribus opera exercere posse, quàm ordinariè: similiter & Magi-stratum de procerum & sanio-ris partis Ecclesiæ consilio plus
units.tr: But these things can be changed only in good order, that is, by the agreement and authority of the Church and the Orthodox magistrate. The former must hold everywhere and in whatever condition the commonwealth is in which the Church exists; the latter vary according to the nature of places, commonwealths and also of minds. For it is not simply true, as the Papists want, that the ecclesiastical government must be tempered to the political government. For that is most absurd concerning those things which are immovable [ἀκίνητα] in the governance of the Church. On this matter an excellent and very learned writer, whoever he is (for the iniquity of the times envies us his name), discusses it briefly but forcefully, and he gave us this year the History of the disturbances of the kingdom of Scotland, p. 245. Thirdly, it is to be observed that in a disturbed state of the Church, and when the supreme magistrate is unwilling to perform his office, the Church, or its sounder part, placed in extreme danger to religion, can exercise more power, together with the nobles and their work, than ordinarily; similarly the magistrate can use more power, by the counsel of the nobles and the sounder part of the Church, than ordinarily,

units.la: (?) 2 potestatis, quàm ordinariè, adhibere posse, ubi Ecclesia ossicium facere, aut rectè facere non vult. Et hoc velut fundamento nititur Reformatio Religionis ejusq; conservatio suscepta ac continuata invitis multis, qui supremas partes tàm in Ecclesiâ Christianâ quam in Republica obtinebant, aut etiammum obtinent. Quartò denique si aut ministri aut Magistratus abutantur potestate sua, notandum; cavendum tunc esse, ne ideò abrogetur ipsis potestas, quam secundùm verbum Dei habent, aut disputetur contra
units.tr: power than ordinarily, where the Church is unwilling to perform its office, or to perform it rightly. And upon this foundation rests the Reformation of religion and its preservation, undertaken and continued against the wishes of many who held, or still hold, the chief place both in the Christian Church and in the commonwealth. Fourthly and finally, if either the ministers or the magistrate abuse their power, it must be noted; one must take care that on that account the power which they hold according to the Word of God is not taken away from them, or disputed against

units.la: PRÆFATIO.
units.tr: PREFACE.

units.la: e im:[?] sed indicandi sunt abusus, & contra[?] eos agendū et ostendendum ex verbo Dei, quare iis acquiescere nefas sit, & ad ve-rum usum omnia sunt revocanda. Nec enim abusus potestatis ipsam potestatem seu auctoritatem tollit. Egregiè insignis ille & per controversias, quas contra Pontificios edidit optimè de Ecclesia meritus Theologus Daniel Chamierus de hac re disserit lib.14.de Pontif.Oecum. cap II. postquam enim respon-disset ad exceptionem Bellarmini, dicentis Abiatharem Sacerdotem à Salomone depositum (?) 3
units.tr: ...but abuses must be pointed out, and action must be taken against them, and it must be shown from the Word of God why it is wrong to acquiesce in them, and everything must be brought back to its true use. For the abuse of power does not abolish the power or authority itself. That distinguished theologian, who through the controversies he published against the Papists has deserved very well of the Church, Daniel Chamier, discusses this matter in book 14 of his Pontifical Oecumenical work, chapter 2, after he had replied to the objection of Bellarmine, who says that Abiathar the priest was deposed by Solomon (?) 3

units.la: PRÆFATIO.
units.tr: PREFACE.

units.la: tanquam à propheta non tanquam à rege, [?] solidi-tatem ipsius effugii ostendisset: respondet ad aliud ipsius [illegible, ~9 letters] dicentis Imperatores Christianos, qui Episcopatu suo privarunt, de facto id, non de jure, præstitisse; & abusos eos sua potestate fuisse. Ait igitur solidissimus ille Theologus: Itaque nihil est novi cum dicuntur Liberius, Silverius, Johannes injustè pulsi. Nam quis nescit Imperatores sæpè abuti auctoritate? Nemo sanus neget injustè etiam Athanasium factum exulem - à Constantino primum; deinde à Constantio: alios etiam Episcopos Catholicos cùm ab hoc, tum ab aliis: sed non sequitur, ex eo, quod quis injustè facit, propterea non habere auctoritatem faciendi: hoc enim sequitur duntaxat, abuti eum suâ auctoritate. Et mox: Solent autem in facto variæ esse iplarum actionum circumstantiæ, aliâs bonæ, aliâs malç[?], sed eas circumstantias non decet attendi. Ejecit, ut dixi,
units.tr: as coming from a prophet and not from a king, [?] had shown the solidity of his escape: he answers another of his [illegible, about 9 letters] saying that Christian emperors who deprived bishops of their see did so in fact, not by right, and that they abused their power. So that most solid theologian says: Thus nothing new is said when Liberius, Silverius and John are said to have been driven out unjustly. For who does not know that emperors often abuse their authority? No sane person would deny that Athanasius was unjustly made an exile, first by Constantine and then by Constantius, and other Catholic bishops too, both by him and by others. But it does not follow from the fact that someone acts unjustly that he therefore lacks the authority to act; this only follows, that he abuses his authority. And soon after: The circumstances of such actions are usually various in fact, some good and some bad, but those circumstances ought not to be attended to. He was expelled, as I said,

units.la: PRÆFATIO.
units.tr: PREFACE.

units.la: Constantinus Arium, Eusebium, Theognin, hæretcos: ejecit & Athanasium. Confer: utrinque ejiciendi autoritatem potestatemque; eandem invenias; & tamen justè illi, hic contra ejectus est. Quî fit ? Non sanè quia in Athanasio deficeret potestas; quæ in reliquis sufficiebat: sed quia cum æquè Athanasii judex esset Imperator ac reliquorum, tamen Athanasii nullum crimen erat; & erat magnum aliorum. Sic de his respondeo: malè ejectos Liberium, Silverium, Johannem; sed malè; quia causa in his nulla erat exilii; non quia in Imperatoribus nulla esset auctoritas.
units.tr: Constantine expelled Arius, Eusebius, and Theognis, heretics, and he also expelled Athanasius. Compare them: you will find that the authority and power of expelling was the same on both sides, and yet those men were justly expelled, while this one was expelled unjustly. How so? Certainly not because the power was lacking in Athanasius' case, when it was sufficient in the others. Rather, although the emperor was judge of Athanasius just as much as of the rest, Athanasius had no crime, while the others had great ones. So I answer concerning these cases: Liberius, Silverius, and John were expelled wrongly, but wrongly because there was no cause for their exile, not because the emperors had no authority.

units.la: Ita Chamierus. Hæ sunt qua-tuor maximæ, ad quas, qui non attendit, facilè omnia sursum deorsum vertet, Ecclesiam & Rcmp.[?] turbabit, Religionem destruet, cædibus et sanguine, quantum in se est, omnia replebit: qui autem eas observabit, prudenter aget magno cum bono Ecclesiæ & Reip. Possent autem eæ maximæ latissime deduci; sed ad hypothesin descendere
units.tr: Thus Chamier. These are the four greatest points. Whoever does not attend to them will easily turn everything upside down, throw Church and commonwealth into confusion, destroy religion, and fill everything, as far as he can, with slaughter and blood. But whoever observes them will act wisely, to the great good of the Church and the commonwealth. These greatest points could be drawn out very widely, but to descend to a hypothesis

units.la: PRÆFATIO.
units.tr: PREFACE.

units.la: id verò justi voluminis & magni est. Qua in re optandum est, non ut Theologi orthodo-xi infestis scriptis inter se concurrant, se convitiis, & calumniis invicem petant; insidias alii aliis struant; scripta, dicta, facta, sententias, consilia affingant innocenti, quæ ei nunquam vel per febrim aut somnium in mentem venerunt; & dira quævis per inauditam malitiam contra eum moliantur: sed ut conjunctis operis & animis inter se conveniant; & omnia, quæ ad hanc rem faciunt in unum aliquod corpus re tota benè ex-pensa
units.tr: Indeed, this is the task of a long and weighty volume. In this matter it is to be wished that orthodox theologians would not clash with hostile writings, attack one another with insults and slanders, lay snares for each other, and attribute to an innocent man writings, sayings, deeds, opinions and plans that never entered his mind, not even in a fever or a dream, and devise every dreadful thing against him out of unheard-of malice; but rather that they would come together in joined labours and minds, and, having weighed the whole matter carefully, gather everything that bears on it into one body

units.la: PRÆFATIO.
units.tr: PREFACE.

units.la: pensa,& probè distinctis iis,quæ ἀκίνητα, quæ κινητὰ in hac materia sunt, congerant. O quantum hoc operæ precium foret! O quantum suspicionum evelleretur, per quas sæpè Magistratus & ministerium maximo cum malo Ecclesiæ & impedimento cursus regni Christi di-vellunt[?]ur! O quanta spei ansa præscinderetur hostibus veritatis, qui sperant fore ut aliqui ex nobis ipsis exsur-gant, qui pontificiam doctrinam illam (quâ stante tota periclitatur Religio, ut experientia Papatus ostendit) in Ecclesias nostras omnibus modis reducturi
units.tr: weigh them, and, having properly distinguished those things which in this matter are immovable [ἀκίνητα] and those which are movable [κινητὰ], gather them together. O how worthwhile this would be! O how many suspicions would be removed, by which the magistrate and the ministry are so often torn apart, to the great harm of the Church and the hindrance of the course of Christ's kingdom! O what an opening for hope would be cut off from the enemies of the truth, who hope that some from among ourselves will arise who are going to bring back into our churches, by every means, that Papist doctrine (with which, if it stands, the whole Religion is put in peril, as the experience of the Papacy shows)

units.la: PRÆFATIO.
units.tr: PREFACE.

units.la: sint, & eâ ratione Magistra-tuum animos exacerbaturi & ab Ecclesiâ cum præsentissimo il-lius malo abalienaturi. Hoc con-silium meum, ut pius placeat & pacis studiosis pectoribus opto; non quòd doctrina quam propo-no, in ambiguo posita sit, & nondum decisa (contrarium e-nim patet ex hac Disputatione in quâ ut dixi non meam priva-tam, sed totius Ecclesiæ Refor-matæ doctrinam propono) verũ[?] ut omnia ordine perfecto digerā-tur; si qui in hac materia non a-deo versati sunt, plenè instruātur, si quæ durius aut generaliùs vel
units.tr: may be, and may arouse the minds of the magistrates and alienate them from the Church, with its most pressing evil. I hope this counsel of mine will please the pious and those whose hearts are devoted to peace; not because the doctrine I set forth is still in doubt and not yet settled (the contrary is clear from this Disputation, in which, as I said, I set forth not my private opinion but the doctrine of the whole Reformed Church), but so that everything may be laid out in perfect order; if some who are not so practised in this matter are fully instructed, and if anything has been stated too harshly or too generally

units.la: PRÆFATIO.
units.tr: PREFACE.

units.la: ab his vel ab illis scripta sint, mitigentur, difficultates & dubia omnia tollantur, & sic ansa de hac re unquam litigandi etiam in omnem posteritatem tollatur: quò ita & pax et religio in perpetuum floreat, quæ votorum meorum summa est. Hoc meum ex pacis studio consilium est: Sed ut illud & cordatis & prudentibus & modestis viris non displicebit: ita jam prævideo temerariis & superbis ingeniis nihil magis in votis fore, quàm ut spretis salutaribus pacis & concordiæ consiliis ac monitis [?] in me involent, & virus suum contra me evomant. Ipsi viderint, & norint Deum resistere superbis, humilibus autem gratiam dare. Cæterum præfixi de hac dissertatione judicium maximi & sincerissimi Theologi D. Andreæ Riveti, cujus candidum, sanum, defæcatum-que animum, incorruptum judi-dium, summam doctrinum, prudentiam, & merita tota Ecclesia novit & ipsi adversarii suspiciunt; cujus etiam vestigia, ut & D. Walæi, p. m. accuratè expressi in hac materia, prout unicuivis legenti patebit. Addidi & Epistolium Clariss-simi
units.tr: from these or those writings be softened, difficulties and doubts all removed, and so the occasion for ever disputing this matter be taken away for all posterity, so that peace and religion may flourish thus in perpetuity, which is the chief of my prayers. This counsel of mine comes from zeal for peace. But just as it will not displease sensible, prudent and modest men, so I already foresee that rash and proud minds will have nothing more at heart than to scorn the salutary counsels and admonitions of peace and concord, fly at me, and vomit their venom against me. Let them see to it, and know that God resists the proud but gives grace to the humble. Moreover, I have prefixed the judgment on this dissertation of the greatest and most sincere theologian Andreas Rivetus, whose candid, sound and purified mind, incorrupt judgment, great learning, prudence and merits the whole Church knows, and even his adversaries admire; whose footsteps, like those of Walaeus of blessed memory, I have accurately expressed in this matter, as will be plain to any reader. I have also added a short letter of the most distinguished

units.la: PRÆFATIO.
units.tr: PREFACE.

units.la: simi Viri D. Joh. Maccovii, Collegæ mei, Theologi celeberrimi; ut unicuique consensus noster palam fieret. Ego igitur, ut cum totâ Ecclesiâ Reformatâ, nec Magistratibus, nec Episcopis & Pastoribus quicquam detraho, quod eis secundùm verbum Dei competit, aut attribuo, quod non competit, sed Cæsari do, quæ sunt Cæsaris, & Deo, quæ Dei sunt; ita Deus sapientiæ, prudentiæ, pacis, concordiæ, mansuetudinis nobiscum omnibus sit. Franecqueræ.
units.tr: ...of the most distinguished man, Dr. Johannes Maccovius, my colleague, a most celebrated theologian, so that our agreement might be made plain to everyone. Therefore I, like the whole Reformed Church, take nothing away from magistrates, bishops and pastors that belongs to them according to the Word of God, nor do I ascribe to them what does not belong to them, but "render to Caesar the things that are Caesar's, and to God the things that are God's." So may God be with us all in wisdom, prudence, peace, concord and gentleness. Franeker.

units.la: Nonis Novembr. 1641.
units.tr: On the Nones of November 1641.

units.la: Legi & expendi Disputationem Theologicam' de Magistratu, adversus Bellarmini librum de Laicis, quam hoc anno edidit Daventriæ Clariss. & Doctiss. Vir. D. Nicolaus Vedelius, S. Th. Doct. & Professor, eamq; in tredecim quæstiones, ordinis & perspicuitatis gratiâ, distribuit. Testor autem nihil à me animadversum esse in ejus responsionibus & solutionibus, quod non judicem [?] convenire cum o-nium. mnium Ecclesiarum Reformatarum, de eodem articulo, doctrinâ, juxta verbum Dei. Specialiter autem, in iis, quę ex meis in Decalogum commentariis citavit, nihil illum mihi affinxisse, sed mentem meam expresisse, & sententiam, quam veram judico. Cum tamen mihi scrupulus quidam injectus suisset ex eo, quod quaest. 3. ubi agitur de depositione Ministrorum, non objectivam solum, sed etiam formalem potestatem Magistratui tribueret, quum verba ex me citata quæst. 6. negarent eam Magistratui in eo convenire: eum plane mihi satisfecisse,cum id ita interpretatus est, ut spectaret tantum depositionem, quę exercitium prohibet Ministerii in districtu Magistratus illius, & coercitionem externam: non autem potestatem,qua ordinatio ministri, quæ fit à solis pastoribus, redderetur irrita, & pastor exauteratus fieret inhabilis ad prędicationem verbi & sa-
units.tr: I have read and weighed the Theological Disputation on the Magistrate, against Bellarmine's book on laymen, which the most distinguished and learned Mr. Nicolaus Vedelius, Doctor and Professor of Sacred Theology, published this year at Deventer, and which he divided into thirteen questions for the sake of order and clarity. I testify that I have noticed nothing in his replies and solutions that I do not judge to agree with the doctrine on this article of all the Reformed Churches, according to the Word of God. In particular, in those things which he cited from my commentaries on the Decalogue, he has not falsely attributed anything to me, but has expressed my mind and the opinion that I judge to be true. Yet a certain scruple was raised in my mind because in question 3, where he treats of the deposition of ministers, he grants to the magistrate not only objective but also formal power, whereas the words cited from me in question 6 deny that this belongs to the magistrate. He has fully satisfied me, since he interpreted it so that it looks only to deposition, which forbids the exercise of the ministry within that magistrate's jurisdiction, and to external coercion; and not to the power by which the ordination of a minister, which is performed by pastors alone, would be rendered void, and a pastor who had been deposed would become unfit for preaching the Word and administering the sacraments. I assert that this power belongs formally to pastors alone, to whom ordination belongs, just as he himself in question 6 interprets the matter from my words and rests content with them.

units.la: cramentorum administrationem, quam formaliter so-lis Pastoribus assero, quibus competit ordinatio; quemadmodū etiam ipse quæst. 6. rem ex meis verbis interpretatur, & in iis acquiescit.
units.tr: (Continuation of the same point: the administration of the sacraments, which I assert belongs formally to pastors alone, to whom ordination belongs; just as he himself in question 6 interprets the matter from my words and rests content with them.)

units.la: In eo etiam quod quæst. 13.[?] ex me citat, circa eminentiam & præcellentiam potestatis politicæ & Ministerii Ecclesiastici, quod dixi, veterum nonnullos & præcipuè Chrysostomum extollentes dignitatem Ecclesiastici muneris supra Politica, non spectasse honorem, præcellentiam, & dignitatem civilem, sed tantum objectum & finem, ab una parte spiritualem, & vitam æternam spectantem, ab altera Rerumpub. & politi-tię temporalis conservationem, nihilque hoc præjudicare dignitati Magistratuum, quandoquidem illa est αὐτοκρατορικὴ[?], cum alia sit tantum Ministerialis, quod pluribus exemplis illustravi, idem paucis, sed verè expressum fuisse à D. Vedelio, per distinctionem eorum,quę ministris competunt per se, vel per accidens. Proinde, hac mea Syngrapha,omnibus testatum volo,virum illum,de Ecclesia bene merito, & qui doctissimis lucubrationibus satis probavit, quàm alienus esset ab omnium novatorum molitionibus, in hoc etiam, de Magistratu, articulo ita se gesisse, ut adversus Pontificios & alios superereminentium potestatum adversarios,veritatem asseruerit, sine prȩjudicio eorum, quę verbi divini
units.tr: Concerning what he cites from me in question 13, on the eminence and pre-eminence of civil power and of the ecclesiastical ministry, I said that some of the ancients, and especially Chrysostom, in extolling the dignity of the ecclesiastical office above the civil, did not have in view honour, pre-eminence and civil dignity, but only the object and the end: on the one hand spiritual, concerning eternal life, and on the other the preservation of the commonwealth and of temporal civil life. I said that this prejudices nothing to the dignity of magistrates, since theirs is autocratic [αὐτοκρατορικὴ] while the other is merely ministerial. I illustrated this at length with many examples. The same thing was expressed by Mr. Vedelius, though briefly, but truly, through the distinction between what belongs to ministers per se and what belongs to them per accidens. Therefore, by this my signed statement, I wish it to be made known to all that this man, who has deserved well of the Church and who has sufficiently shown by his most learned labours how far removed he is from the undertakings of all the innovators, has in this article also, concerning the magistrate, so conducted himself that against the Papists and other opponents of the supreme powers he has asserted the truth, without prejudice to those things of the divine word which

units.la: Ministris & Ecclesiarum rectoribus, juxta Canonem scripturæ, & Ecclesiasticos ex eo deductos canones competunt: nullamq; me videre rationem, cur Orthodoxus quilquam ei, circa hoc negotium litem ullam intendat. Scripsi Hagæ Comitis, ultimo Februarii stylo novo, anno 1638.
units.tr: Written at The Hague, Count's Court, on the last day of February, new style, in the year 1638. (Note: this unit is the close of the testimony of Rivetus.)

units.la: ANDREAS RIVETVS.
units.tr: ANDREAS RIVETUS.

units.la: S.
units.tr: S.

units.la: VIr Clariss. Disputationem tuam de Magistratu Politico adversus Bell. eò diligentius legi, quò videre potui, eam accuratius esse conscriptam, & deprehendi non tantum argumentorum gravissimorum veritate, sed & Clariss. Theologorum authoritate undecumque suffultam ac munitam. Non dubito, quin rem gratiss. feceris iis, qui materiam hanc accuratius pernoscere cupiunt. Me certè tibi devinctum hoc nomine habes, & quia nos pudere non debet profiteri, per quem profecerimus, fateor me tractatu hoc tuo doctiss. in iis, in quibus fluctuabam ante, expeditum & quae nesciebam, edoctum. Deus tibi sufficiat porrò vires ad bene merendum de Ecclesia Dei.
units.tr: Most distinguished Sir, I have read your disputation on the Political Magistrate against Bellarmine all the more carefully because I could see that it was written with greater precision, and I have found it supported and fortified not only by the truth of most weighty arguments but also by the authority of most distinguished theologians from every quarter. I do not doubt that you have done a most welcome service to those who desire to know this matter more thoroughly. I am certainly bound to you on this account, and since we ought not to be ashamed to confess by whom we have profited, I acknowledge that in this your most learned treatise I have been freed from my wavering on the points where I was uncertain before, and have been taught what I did not know. May God grant you strength henceforth to deserve well of the Church of God.

units.la: Cl.T.
units.tr: Most distinguished T.

units.la: devinctiss.
units.tr: most devoted.

units.la: J. MACCOVIUS.
units.tr: J. MACCOVIUS.

units.la: DE EPISCOPATU Constantini Magni, SEU De Potestate Magistratus in rebus Ecclesiasticis, DISPUTATIO.
units.tr: ON THE EPISCOPACY OF CONSTANTINE THE GREAT, OR ON THE POWER OF THE MAGISTRATE IN ECCLESIASTICAL MATTERS: A DISPUTATION.

units.la: Egimus Disputatione præcedente de Naturâ Ecclesiæ & Concilиis, & anatomen proposuimus librorum quatuor Bellarmini. Sequitur ut agamus de membris Ecclesiæ militantis, inter quæ præcipuum membrum est Magistratus, quamvis eum Bellarminus adeò deprimat, ut in Ecclesiâ infimum locum ei post quosvis Clericos adscribat contra verbum Dei, cujus nos ordinem sequemur, ut etiam quæstione præcedente à nobis factum est.
units.tr: In the preceding disputation we treated of the nature of the Church and of councils, and we set out an analysis of the four books of Bellarmine. It follows that we should now treat of the members of the militant Church. Among these the chief member is the magistrate, although Bellarmine so belittles him that he assigns him the lowest place in the Church, after any clergy whatever, contrary to the Word of God. We shall follow the order of God's Word, as we also did in the previous question.

units.la: De Magistratu autem agit libro toto de Laicis: hoc enim nomine contumeliosè & contra usum Scripturæ Sacræ (quæ expresse Magistratum à Laicis distinguit, qui בְּנֵי הָעָם[?] 2. Chron. 35. 5.7. vocantur) unctos Domini designat. Ita autem agit contra nos (nam quæ adversum Anabaptistas aut alios disputat, nos non tangunt) de Magistratu, ut non tractet aliâ de re, quàm de potestate seu jure & officio ejus in rebus Ecclesiasticis; quemadmodum etiam in aliis libris quibusdam eam materiam inspergit. Nos inpræsentiarum sequuti filum & ordinem instituti nostri contra eum agemus, ita ut, quandoquidem hæc materia vulgò minus nota est, distinctè proponamus & ipsius doctrinam, & doctrinam Ecclesiarum Reformatarum, hancque quantum postulat necessitas & chartæ hujus angustia patitur, probemus ex verbo Dei, & contrariam doctrinam refutemus, aut indicemus, apud quos auctores probationes & objectionum solutiones sint quærendæ. Est autem controversia illa non nova, sed in vetere etiam Ecclesia motafuit. Temporibus enim S. Augustini Donatistæ contendebant, ad Magistratum non pertinere cognitionem causarum Ecclesiasticarum: Quid est Imperatori cum Ecclesiâ? dicebat Donatus apud Optatum Milevitanum lib. 3. cont. Parmen. Horum furori se opposuerunt Augustinus & Optatus. Anabaptistæ & Sociniani Donati vestigia sequuntur hodie, & sic in defectu gravissimè peccant. Arminiani è contrario in excessu peccant. Etenim ante Synodum Dordracenam conten-debant, sub Magistratu orthodoxo Ecclesiam per se nullam habere potestatem spiritualem: ministros Ecclesiæ officio suo defungi nomine Magistratus, ita ut Magistratus, quia ipse per alia negocia concionari &c. non possit, per ministros doceat, qui vices ipsius gerant in docendo &c. quemadmodum vicarius Trajani Imperatoris vices gerebat sui Imperatoris. Et sic ministros non habere suam potestatem à Christo, sed à Magistratu, qui & quidem solus eam potestatem immediatè à Christo acceperit. Adeoque Magistratum in locum Papę constituebant, imò plus ei tribuebant, quam Romanenses Pontifici. Gubernationem etiam Ecclesiæ assignabant sòli Magistratui; ab eâ excludentes Ministros, nisi in quantum essent vicarii & instrumenta seu servi Magistratus. Speciatim electionem ministrorum seu vocationem, item depositionem tribuebant soli Magistratui, & quidem non solùm summo, sed etiam subalternis Magistratibus, qui oppidatim vices gerunt summi Magistratus; statuebantque penes eos esse distribuere officia Ecclesiastica, non secus atque in ipsorum potestate est distribuere officia Politica. Contendebant etiā ad solum Magistratum immediatè sub Christo pertinere judicium, quando controversiæ fidei ortę sunt in Ecclesiâ. Quæ doctrina à diversis Theologis tunc fuit refutata, speciatim à Cl. Walæo tract. de off. ministror. & auctoritate atq; inspectione quā magistratus super ministros habere debet: contra Joh. Vtenbogard. Post Synodum in Confess. sua [?] & Apol. c. 25. §. 4. tribuunt quidē etiam Magistratui potestatem architectonicam in Ecclesia immediatè sub Christo; sed negāt ejus jus aut officiū esse, ad decreta Synodica, ut ut verbo Dei conformia sint, observanda obligare homines suâ auctoritate, & potestate ullâ coactivâ uti in eâ parte. Negant etiam Magistratum jus habere in privatos cōventus, sed tantùm in exercitia quæ in Tēplis seu locis publicis ad Magistratum pertinentibus instituuntur, ibid. Apol. sol. 297. &c. Quibus duabus posterioribus negationibus revera tantum detrahunt Magi-stratus potestati, quantum ei in cæte-ris volunt videri tribuere; ut jamnon dicam eos sibi non constare quantum ad hæc duo attinet. Nam cùm rebus suis ita consultum putarent, aliter statuebant & contrarium, quemadmodum alibi à nobis est ostensum. Pontificii, speciatim Bellarminus, volunt videri plus tribuere Magistratui, quàm Anabaptistæ circa res Ecclesiasticas, sed revera etiam in defectu peccant, & in substantia conveniunt cum eis, nisi quod ex Magistratu lictores & mancipia, imò carnifices Ecclesiasticorum faciunt, prout ex sequentibus quæstionibus palam fiet. Observetur autem in antecessum, quæcumque à nobis & aliis Theologis Reformatis hîc dicuntur, accipienda esse de Magistratu summo & Orthodoxo, qui adeoq; ipse membrum Ecclesiæ sit; quo deficiente Ecclesia sola sub Christo secundum verbum ejus prospicere debet conservationi veræ religionis & ordinis exterioris à Christo insti-tuti.
units.tr: Bellarmine treats of the magistrate in his book on laymen. By this term he contemptuously, and contrary to the usage of Holy Scripture (which expressly distinguishes the magistrate from the laity, who are called the sons of the people [בְּנֵי הָעָם] in 2 Chron. 35. 5, 7), designates the anointed of the Lord. He argues against us in this way (for what he disputes against the Anabaptists or others does not touch us) concerning the magistrate, and he treats of no other matter than the power, or the right and office, of the magistrate in ecclesiastical affairs, just as he also sprinkles this material through certain other books. For our part, following the thread and order of our own undertaking, we shall argue against him. Since this subject is commonly less well known, we shall set out distinctly both his doctrine and the doctrine of the Reformed Churches, and, as far as necessity demands and the limits of this paper allow, we shall prove it from the Word of God. We shall refute the contrary doctrine, or at least indicate among which authors the proofs and the answers to objections are to be sought. This controversy is not new, however; it was stirred already in the ancient Church. In the time of St. Augustine the Donatists contended that the hearing of ecclesiastical causes did not belong to the magistrate: "What has the Emperor to do with the Church?" said Donatus, according to Optatus of Milevis, book 3 against Parmenian. Augustine and Optatus opposed themselves to this fury. The Anabaptists and Socinians follow the footsteps of Donatus today, and so in deficiency they sin most grievously. The Arminians, on the contrary, sin by excess. For before the Synod of Dort they contended that, under an orthodox magistrate, the Church has by itself no spiritual power; that the ministers discharge their office in the name of the magistrate, so that the magistrate, since he cannot himself preach through other business, teaches through ministers who act in his place in teaching, just as the deputy of the Emperor Trajan acted in place of his Emperor. Thus the ministers do not have their power from Christ but from the magistrate, who alone, they said, received that power immediately from Christ. Accordingly they put the magistrate in the place of the Pope, and attributed even more to him than the Romanists attribute to the Pontiff. They also assigned the government of the Church to the magistrate alone, excluding the ministers from it except insofar as they were vicars, instruments, or servants of the magistrate. Specifically, they gave the election or calling of ministers, and likewise their deposition, to the magistrate alone, and not only to the supreme magistrate but also to subordinate magistrates, who act in the towns as deputies of the supreme magistrate. They held that it lay with these to distribute ecclesiastical offices, just as it lies in the power of the civil authorities to distribute civil offices. They further contended that judgment, when controversies of faith arose in the Church, belonged immediately under Christ to the magistrate alone. This doctrine was then refuted by various theologians, especially by the distinguished Walaeus in his treatise on the office of ministers and on the authority and oversight which the magistrate ought to have over the ministers, against Johannes Uytenbogaert. After the Synod, in their Confession and Apology, ch. 25, §4, they indeed grant to the magistrate an architectonic power in the Church immediately under Christ; but they deny that it is his right or office to bind people by his own authority to observe synodal decrees, however much they may agree with the Word of God, and to use any coercive power in that respect. They also deny that the magistrate has any right over private assemblies, but only over exercises which are carried on in temples or public places belonging to the magistrate (ibid., Apology, p. 297, etc.). By these two latter denials they really take away from the magistrate's power just as much as they seem willing to grant him in other matters, not to mention that they do not agree with themselves as far as these two points are concerned. For when they thought their own interests were served in this way, they held otherwise and the contrary, as we have shown elsewhere. The Papists, especially Bellarmine, wish to seem to grant more to the magistrate in ecclesiastical affairs than the Anabaptists do, but in truth they too sin by deficiency and agree with them in substance, except that they make the magistrates into lictors, slaves, and even executioners of the clergy, as will become plain from the following questions. It should be noted beforehand, however, that whatever is said here by us and by other Reformed theologians is to be understood of the supreme and orthodox magistrate, who is himself a member of the Church. Where such a magistrate is wanting, the Church alone, under Christ and according to his Word, must provide for the preservation of true religion and of the external order instituted by Christ.

units.la: QUÆST. PRIMA. An Magistratus nullam pote- statem habeat in rebus Ecclesiasticis, quam ut sit defensor Ecclesiæ & executor sententiæ illius?
units.tr: QUESTION 1. Does the magistrate have no power in ecclesiastical matters beyond being the defender of the Church and the executor of its sentence?

units.la: Ita Bellarm. cum cæteris Pontifi-ciis maximè Iesuitis sentit lib. de Laicis capp. 17. 18. & aliis in libris, prout etiam distinctius ex omnibus locis, quę allegabimus, patebit. Contra istam opinionem nos hanc propositionem formamus: Quemadmodum certissimum est & extra omnem controversiam positum, Magistratum esse defensorem Ecclesiæ, & propugnatorem ordinis divinitus instituti, adeoq; potestatis quam Deus dedit Ecclesiæ suæ; ita falsissimum est eum tantum defensorem esse Ecclesiæ & exequutorem sententiæ illius. Hæc propositio est doctrina totius Ecclesiæ Reformatæ, adeò ut Zanchius in Locis Communibus cap 26. §. 9. haud obscurè eos illudere Magistratui indicet, qui secus statuunt: Improbamus, inquit, & illos qui auctoritatem in Religione DICIS TANTUM CAUSSA attribuunt Magistratibus &c. dum illos aliud esse nolunt, quam eorum, quae ab Episcopis definiuntur executores. Vide de hac propositione Confessionem Ecclesiarum Gallicarum art. 39. 40. Anglicam art. 37. Belgicam art. 36, Bohemicam art. 16. Calvinum Instit. lib. IV. cap. 11. §. 16. Bullingerum de Episcoporum institutione & functione cap. 1. Petrum Martyrem in 1. Sam. cap. 8. de quo commentario Iosias Simlerus Theologus Tigurinus in praefatione ait: nihil eum continere quod non Orthodoxum sit. Eundem in locis communibus lib. 4. c. 13. & in Appendice locorum communium Quaestione, Regi, Principi, Magistratui, liceatne de Religione statuere? Bucerum lib. 1. de Regno Christi. Ivellum Episcopum Sarisburiensem in Apolog. Ecclesię Anglicanae capp. 9. 10. 11. 12. 13.14.
units.tr: Thus Bellarmine, together with the other Papists, especially the Jesuits, holds in his book On Laymen, chapters 17 and 18, and in other books, as will also become clearer from all the passages we shall cite. Against that opinion we set forth this proposition: "Just as it is most certain and beyond all controversy that the magistrate is the defender of the Church and the champion of the order instituted by God, and therefore of the power that God gave to his Church, so it is most false that he is only the defender of the Church and the executor of its sentence." This proposition is the doctrine of the whole Reformed Church, so much so that Zanchius, in his Common Places, chapter 26, section 9, plainly indicates that those who think otherwise mock the magistrate: "We disapprove," he says, "of those too who attribute authority in religion to magistrates merely for show, while they will not have them to be anything other than executors of what the bishops define." On this proposition see the Confession of the French Churches, articles 39 and 40; the English, article 37; the Belgic, article 36; the Bohemian, article 16; Calvin, Institutes, book 4, chapter 11, section 16; Bullinger, On the Institution and Function of Bishops, chapter 1; Peter Martyr on 1 Samuel, chapter 8, on whose commentary Josias Simler, the Zurich theologian, says in the preface that it contains nothing that is not orthodox. The same Peter Martyr in his Common Places, book 4, chapter 13, and in the appendix to the Common Places, on the question "Whether a king, prince or magistrate may decide about religion?"; Bucer, book 1, On the Kingdom of Christ; Jewel, bishop of Salisbury, in his Apology of the Church of England, chapters 9 to 14.

units.la: Vir Clariss. Disputationem tuam de Magistratu Politico adversus Bell. eò diligentius legi, quò videre potui, eam accuratius esse conscriptam, & deprehendi non tantum argumentorum gravissimorum veritate, sed & Clariss. Theologorum authoritate undecumque suffultam ac munitam. Non dubito, quin rem gratiss. feceris iis, qui materiam hanc accuratius pernoscere cupiunt. Me certè tibi devinctum hoc nomine habes, & quia nos pudere non debet profiteri, per quem profecerimus, fateor me tractatu hoc tuo doctiss. in iis, in quibus fluctuabam ante, expeditum & quae nesciebam, edoctum.Deus tibi sufficiat porrò vires ad bene merendum de Ecclesia Dei.
units.tr: To the most distinguished man: I have read your Disputation on the Political Magistrate against Bellarmine all the more carefully because I could see that it was written with greater precision, and I have found it supported and fortified not only by the truth of the most weighty arguments but also by the authority of the most distinguished theologians from every quarter. I have no doubt that you have done a most welcome service to those who wish to know this subject more thoroughly. Indeed you have bound me to yourself on this account, and since I need not be ashamed to acknowledge through whom I have made progress, I confess that by your most learned treatise I have been set free on those points about which I was wavering before, and taught what I did not know. May God grant you further strength to deserve well of the Church of God.

units.tr: To the most distinguished T.

units.la: DE EPISCOPATU Constantini Magni, SEU De Potestate Magistratus in rebus Ecclesiasticis, DISPUTATIO.
units.tr: ON THE EPISCOPATE of Constantine the Great, OR On the Power of the Magistrate in Ecclesiastical Affairs, A DISPUTATION.

units.la: EGimus Disputatione præcedente de Naturâ Ecclesiæ & Conciliis, & anatomen proposuimus librorū quatuor Bellarmini. Sequitur ut agamus de membris Ecclesiæ militantis, inter quæ præcipuum membrum est Magistratus, quamvis eum Bellarminus adeò deprimat, ut in Ecclesiâ infimum locum ei post quosvis Clericos adscribat contra verbum Dei, cujus nos ordinem sequemur, ut etiam quæstione præcedente à nobis factum est.
units.tr: In the preceding disputation we dealt with the nature of the Church and with councils, and we set out an analysis of the four books of Bellarmine. It follows that we treat of the members of the militant Church. The chief of these members is the magistrate, although Bellarmine so depresses him that he assigns him the lowest place in the Church, after any clergy whatever, contrary to the Word of God. We shall follow the order of that Word, as we also did in the previous question.

units.tr: Bellarmine treats of the magistrate throughout his book on laymen. By this term he contemptuously designates, against the usage of Holy Scripture, the anointed of the Lord. Scripture expressly distinguishes the magistrate from laymen, who are called [בְּנֵי] (2 Chron. 35. 5, 7). He argues against us in such a way (for what he disputes against the Anabaptists or others does not touch us) that he treats of the magistrate on no other subject than the power, or the right and office, of the magistrate in ecclesiastical affairs, as he also scatters this material through certain other books. For the present we shall follow the thread and order of our undertaking and argue against him. Since this subject is commonly less well known, we shall set out clearly both his doctrine and the doctrine of the Reformed Churches. As far as necessity demands and the limits of this paper allow, we shall prove the latter from the Word of God, and we shall refute the opposing doctrine or indicate where proofs and answers to the objections are to be sought. This controversy is not new; it was already stirred in the ancient Church. In the time of St. Augustine the Donatists contended that the magistrate had no part in judging ecclesiastical causes: "What has the Emperor to do with the Church?" said Donatus, as reported by Optatus of Milevis, book 3 against Parmenian. Augustine and Optatus opposed themselves to this fury. The Anabaptists and Socinians follow the footsteps of Donatus today, and in this defect they sin most gravely. The Arminians, on the contrary, sin by excess. For before the Synod of Dort they maintained that, under an orthodox magistrate, the Church has no spiritual power of its own. They held that the ministers discharge their office in the name of the magistrate, so that, since the magistrate cannot himself preach through other business, he teaches through ministers who act in his place in teaching, just as a vicar of the Emperor Trajan acted in the place of his emperor. Thus they held that the ministers do not have their power from Christ but from the magistrate, who alone, they said, received that power immediately from Christ. Accordingly they set the magistrate in the place of the Pope, and even attributed more to him than the Romanists attribute to the Pontiff. They also assigned the government of the Church to the magistrate alone, excluding the ministers from it except insofar as they were vicars, instruments, or servants of the magistrate. Specifically, they gave the election or calling of ministers, and likewise their deposition, to the magistrate alone, and not only to the supreme magistrate but also to the subordinate magistrates who act as deputies of the supreme magistrate in each town. They held that it lay with these to distribute ecclesiastical offices, just as it lies in the power of the magistrates to distribute civil offices. They also contended that judgment belongs immediately under Christ to the magistrate alone whenever controversies of faith arise in the Church. This doctrine was then refuted by various theologians, especially by the distinguished Walaeus in his treatise On the Office of Ministers, and on the Authority and Oversight which the Magistrate ought to have over the Ministers, against Johannes Uytenbogaert. After the Synod, in his Confession and Apology, chapter 25, section 4, they indeed grant to the magistrate an architectonic power in the Church, immediately under Christ. But they deny that it is his right or office to bind men by his own authority to observe synodal decrees, however conformable to the Word of God they may be, or to use any coercive power in that respect. They also deny that the magistrate has a right over private assemblies, and assert it only over the exercises instituted in temples or in public places belonging to the magistrate (ibid., Apology, pp. 297 and following). By these last two denials they really take from the magistrate's power just as much as they wish to seem to grant him in other matters, not to mention that they are inconsistent with themselves as far as these two points are concerned. For when they thought their own interests were served in this way, they set down otherwise and the contrary, as we have shown elsewhere. The Papists, especially Bellarmine, wish to seem to attribute more to the magistrate in ecclesiastical affairs than the Anabaptists do, but in truth they too sin by defect, and they agree with them in substance, except that they make the magistrates into lictors, slaves, and even executioners of the clergy, as will become plain from the following questions. It should be noted in advance that whatever is said here by us and other Reformed theologians must be understood of a supreme and orthodox magistrate, who is himself a member of the Church. Where such a magistrate is lacking, the Church alone, under Christ and according to his Word, must provide for the preservation of true religion and of the external order instituted by Christ.

Contra istam opinionem nos hanc propositionem formamus: Quemadmo-dum certissimum est & extra omnem controversiam positum, Magistratum esse defensorem Ecclesiæ, & propugnatorem ordinis divinitus instituti, adeoq; potestatis quam Deus dedit Ecclesiæ suæ; ita falsissimum est eum tantùm defensorem esse Ecclesiæ & exequutorem sententiæ illius. Hæc propositio est doctrina totius Ecclesiæ Reformatæ, adeò ut Zanchius in Locis Communibus cap 26. §. 9. haud obscurè eos illudere Magistratui indicet, qui secus statuunt: Improbamus, inquit, & illos qui auctoritatem in Religione DICIS TANTUM CAUSSA attribuunt Magistratibus &c. dum illos aliud esse nolunt, quàm eorum, quæ ab Episcopis definiuntur exequutores. Vide de hac propositione Confessionem Ecclesiarum Gallicarum art. 39. 40. Anglicam art. 37. Belgicam art. 36, Bohemicam art. 16. Calvinum Instit. lib. IV. cap. 11. §. 16. Bullingerum de Episcoporum institutione & functione cap. 1. Petrum Martyrem in 1. Sam. cap. 8. de quo commentario Iofias Simlerus Theologus Tigurinus in præfatione ait: nihil eum continere quod non Orthodoxum sit. Eundem in locis communibus lib. 4. c. 13. & in Appendice locorum communium Quæstione, Regi, Principi, Magistratui, liceatne de Religione statuere? Bucerum lib. 1. de Regno Christi. Iuellum Episcopum Sarisburiensem in Apolog. Ecclesiæ Anglicanæ capp. 9. 10. 11. 12. 13.14.
units.tr: So Bellarmine thinks, together with the other Papists, especially the Jesuits, in his book On Laymen, chapters 17 and 18, and in other books, as will also become clearer from all the passages we shall cite. Against that opinion we set forth this proposition: Just as it is most certain and beyond all controversy that the magistrate is the defender of the Church and the champion of the order instituted by God, and therefore of the power God gave to his Church, so it is most false that he is only the defender of the Church and the executor of its sentence. This proposition is the doctrine of the whole Reformed Church, so much so that Zanchius in his Common Places, chapter 26, section 9, plainly indicates that those who hold otherwise mock the magistrate. We disapprove, he says, of those who attribute authority in religion to magistrates merely for the sake of order, etc., since they wish them to be nothing other than the executors of what is defined by the bishops. On this proposition see the Confession of the French Churches, articles 39 and 40; the English article 37; the Belgic article 36; the Bohemian article 16; Calvin, Institutes, book 4, chapter 11, section 16; Bullinger, on the institution and function of bishops, chapter 1; Peter Martyr on 1 Samuel, chapter 8, of whose commentary Josias Simler, the Zurich theologian, says in the preface that it contains nothing that is not orthodox. The same author in his Common Places, book 4, chapter 13, and in the appendix to the Common Places, the question whether a king, prince or magistrate may legislate about religion; Bucer, book 1, On the Kingdom of Christ; Jewel, bishop of Salisbury, in the Apology of the Church of England, chapters 9 to 14.

units.la: 15. Item ejusdem Antapologiam contra Hardingum capp. 9. 10. &c. Zanchium in locis communibus tit. de Magistratu. Vrsinum in catech. ad praeceptum quintum. Wittakerum lib. de Conciliis & Ecclesia. Franciscum Junium libris iisdem. Polanum Syntag. lib. 1. c. 45. & lib. 7. c. 19. Chamierum de Oecumenico Pontifice hinc inde. Tareum Comment. in epist. ad Romanos cap. 13. Item in Aphorismis doctrinae Ecclesiarum Reformatarum art. 11. §. 17. 18. Bucanum loco de Magistratu. Piscatorem in Aphorismis & earum Explicatione de Magistratu. Sibbrandum Lubbertum contra Grotii pietatem Ordinum Hollandiæ hinc inde. Bogermannum contra eundem Grotium in Appendice ex Junio. Cl. Molinaeum de novitate Papismi libris 4. 5. 6. Jacobi Capelli Historiam sedis Romanæ contra Ferrerium speciatim. Syno-psin purioris Theologiae Cl. Professorum Leydensium loco de Magistratu, item loco de Disciplinâ Ecclesiasticâ, item de Vocatione Pastorum, item de conciliis. Eorundem Censuram Confessionis Remonstrantium cap. 25. Cl. Rivetum in Commentario in Decalogum ad præceptum quintum. Cl. Walæum de Officio ministrorum &c. per totum. Amesii Medullam Theologicam loco de Magistratu. Altstedii Supplementum in Panstrat. Chamierii lib. de jurisdict. Ecclesiæ Milit. capp. 3. 4. &c. item alios recentiores Anglos Theologos, ut L. Cicestrensis tortuīram Torti[?]. Bilsonium de perpetuâ gubernatione Ecclesiæ, & alios. Ut jam Musculum non allegem, qui in hac materiâ circa quædam recedere à communi consensu Doctorum Reformatorum odio disciplinæ Anabaptisticæ videtur, & pastoribus minus tribuere nonnullibi quàm par est; Theologus alioquin insignis & de Ecclesia bene meritus. In summa hæc est doctrina omnium Theologorum Reformatorum, qui ante & post Synodum Dordracenam de hac materia scripserunt.
units.tr: 15. Also the same author's Antapologia against Harding, chapters 9, 10, etc.; Zanchius in his Common Places, the title on the magistrate; Ursinus in the catechism on the fifth commandment; Whitaker, book on councils and the Church; Franciscus Junius, the same books; Polanus, Syntagma, book 1, chapter 45, and book 7, chapter 19; Chamier, on the Ecumenical Pope, passim; Tarnovius, commentary on the Epistle to the Romans, chapter 13, and also in the Aphorisms of the Doctrine of the Reformed Churches, article 11, sections 17 and 18; Bucanus, the place on the magistrate; Piscator in the Aphorisms and their explanation, on the magistrate; Sibrandus Lubbertus against Grotius's Piety of the Orders of Holland, passim; Bogerman against the same Grotius in the appendix from Junius; Cl. Molinaeus, on the novelty of Papism, books 4, 5 and 6; James Capellus, History of the Roman See, especially against Ferrerius; the Synopsis of Purer Theology of the illustrious professors of Leiden, the place on the magistrate, likewise the place on church discipline, likewise on the calling of pastors, likewise on councils; the same men's Censure of the Confession of the Remonstrants, chapter 25; Cl. Rivetus, commentary on the Decalogue, on the fifth commandment; Cl. Walaeus, on the office of ministers, etc., throughout; Ames's Marrow of Theology, the place on the magistrate; Alsted's Supplement to the Panstratia of Chamier, the book on the jurisdiction of the militant Church, chapters 3, 4, etc.; likewise other more recent English theologians, such as the bishop of Chichester, Bilson on the perpetual government of the Church, and others. I do not now cite Musculus, who in this matter seems, out of hatred of Anabaptist discipline, to depart somewhat from the common consent of the Reformed doctors, and in some places to grant ministers less than is right; otherwise he is a distinguished theologian and deserving of the Church. In sum, this is the doctrine of all the Reformed theologians who wrote on this matter before and after the Synod of Dort.

units.la: Probatur autem hæc propositio.
units.tr: This proposition is proved as follows.

units.la: 1. Quia qui Magistratibus aliud non tribuunt, quàm ut sine ullâ potestate aliâ in rebus Ecclesiasticis tantùm sint defensores & exequutores Ecclesię; faciunt ex iis mancipia imò lictores & carnifices Episcoporum seu ministrorum Ecclesię. Hoc argumentum est Parei Comm. Rom. 13. p. 1084. Cl. Riveti comment. in Decal. p. 164. a. & aliorum.
units.tr: 1. Because those who grant magistrates nothing more than that, without any other power in ecclesiastical affairs, they are merely defenders and executors of the Church, make them the slaves, indeed the lictors and executioners, of the bishops or ministers of the Church. This argument is Pareus's, Commentary on Romans 13, p. 1084, and of Cl. Rivetus, commentary on the Decalogue, p. 164a, and of others.

units.la: 2. Probatur ex eo, quia Magistratus ossicium extendit se præter defensionem Religionis & Ecclesiæ etiam ad alia, ut ex sequentibus omnibus patebit. Quæ Bellarminus pro suâ sententiâ affert, refutata sunt à multis ex modo laudatis Theologis.
