units.tr: 2. It is proved from the fact that the office of the magistrate extends, beyond the defence of religion and the Church, also to other matters, as will be clear from all that follows. What Bellarmine brings forward for his opinion has been refuted by many of the theologians just cited.

units.la: Annotationes seu Interrogata
units.tr: Annotations, or Questions

units.la: Ad Quæst. Primam.
units.tr: On the First Question.

units.la: Cum negatur Magistratum tantùm esse defensorem Ecclesiæ & executorem sententiæ illius: An non indicandum erat quid ergo sit Magistratus respectu Ecclesiæ? Negativa enim ejusmodi propositio nimium est generalis, cùm negatâ unâ specie, aliæ plures restent, vel affirmanda, vel neganda. Estne ergo Magistratus Dominus aut caput Ecclesiæ: an vero habet munus aliquod in Ecclesiâ? Certè Magistratus non est quidem stupidus aut cæcus Ecclesiæ defensor, aut debet sententiam Ecclesiæ defendere, quæcunque demum illa sit: attamen si Magi-stratus aliud quid est, præterquam Ecclesiæ defensor, quæso quid demum est? Quamvis ii, qui volunt, ut Magistratus stupidè & cæcè Ecclesiam tueantur, ejusque exequantur sententiam (quod volunt Papæ Romani sectatores) illos faciunt Mancipia Episcoporum, id tamen tribuendum non est illis, qui volunt veram re-ligionem veramque Ecclesiam à Magistratu è verbo Dei cognosci, & cognitam defendi, eoque sensu Magistratum Ecclesiæ defensorem faciunt.
units.tr: When it is denied that the magistrate is only the defender of the Church and the executor of its sentence, should it not be stated what the magistrate is, then, with respect to the Church? For a negative proposition of this kind is too general, since with one kind denied, several others remain, which must either be affirmed or denied. Is the magistrate then the lord or head of the Church, or does he have some office in the Church? Certainly the magistrate is not a dumb or blind defender of the Church, nor must he defend the Church's opinion, whatever it may be; yet if the magistrate is something other than a defender of the Church, I ask, what then is he? Although those who want the magistrate to protect the Church stupidly and blindly, and carry out its sentence (which is what the followers of the Roman Pope want), make him the slave of the bishops, that charge must not be laid on those who want the true religion and true Church to be recognised by the magistrate from the Word of God, and, once recognised, defended; and in that sense they make the magistrate the defender of the Church.

units.la: Dices: Ergo Magistratus judicat de Ecclesiâ & de rebus Ecclesiasticis. Certè (inquam) judicat etiam de religione. Sed & Pastor judicat, & fidelis quilibet. Pastor, ut veram religionem doceat, & res Ecclesiasticas rite administret: fidelis quilibet, ut Deum recte colat: Magistratus, ut veram religionem & Ecclesiam tueatur atqz defendat, non falsam.
units.tr: You will say: therefore the magistrate judges concerning the Church and ecclesiastical affairs. Certainly (I reply) he also judges concerning religion. But so too does the minister, and every believer. The minister judges so that he may teach the true religion and administer ecclesiastical affairs rightly; every believer so that he may worship God correctly; the magistrate so that he may protect and defend the true religion and Church, not a false one.

units.la: Resp.
units.tr: Answer.

units.la: Proponuntur in Annotationibus mul-tæ Quæstiones solvendæ. Sed impossibile, fuit illa quæ in iis continentur, in exercitio merè Scholastico tractare: Certè id justi voluminis est, & quod in usum publicum totius Ecclesiæ quis edere vellet, non autem disputationis Scholasticæ. Profecto Cll. DD. Proff. Leydd. etiam tractârunt hanc materiam, & quidem non in unâ, sed in variis disputationibus, quas in publicum totius Ecclesiæ usum tanquam Synopsin purioris doctrinæ ediderunt, eandemque doctrinam tradunt quam ego, & tamen illas quæstiones non attingunt. Nulla etiam est ex illis Confessionibus fidei, nullus ex authoribus, quos ego allegavi, qui ad ista quæsita omnia aut majore ex parte respondeat vel explicationes contineat, quæ in eo privato exercitio Scholastico postulantur; quamvis ex professo & justis voluminibus quidam eam materiam tractârint, inter quos facile primas fert Cl. V.Valæus in tractatu suo insigni. An ideò Ecclesiis, quarum illæ Confessiones sunt & Theologis illis omnibus lis erat aut etiamnum est movenda? Certè si alicui lis est movenda propter omissa in disputatione aliquâ aut exercitio Academico, unâ litura obducî possent scripta Theologica ferè omnia, maximè autem Disputationes. Adde, quòd ea, quæ à me ibi proposita sunt, sufficiunt adversus Bellarminum, cui & sociis ipsius tantùm opposui Disputationem illam, ita postulante ordine ac serie disputationum & Lectionum mearum. Dices, ideò proponi dubia illa, quò explicentur in usum Ecclesiæ ob temporum pericula, ea quæ ambiguè à me dicta sint. Sed profectò si in usum totius Ecclesiæ voluissem disputationem edere; nemo qui me novit dubitare debet, quin uberius & explicatius omnia tractaturus fuissem. Et verò Confessiones ut & scripta illa, quorum memini, edita sunt temporibus æquè periculosis, imò quædam etiam longè periculosioribus, quàm moderna sunt. Nec denique affectæ ambiguitatis quicquam in eâ Disputatione est, nec quicquam ibi deprehendi potest, quod alicui obscurum aut ambiguum videri queat, quod non ibidem pro instituti ratione ac brevitate vel meis vel aliorum verbis explicatum sit & clarius dictum. Hæc in genere.
units.tr: Many questions to be solved are proposed in the Annotations. But it was impossible to treat in an exercise that is purely scholastic all that is contained in them. Indeed that would be the work of a large volume, and something one would wish to publish for the public use of the whole Church, not a scholastic disputation. Certainly the illustrious doctors and professors of Leiden also treated this matter, and not in one but in several disputations, which they published for the public use of the whole Church as a Synopsis of Purer Doctrine, and they teach the same doctrine as I do, yet they do not touch on those questions. Nor is there any one of those Confessions of faith, nor any one of the authors I cited, who answers all those questions, or the greater part of them, or contains the explanations that are demanded in that private scholastic exercise; although some have treated that matter ex professo and in large volumes, among whom Cl. V. Valaeus in his notable treatise easily bears the palm. Ought the Churches, whose those Confessions are, and all those theologians, therefore to be troubled, or is any dispute to be raised against them even now? Certainly if any dispute is to be raised because of things omitted in some disputation or academic exercise, almost all theological writings, and especially disputations, could be wiped out with one stroke of the pen. Add that what I have set out there is sufficient against Bellarmine, and against his followers I only opposed that disputation, since the order and sequence of my disputations and lectures demanded it. You will say that those doubts were proposed so that what I have said ambiguously might be explained for the use of the Church, given the dangers of the times. But certainly, if I had wished to publish the disputation for the use of the whole Church, no one who knows me ought to doubt that I would have treated everything more fully and more explicitly. Indeed the Confessions, and those writings I have mentioned, were published in times no less dangerous, and some even far more dangerous than the present ones. Nor finally is there anything of deliberate ambiguity in that disputation, nor can anything be detected in it that could seem obscure or ambiguous to anyone, which was not there explained and stated more clearly, in my words or those of others, according to the plan and brevity of the work. So much in general.

units.la: Nunc in specie ad singulas Considerationes respondebo, & quidem breviter. Nam omnia adferre, quæ ad eas aut similes alias Quæstiones dicere possum, justi voluminis est, ut dictum.
units.tr: Now I will answer each of the Considerations in particular, and briefly. To bring forward everything I could say to these or similar questions would require a volume of considerable size, as I have said.

units.la: Responsio specialis ad Annotationes
units.tr: Special Reply to the Annotations

units.la: Circa Quæst. primam.
units.tr: On the First Question.

units.la: I. Quærere quid præterea sit Magistratus respectu Ecclesiæ, est revera aliud nihil quàm quærere: Quam nam potestatem habeat Magistratus in Ecclesiâ seu circa Ecclesiam & res Ecclesiasticas, præter illam quam Bellarm. ei assignat[?] prout à me Quæstio formata est conceptis verbis. Atqui hoc ipsum tractatur tum in genere Qq. 1. 2. 3. tum in specie Qq. 4. 5. 6. 7. 8. 9. 10. 11. 12. II. Si quis tamen velit (quamvis opus non sit) non in casu obliquo, non paronymicè, sed in casu recto & Synonymicè formari enunciationis prædicatum, dico: Magistratus respectu Ecclesiæ est præcipuum membrum Ecclesiæ, & eo respectu partes etiam suas habet in vocatione Ministrorum, quia vocatio ministrorum ad totam Ecclesiam pertinet. item: Magistratus respectu Ecclesiæ est director Ordinis externi Ecclesiæ, imperio & gladio armatus, & ideo potestatem habet reliquam, quam ipsi in disputatione attribuo, ut custos ac vindex utriusque tabulæ legis. Quod quæritur: An Magistratus sit Dominus aut caput Ecclesiæ? Respondeo breviter, me malle cum Scriptura loqui, quæ illum honorem Soli Christo tribuit; & voces duriores suis auctoribus relinquere, qui sese ipsos explicare debent, prout etiam Orthodoxi, qui illa Epitheta Magistratui tribuunt, sese explicant. Ad quæstionem: An Magistratus habeat munus aliquod in Ecclesia? Respondeo, eum proprie loquendo munus in ecclesia non habere. Proprie enim & formaliter munus in Ecclesia habere est defungi ministerio aliquo Ecclesiastico, quæ quatuor recensentur in Constitut. Dordrac. art. 2. &c. Constat autem Magistratum nullum ex iis ministeriis habere. Sed habet potestatem coactivam externam in Ecclesia, seu potius circa Ecclesiam sive circa res & personas Ecclesiasticas, tanquam custos ac vindex utriusque tabulæ legis, & tanquam nutricius ac defensor Ecclesiæ. Quæ quidem potestas exponitur in Corollario Interrogatorum, distinctione Regni generalis & specialis Dei, &c. Eam Cl. V Valæus[?] hinc inde vocat surintendence fur l' office des ministres inspectionem supra officium ministrorum; alii vocant Politicam gubernationem Ecclesiæ, item Primatum Regium, item Primatum quoad curam Religionis & cultus Dei, ut Polanus System. lib.7. cap. 19.& alibi. Alii Orthodoxi vocant potestatem regiam circa Ecclesiasticam, ut Pareus Comment. Rom. 13. p. 1075. item jurisdictionem Ecclesiasticam ib.p.1078. item potestatem Ecclesiasticam non internam, quæ ab Ecclesiasticis Ecclesiastice in Ecclesiâ exercetur docendo, solvendo, ligando, administrando Sacramenta, &c. sed externam, quæ est νομοθετικὴ [?] & circa Ecclesiasticas res & personas extra templum civiliter exercetur ib. p. 1097. De quâ ultimâ locutione Cl. Rivetus in Decal. p. 261. ita loquitur: Quam igitur jurisdictionis potestatem in Ecclesiasticis & spiritualibus rebus Magistratui adscribamus, videndum est. Eam Spiritualem & Ecclesiasticam si quis dicat, id ita intelligi debet, ut non formaliter, ut ita dicam, Spiritualis & Ecclesiastica dicatur: Est enim pars potestatis politicæ & temporalis; sed objectivè ita appelletur, quia exercetur circa res Ecclesiasticas & Spirituales, tenditque ad eas asserendas & conservandas, &c. Quod denique dicitur de mente Orthoxorum, qui Magistratum Ecclesiæ defensorem vocant, cant, contra me non militat; tùm quia ipse in thesi conceptis verbis dixi, extra dubium esse, quòd Magistratus defensor Ecclesiæ sit, tùm quia nullus Orthodoxus Theologus unquam scripsit hactenus Magistratum nullam aliam potestatem habere in rebus Ecclesiasticis, quàm ut sit defensor Ecclesiæ, quod consequen-ter est τὸ κρινόμενον[?] non inter me & Orthodoxos, contra quos non disputo, sed inter me & Pontificios, contra quos di-sputo.
units.tr: I. To ask what further authority the magistrate has with respect to the Church is really nothing other than asking what power the magistrate has in the Church, or around the Church and ecclesiastical matters, beyond the power which Bellarmine assigns to him. That is how I have framed the question in plain words. This very matter is treated both in general in Questions 1, 2 and 3, and in particular in Questions 4 to 12. II. If anyone nevertheless wishes (though there is no need) to frame the predicate of the proposition not in an oblique case or paronymously, but in the nominative and synonymously, I say: with respect to the Church the magistrate is a principal member of the Church, and in that respect he also has a share in the calling of ministers, because the calling of ministers pertains to the whole Church. Likewise: with respect to the Church the magistrate is the director of the external order of the Church, armed with command and sword, and therefore has the remaining power which I attribute to him in the disputation, as guardian and avenger of both tables of the law. As for the question, Is the magistrate the lord or head of the Church? I answer briefly that I prefer to speak with Scripture, which gives that honour to Christ alone, and to leave harsher expressions to their authors, who must explain themselves. The Orthodox who ascribe those titles to the magistrate also explain themselves. To the question, Does the magistrate have some office in the Church? I answer that, properly speaking, he does not have an office in the Church. For to have an office in the Church, properly and formally, is to perform some ecclesiastical ministry, and four such ministries are listed in the Constitution of Dort, art. 2, etc. It is certain, however, that the magistrate holds none of those ministries. But he has a coercive external power in the Church, or rather over the Church, that is, over ecclesiastical matters and persons, as guardian and avenger of both tables of the law, and as nurse and defender of the Church. This power is set out in the Corollary to the Questions, in the distinction of the general and special kingdom of God, etc. The distinguished Valaeus calls it, in various places, surintendence sur l'office des ministres (oversight of the office of the ministers). Others call it the political government of the Church, likewise royal primacy, likewise primacy in the care of religion and the worship of God, as Polanus does in System, book 7, chapter 19, and elsewhere. Other Orthodox writers call it royal power over ecclesiastical matters, as Pareus does in his Commentary on Romans 13, p. 1075, likewise ecclesiastical jurisdiction, ibid. p. 1078, and likewise ecclesiastical power, not internal, which is exercised ecclesiastically by churchmen within the Church by teaching, absolving, binding, administering the sacraments, etc., but external, which is legislative [νομοθετικὴ] and is exercised civilly over ecclesiastical matters and persons outside the temple, ibid. p. 1097. Concerning this last expression, the distinguished Rivetus, in his Decalogue, p. 261, speaks thus: Let us see, then, what power of jurisdiction in ecclesiastical and spiritual matters we ascribe to the magistrate. If anyone calls it spiritual and ecclesiastical, that must be understood in such a way that it is not called spiritual and ecclesiastical formally, so to speak. For it is a part of political and temporal power; but it is called such objectively, because it is exercised over ecclesiastical and spiritual matters and tends to asserting and preserving them, etc. Finally, what is said about the mind of the Orthodox, who call the magistrate defender of the Church, does not tell against me. This is both because I myself stated in plain words in my thesis that it is beyond doubt that the magistrate is defender of the Church, and because no Orthodox theologian has ever yet written that the magistrate has no power in ecclesiastical matters other than to be defender of the Church. That consequently is [τὸ κρινόμενον] the point at issue, not between me and the Orthodox, against whom I do not dispute, but between me and the Papists, against whom I do dispute.

units.la: QUÆST· II. An ad Magistratum non perti- neat cura verae Religionis nisi ad præscriptum ministrorum Ecclesiæ?
units.tr: QUESTION II. Does the care of true religion not belong to the magistrate, except as prescribed by the ministers of the Church?

units.la: Ita quidem Bellarm. lib. de Laicis cap. 1 8. ubi statuit; Principum esse dare operam, ut ea fides servetur, quam Episcopi Catholici, & præcipuè summus Pontifex docet esse tenendam; quo aliud nihil vult, quam ejus curam debere tantùm sequi judicium latum ab Ecclesiâ; & aliam nullam esse debere, quàm ut tueatur & exequatur, quod à PastoPastoribus est prescriptum, ut Q. præcedente[?] dictum; alioquin eum non debere curam ullam rerum Eccle-siasticarum habere, nec ante, nec post dictamen Pastorum. Hinc clarius se exprimit lib. 1. de Pontif. cap 17. ubi contendit: Magistratui nullo modo convenire regimen Ecclesiæ, quod ipse vocat rebus Ecclesiasticis se immiscere. Et ibid. dicit, Magistratum regere homines, ut homines sunt, non autem ut Christiani, & pro fine habere temporalem quietem & salutem populi, non autem vitam & felicitatem sempiternam, hunc enim esse finem tantum Episcoporum seu ministrorum Ecclesiæ, & lib 5. cap. 6. Politica potestas pro fine habet temporalem pacem; Ecclesiastica salutem æternam. Nos affirmamus, & contra Bellarminum hanc propositionem formamus: Magistratus pro fine præcipuo debet habere salutem & felicitatem populi non temporalem solum, sed etiam æternam; adeoque ad eum pertinet cura vera Religionis, quâ ipse per se tenetur sollicittus esse, de eâ introducendâ ubi nondum exercetur, conservandâ ubi in usu est, vindicandâ ubi corrumpitur, restaurandâ ubi collapsa est, & quidem haec omnia secundum praescriptum verbi Dei. Haec propositio est etiam totius Ecclesiae Reformatae doctrina, quemadmodum recte pronunciat Sibbrandus contra Grotium p. 115. &c. & Cl Walæus lib. allegato p. 58. ait; omnes Reformatos Theologos fateri Magistratui competere inspectionem etiam & potestatem in rebus Religionis. Vide loca & Confess. modo laudatas, speciatim Belgic. art. 36. Helv. c. 30. Scot. art. 24.
units.tr: Bellarmine, in book 1 of On Laymen, chapter 18, does indeed hold this, where he lays down: It is the duty of princes to see that the faith is kept which the Catholic bishops, and above all the supreme Pontiff, teach must be held. By this he means nothing else than that the magistrate's care ought only to follow the judgment delivered by the Church, and that it ought to be nothing else than to protect and carry out what has been prescribed by the ministers, as was said under the preceding question. Otherwise he should have no care at all for ecclesiastical matters, either before or after the ministers have pronounced. He expresses himself more clearly in book 1, On the Pontiff, chapter 17, where he contends: It by no means belongs to the magistrate to govern the Church, which he calls meddling in ecclesiastical matters. And in the same place he says that the magistrate governs men as men, not as Christians, and has as his end the temporal peace and welfare of the people, not eternal life and happiness; for this, he says, is the end only of bishops or ministers of the Church. And in book 5, chapter 6: Political power has temporal peace as its end; ecclesiastical power, eternal salvation. We affirm, and against Bellarmine we frame this proposition: The magistrate ought to have as his chief end the salvation and happiness of the people, not only temporal but also eternal; and therefore the care of true religion belongs to him, and he is himself bound to be solicitous about it: to introduce it where it is not yet practised, to preserve it where it is in use, to vindicate it where it is corrupted, and to restore it where it has fallen, and indeed all these things according to the prescription of the Word of God. This proposition is also the doctrine of the whole Reformed Church, as Sibrandus rightly declares against Grotius, p. 115, etc., and the distinguished Walaeus, in the book cited, p. 58, says: All Reformed theologians confess that the magistrate has the oversight and also the power in matters of religion. See the passages and the Confessions just cited, especially the Belgic Confession art. 36, the Helvetic chapter 30, and the Scottish art. 24.

units.la: Probatur haec propositio 1. ex Deut. 17. 18. 19. 20. 2. Reg. 18. 6. Rom. 13, 4. 1. Tim 2. 2. Deinde ex praxi piorum Regum ac PrincipuV.[?] T. qui summopere laudantur ob curam illam quemadmodum è contrario vituperantur ii principes qui curam illam verè religionis non habuerunt. Ubi observandum omnes pios Principes curam gessisse verae Religionis ex mandato generali Deut. 17. quosdam etiam de officio illo suo edoctos fuisse revelatione speciali, prout tunc Deus ad Ecclesiæ suæ ætatem & captum se accommodabat; utrovis modo edocti fuerint, certum tamen est, eos nihil in ea re præter aut contra officium suum fecisse. Horum exemplum sequuti sunt Imperatores pii, & hodie sequuntur Reges ac Principes & Magistratus Orthodoxi omnes. Tertio patet ex noxio effectu contrarii. Nam quando deest cura Magistratus circa veram Religionem, eam facile corrumpi & idololatriam introduci testatur experientia tum Ecclesiæ Israëlitiæ Judic. 17. 3. 4. 5. 6. cap. 18. 1. tum Ecclesiæ Christianæ sub Papatu. Denique patet ex eo, quod ipsum jus naturæ hoc docuit Ethnicos sapientiores, qui ut rectè ait gravissimus Theologus Pareus, unanimi consensu Regibus suis demandarunt curam Religionis. Aphor. art. 11. §. 18. item in comment. ad Rom. cap. 13. Hęc argumenta & alia modo laudati Theologi afferunt. Excipit quidem Bellarm. & alii Pontificii ad argumentum secundum, Mosem cultum Dei instituisse &c. ut summum Sacerdotem & Prophetam; Reges idem fecisse extraordinariâ auctoritate non tam ut Reges, quàm ut Prophetas lib. 1. de Pontif. cap. 7. Sed futile est & ineptum hoc effugium, ut ostensum est à Wittakero, Martyre, Junio, Pareo, Clarissimo Riveto, & aliis.
units.tr: This proposition is proved, first, from Deuteronomy 17:18–20, 2 Kings 18:6, Romans 13:4 and 1 Timothy 2:2. Second, from the practice of the godly kings and princes, who are greatly praised for that care, just as, on the contrary, those princes who did not have this care for true religion are blamed. Here it must be observed that all the godly princes exercised care for true religion by the general command of Deuteronomy 17, and some were also instructed in that duty of theirs by special revelation, as God then accommodated himself to the age and capacity of his Church. However they were instructed, it is certain that in this matter they did nothing beyond or against their office. Godly emperors followed their example, and today all Orthodox kings, princes and magistrates follow it. Third, it is evident from the harmful effect of the contrary. For when the magistrate's care for true religion is lacking, experience shows that it is easily corrupted and idolatry introduced: both in the Israelite Church, Judges 17:3–6 and chapter 18, and in the Christian Church under the Papacy. Finally, it is evident from the fact that natural law itself taught this to the wiser Gentiles, who, as the most weighty theologian Pareus rightly says, by unanimous consent entrusted the care of religion to their kings. Aphorisms, art. 11, §18, and likewise in his commentary on Romans, chapter 13. These arguments, and others, are offered by the theologians just cited. The Cardinal and other Papists do indeed except to the second argument, saying that Moses instituted the worship of God as chief priest and prophet, and that the kings did the same by an extraordinary authority, not so much as kings but as prophets (On the Pontiff, book 1, chapter 7). But this escape is futile and inept, as has been shown by Whitaker, Martyr, Junius, Pareus, the most distinguished Rivetus, and others.

units.la: Objicit Bellarm. ibidem, Regem non debere fungi officio sacerdotum & affert inter alia exemplum Vziæ Regis volentis thus adolere, qui ideò lepra à Deo percussus fuit; quod exemplum Pontificii decimo quoque verbo ingerunt. Sed ineptè & non ad rem, ut ostensum est ab iisdem Theologis. Inter quos Petrus Martyr de Vzia ait; Ille contra Dei præscriptum sacrificare voluit, at si sacerdotem delinquentem coërcuisset, aut in ordinem rederedegisset, nihil illi mali ea de causâ contigisset. Locis communib. append. alleg. p. 723. Affert etiam Bellar. Conciliorum & Patrum dicta, quæ nisi accipiantur de proprio officio ministrorum, nimirum quòd reges non debeant concionari, Sacramenta administrare, ligare & solvere, item quod non habeant potestatem absolutam circa res Ecclesiæ, quidvis pro lubitu & contra verbum Dei statuendi; denique de Regibus & Magistratibus qui adversarii sunt Ecclesiæ ac Religionis, merito rejiciuntur à Pareo comment. Rom. p. 1077. tanquam erronea & quę ad Papatum viam straverunt, ut in aliis dogmatibus, ita etiam in hac materia.
units.tr: Bellarmine objects in the same place that the king must not exercise the office of priests, and among other things he cites the example of King Uzziah, who wished to burn incense and for that reason was struck with leprosy by God. The Papists thrust this example at us at every turn. But it is clumsy and beside the point, as the same theologians have shown. Among them Peter Martyr says of Uzziah: He wished to sacrifice against God's prescription; but if he had restrained a priest who was at fault, or brought him back into order, no harm would have come to him for that reason. Common Places, appendix, cited passage, p. 723. Bellarmine also cites sayings of Councils and Fathers. Unless these are understood of the proper office of ministers, namely that kings ought not to preach, administer the sacraments, bind and loose, and that they have no absolute power over the affairs of the Church to decree whatever they please and against the Word of God, and finally of kings and magistrates who are enemies of the Church and of religion, they are rightly rejected by Pareus in his commentary on Romans, p. 1077, as erroneous and as having paved the way to the papacy, in this matter as in other dogmas.

units.la: QUÆSTIO III. An potestas Magistratus sese extendat ad omnes partes officij mini- strorum Ecclesiæ?
units.tr: QUESTION III. Does the power of the magistrate extend to all parts of the office of the ministers of the Church?

units.la: BEllarminus negativam tuetur, ut ex præcedentibus patet & porro ex sequentibus manifestum fiet.
units.tr: Bellarmine defends the negative, as is clear from what precedes and will become still more evident from what follows.

units.la: Contrà formamus hanc propositionem: Potestas Magistratus se extendit ad omnes partes officii Episcoporum seu ministrorum Ecclesiæ. Hanc totius Ecclesiæ Reformatæ doctrinam esse patebit ex sequentibus, quam D. Amesius paucis his verbis complexus est: Nulla res, persona aut causa tam est Ecclesiastica, quin aliquâ ratione pertineat ad jurisdictionem Magistratus. Medull. Theol. de Magistratu p. 325. Quâ in re sequutus est Petrum Martyrem, qui Locis commun. Classe IV. cap. 13. §. 9. ait: Rursus Politica potestas ad omnia extenditur, quæ ad potestatem Ecclesiasticam (in quibusdam exemplaribus legitur Politicam, sed errore typographico, ut ex toto orationis filo, unusquisq; videt) pertinent. Sed quonam tandem modo? An requirit civilis potestas bonos animi motus & intimam pœnitentiam. Non potest ipsa hæc effi-cere: optabit tamen ut habeantur, & utetur iis medijs, per quae haberi possint. Curabit enim ut Episcopi, Pastores & Doctores in Ecclesia purè doceant, paternè reprehendant, & ex verbo Dei administrent Sacramenta. Haec quidem per se non facit Magistratus; sed curare debet, ut sint ad manus, qui ea rectè faciant. Proinde utraque potestas latissimè patet, & omnia complectitur, sed non eodem modo. Similiter Sibbrandus contra Grot. p. 120. ait: Regis esse curare ut OMNIA rectè & legitimè fiant, non tantum in politiâ, sed etiam in Ecclesiâ. Ivellus Episcopus Sarisburiensis (quem idem Sibbrandus merito vocat magnum illum Ivellum & non tantum Angliæ, sed etiam totius Christiani orbis decus ibid. p. 183.) in Antapologia, cap. 9. idem affirmat, & simul exponit, ut P. Martyr exposuit, quomodo ista propositio sit intelligenda; Tametsi, inquit, penes & Principem & Episcopum Ecclesiæ procurationem esse concedimus, non eodem tamen genere procurat uterque. Hujus enim procuratio illis
units.tr: On the contrary, we set forth this proposition: the power of the magistrate extends to all parts of the office of the bishops, or ministers, of the Church. That this is the doctrine of the whole Reformed Church will be plain from what follows. Our own Amesius summed it up in these few words: No thing, person or cause is so ecclesiastical that it does not in some way pertain to the jurisdiction of the magistrate. Medulla of Theology, on the magistrate, p. 325. In this matter he followed Peter Martyr, who in the Common Places, Class IV, ch. 13, §9, says: Again, the political power extends to all things which pertain to ecclesiastical power (in some copies it is read as "political", but by a typographical error, as anyone can see from the whole thread of the argument). But in what way, pray? Does civil power require good movements of the mind and inward repentance? It cannot bring these about itself; yet it will wish that they be present, and it will use those means by which they may be obtained. For it will see to it that the bishops, pastors and teachers in the Church teach purely, rebuke fatherly, and administer the sacraments according to the Word of God. The magistrate does not do these things himself; but he must take care that there are at hand those who do them rightly. Therefore both powers extend most widely and embrace all things, but not in the same way. Similarly Sibrandus, against Grotius, p. 120, says: It is the king's business to see that ALL things are done rightly and lawfully, not only in the state but also in the Church. Ivellus, bishop of Salisbury (whom Sibrandus rightly calls that great Ivellus, the glory not only of England but of the whole Christian world, ibid. p. 183), in his Apologia, ch. 9, affirms the same, and at the same time explains, as Peter Martyr did, how this proposition is to be understood: Although, he says, we grant that the care of the Church rests both with the prince and with the bishop, they do not exercise it in the same manner. For the bishop's care is concerned with these things:

units.la: B rebus continetur: Euangelium docendo, Sacramenta administrando, Sacerdotes initiando, excommunicando, absolvendo &c. illius autem non in eo versatur, ut istorum quicquam faciat ipsemet, sed in hoc tantum, ut ab Episcopis & fieri hæc curet, & verò recte ac fideliter fieri. Vide etiam Cl. Rivetum in Explicatione Decal. p.260.261. Et hoc est, quod Constantinus Magnus apud Eusebium lib. 4. c. 24. de Vita ipsius, dicebat memorabili voce Episcopis: Vos estis Episcopi intra Ecclesiam, ego extra Ecclesiam, hoc est, templum, ut rectè Cl. Rivetus exponit. Summa: Magistratus potestas habet se ad quasdam partes officii ministrorum objectivè tantum seu directivè, non autem formaliter, non n. ipse administrat Sacramenta &c. sed tantum curat, ut illa rectè fiant. Ad alias autem habet se & formaliter & objectivè; ut enim Pastores habent jus vocandi alios pastores, monendi suos Symmystas officii, judicandi in Synodis, constitutiones Ecclesiasticas in Synodis sanciendi, præsidendi in conventibus Ecclesiasticis,deponendi ministros; ita Magistratus & unâ cum ministris omne illud jus habet, & præterea, pro imperio & potestate suâ coactivâ externâ, quam habet, dirigit ordinem externum & curat, jubet, ut ministri omnia illa rectè faciant, seu actionibus illis rectè defungantur. Et potest hæc distinctio optimè intelligi per analogiam ac similitudinem officii Doctorum seu Professorum Theologiæ. Horum enim officium est etiam ministerium Ecclesiasticum ordinarium à Christo institutum Rom. 12. 7. Eph. 4. 11. 12. 13. 14. & in eo consistit, ut tùm viva voce in Scholis, tùm scriptis in totâ Ecclesiâ doceant veram cognitionem & cultum Dei; adeoq; extendit sese ut ad omnes alias res divinas in verbo Dei revelatas, ita etiam ad omnes partes officii ministrorum Ecclesiæ: sed cum hoc discrimine, quòd quasdam actiones pastorum formaliter exercent, circa alias autem objectivè tantùm se habent.
units.tr: B preaching the gospel, administering the sacraments, ordaining priests, excommunicating, absolving, and so on; but the prince's care does not consist in doing any of these things himself, but only in seeing to it that the bishops both do them and do them rightly and faithfully. See also the distinguished Rivetus in his Explanation of the Decalogue, pp. 260–261. And this is what Constantine the Great, according to Eusebius, Life of Constantine, book 4, ch. 24, memorably said to the bishops: You are the bishops within the Church, I am the bishop outside the Church, that is, outside the temple, as the distinguished Rivetus rightly explains. In short: the power of the magistrate relates to some parts of the ministers' office only objectively or directively, not formally, for he does not himself administer the sacraments and so on, but only sees to it that they are done rightly. With regard to other parts, however, it relates both formally and objectively. For just as pastors have the right to call other pastors, to admonish their fellow ministers in their office, to judge in synods, to enact ecclesiastical constitutions in synods, to preside at ecclesiastical assemblies, and to depose ministers, so the magistrate, together with the ministers, has all this right, and besides, by his external power of command and coercion, he directs the external order and sees to it, and orders, that the ministers perform all those things rightly, or discharge those duties well. This distinction can be best understood by analogy with the office of the teachers, or professors, of theology. For their office is also an ordinary ecclesiastical ministry instituted by Christ (Rom. 12:7; Eph. 4:11–14), and it consists in teaching the true knowledge and worship of God, both by the living voice in the schools and by writings throughout the whole Church. It therefore extends, as much to all the other divine matters revealed in God's Word, as to all parts of the office of the ministers of the Church. But with this difference: they exercise some of the pastors' actions formally, while with regard to others they stand only objectively.

units.la: Formaliter quoad doctrinam verbi divini & veram Religionem, quam utriq; tenentur docere & tueri con-tra Hæreticos & alios errantes; item consequenter quoad judicium serendum de rebus fidei, tùm extra Synodum, tùm in Synodis. Objectivè autem quoad specialem doctrinam de officio pastorum. Nam quamvis ipsi, (si ad officium Pastorum vocati non sint) haud habeant potestatem concionandi, Sacramenta administrandi, disciplinam Ecclesiasticam exercendi, pastores vocandi, Leges ferendi Ecclesiasticas, tamen docent ex verbo Dei, quam doctrinam populo annunciare debeant veri pastores, quomodo Sacramenta administrare, disciplinam Ecclesiasticam exercere, in externo ordine Ecclesiæ se gerere debeant tàm erga Magistratum, quàm erga se ipsos[?] & quosvis homines tùm orthodoxos, tùm errantes,item quæ ad legitimam vocationem Pastorum requirantur, quę sit natura Legum Ecclesiasticarum, quousque denique se potestas eorum seu potius ministerium extendat. Similis est ut ut longè excellentior ratio Magistratus quantum hoc attinet. Is enim etiam circa actiones omnes Pastorum versatur, partim formaliter, partim objectivè; sed cum hoc di-scrimine, quod Doctores Ecclesiæ docendo in Scholis vivâ voce, & in Ecclesiâ totâ scriptis circa eas versantur; Magistratus autem operando, præcipiendo cum imperio ac potestate directivâ & coactivâ quoad ordinem externum, ut exseqq. porrò patebit. Vulgò distinguunt officium pastorum in potestatem ordinis &c jurisdictionis. Illam constat non habere Magistratum; nec etiam hanc quatenus consistit in censuris Ecclesiasticis, hoc est; retinendo aut remittendo peccata: sed quatenus con[?]stit in exteriore regimine seu directione ordinis externi & officii ministrorum.
units.tr: Formally, as to the doctrine of the divine Word and the true religion, which both are bound to teach and defend against heretics and other errorists; likewise consequently as to passing judgment on matters of faith, both outside the synod and in synods. Objectively, however, as to the special doctrine of the office of pastors. For although they (if they have not been called to the office of pastors) do not have the power to preach, administer the sacraments, exercise church discipline, call pastors, or make ecclesiastical laws, nevertheless they teach from God's Word what doctrine the true pastors ought to announce to the people, how they ought to administer the sacraments, exercise church discipline, and conduct themselves in the external order of the Church, both towards the magistrate and towards themselves and any men whatever, orthodox or erring; also what is required for the lawful calling of pastors, what the nature of ecclesiastical laws is, and finally how far their power, or rather their ministry, extends. The reasoning concerning the magistrate is similar, though far more excellent so far as this goes. For he too is concerned with all the actions of the pastors, partly formally and partly objectively; but with this difference: the teachers of the Church are concerned with them by teaching in the schools by the living voice and throughout the whole Church in writing, whereas the magistrate is concerned by acting, and by commanding with authority and directive and coercive power as regards the external order, as will further become clear in what follows. It is commonly distinguished that the office of pastors consists of the power of order and of jurisdiction. It is agreed that the magistrate does not have the former; nor the latter either, insofar as it consists in ecclesiastical censures, that is, in retaining or remitting sins; but insofar as it consists in the external government, or direction, of the external order and of the office of the ministers.

units.la: Cæterum veram esse hanc propositionem, patebit ex inductione, quam sequentibus Quæstionibus exhibebimus, ubi speciatim & distinctè post has generales propositiones tres, sa[?]gemus de partibus potestatis Magistratus circa res Ecclesiasticas. Quæ contra objicit Bellarminus lib 1. de Clericis c. 18. & lib. de Laicis c. 17. item de Pontif. Rom. lib. 1. c. 7. quæ item alii Pontificii afferunt pro sua opinione futilia esse ostenderunt inter alios, Ivellus, Pareus, Junius, Chamierus, alii locis citatis.
units.tr: Moreover, that this proposition is true will be clear from the induction which we shall set out in the following questions, where, after these three general propositions, we shall treat specifically and distinctly of the parts of the magistrate's power in ecclesiastical affairs. As for what Bellarmine objects against it in book 1 of On the Clergy, ch. 18, and in book on Laymen, ch. 17, and likewise in On the Roman Pontiff, book 1, ch. 7, and what other Papists also allege in support of their opinion, they have been shown to be futile by, among others, Ivellus, Pareus, Junius and Chamierus, in the places cited.

units.la: Ad Quest tertiam.
units.tr: To the Third Question.

units.la: Nisi bene distinguatur thesis ista, & explicetur quo pacto Magistratus potestas se extendat ad omnes partes officii ministrorum Ecclesiæ, an non datur Magistratui occasio involandi in omnes partes muneris & Ministerii Ecclesiastici?
units.tr: Unless this thesis is carefully distinguished and explained, showing how far the power of the magistrate extends to all parts of the office of the ministers of the Church, does not the magistrate thereby receive an opportunity to intrude into every part of the duty and ministry of the Church?

units.la: Resp.
units.tr: Answer.

units.la: Per totam disputationem id explicatur; & & primò quidem In genere Q. III. paginis fere integris duabus distinctione potestatis Magistratus formaliter & objectivè consideratę; tum in specie Quæstionib.seqq. Quemadmodum etiam hinc inde in Disputat. speciatim in Conclusione, inculcatur, Magistratum non debere involare in partes eas, quæ ministerio Ecclesiastico propriæ sunt. Non non potest, aut debet Magistratus ipse cōcionari, administrare Sacramenta, exercere disciplinā [?] Ecclesiasticam, ut non semel indisputatione moneo. Nec etiā sibi debet arrogare potestatem talem, quam ipse à Christo & quidem solus immediatè accepit, ita ut ministri, aut nomine ipsius concionentur, Sacramenta administrent, disciplinam exerceant, Ecclesiam gubernent; aut excludantur ab Electione seu vocatione ministrorum & à judiciis Ecclesiasticis, quos errores Arminianorum statim in proœmio longissimè & expressissimè rejeci.
units.tr: The whole disputation explains this. First, in general, in Question III, over almost two full pages, by the distinction between the power of the magistrate considered formally and objectively. Then in particular, in the following questions. Likewise, here and there throughout the disputation, and especially in the conclusion, it is impressed that the magistrate ought not to intrude into those parts which belong properly to the ecclesiastical ministry. The magistrate himself can neither preach, administer the sacraments, nor exercise ecclesiastical discipline, as I warn more than once in the disputation. Nor should he arrogate to himself that power which he himself received immediately from Christ, and indeed he alone received it, so that ministers preach, administer the sacraments, exercise discipline, and govern the Church in his name; or so that they are excluded from the election or calling of ministers and from ecclesiastical judgments. These errors of the Arminians I rejected at length and most expressly at the very beginning, in the preface.

units.la: QUÆST. IV. An Magistratus habeat pote- statem vocandi Pastores seu ministros Ecclesiæ?
units.tr: QUESTION IV. Whether the magistrate has the power of calling the pastors or ministers of the Church?

units.la: BEllar. neg. l. 1. de Pontif. c.4 de Cleric. c.47. de Laic. c.17. quiēadmodum etiam affirmat Electionē Episcoporum jure divino ad solum Pontificem Romanum pertinere, de Cleric. c.8. Nos affirmamus, adeoq; è contrario hanc propositionem formamus: Vocatio pastorum pertinet ad potestatem Magistratus & formaliter & objectivè. Seu clarius loquendo: Non soli ministri & personæ Ecclesiastica, sed etiam Magistratus de jure divino potestatem habent vocandi pastores Ecclesiæ: insuper quoque Magistratus ossicium est curam habere, ut ab ipsis ministris in vocatione pastorum omnia recte fiant, & abusus impedire imperio & potestate suâ. Propositio igitur hæc est bimembris. Prius membrum est: Etiam ad Magistratum pertinere formaliter jus vocandi ministros: Hæc doctrina est totius Ecclesiæ Reformatæ, expressa etiam constitutionibus Ecclesiasticis speciatim Synodi Dordracenæ art. 4. 5. quemadmodum etiam ex praxi Ecclesiarum Reformatarum patet. Unde in celeberrimâ & optimè constitutâ Ecclesiâ Genevensi, quando pastori successor dandus videtur, Senatus Ecclesiasticus, antequam ad nominationem procedat, petit facultatem à Magistratu: quam si non impetrat, suspendit aut planè omittit nominationem, si impetrat, progreditur, & tunc Magistratui proponit eum, qui ipsi maximè placuisset; qui si approbetur Magistratui, res rata est salvo jure totius Ecclesiæ; si displicet Magistratui, alius eligitur. Et recte atque prudenter observat Wernerus Helmichius olim Ecclesiæ Ultrajectinæ Pastor, indifferens esse ex se, ut vel Magistratus, si alicujus operâ uti velit in ministerio eum proponat Consistorio, vel Consistorium aut Ecclesia si quem cupiat vocari, eum Magistratui proponat; in Tractatu Belgico de vocatione ministrorum. Quę prudētia etiam placet Sibbrando cont. Grot. p. 172. ubi inter alia ait se de formuleitatibus cum nemine contendere velle. Et Cl. Walæus eam Helmichii sententiam quoque approbat p. 174. Quod & ipsum in Ecclesia Genevensi observatur. Nec puto ullum modestum virum negaturum istam libertatem Magistratui, modò Ecclesiæ salva maneat sua libertas.
units.tr: Bellarmine denies it in book 1 on the Pope, c. 4; on the Clergy, c. 47; and on the Laity, c. 17. In the same way he also asserts that the election of bishops belongs by divine right to the Roman Pontiff alone, On the Clergy, c. 8. We affirm the contrary, and so we frame this proposition: The calling of pastors pertains to the power of the magistrate both formally and objectively. Or, to speak more clearly: not only the ministers and ecclesiastical persons, but also the magistrate, by divine right, has the power of calling the pastors of the Church. Moreover, it is also the office of the magistrate to take care that everything is done rightly by the ministers themselves in the calling of pastors, and to prevent abuses by his command and authority. The proposition is therefore twofold. The first member is: The right of calling ministers also pertains formally to the magistrate. This doctrine belongs to the whole Reformed Church, and it is also expressed in the ecclesiastical constitutions, especially those of the Synod of Dort, articles 4 and 5, as is also evident from the practice of the Reformed Churches. Hence, in the most renowned and best-ordered Church of Geneva, when a successor to a pastor seems to be needed, the ecclesiastical Senate, before proceeding to nomination, asks permission from the magistrate. If it does not obtain this, it suspends or entirely drops the nomination; if it obtains it, it goes forward, and then proposes to the magistrate the man it most favoured. If this is approved by the magistrate, the matter is settled, the right of the whole Church being preserved; if it displeases the magistrate, another is chosen. Wernerus Helmichius, formerly pastor of the Church of Utrecht, rightly and prudently observes that it is in itself indifferent whether the magistrate, if he wishes to use someone's services in the ministry, proposes him to the consistory, or whether the consistory or the Church, if it wishes someone to be called, proposes him to the magistrate; in the Belgic treatise on the calling of ministers. This prudence also pleases Sibrandus, against Grotius, p. 172, where, among other things, he says he wishes to contend about formalities with no one. The learned Walaeus also approves Helmichius's opinion, p. 174, and this too is observed in the Church of Geneva. Nor do I think any modest man will deny this liberty to the magistrate, provided the liberty of the Church remains intact.

units.la: Competit autem Magistratui jus vocandi ministros non ex privilegio humano speciatim Pontificum, sive eo quod jus Patronatus vocant, sive alio aliquo simili privilegio; sed de jure divino, & quidem duplici nomine, tùm ratione personæ, tùm præcipuè ratione muneris, ut mox patebit, quemadmodum recte observat Cl Rivetus p. 267.
units.tr: The right of calling ministers belongs to the magistrate, however, not by human privilege, especially that of the Pontiffs, whether what they call the right of patronage or some other similar privilege; but by divine right, and indeed on a twofold ground: both by reason of his person, and above all by reason of his office, as will soon become clear. The distinguished Rivetus rightly observes this, p. 267.

units.la: Quod de pastoribus diximus, etiam de Seniorum vocatione esse intelligen-dum, ait T. Martyr in 1. Sam. c. 8, dicens, eo sensu Seniorum constitutionem esse de jure à Magistratu. Ubi etiam observandum quod Cl. Walæus monet p. 173. non solùm ad MagiMagistratus summos pertinere jus vocandi pastores; Sed etiam Magi-stratum subalternum seu inferiorem tan-quam principale membrum cujusque Ec-clesiae in eâ re esse agnoscendum, quamvis lege speciali summi Magistratus ad eam rem auctoritatem non accepisset. Et approbat praeterea cum multis Doctoribus Reformatis speciatim cum Calvino Institut. IV. c. 4. §. 12. sententiam Leonis Episcopi Romani, qui dicit etiam aliorum membrorum notabilium & virorum honoratorum judicia & testimonia, nec non desideria civium attendenda esse,eorumque rationem in electione pastorum habendam. Ita enim Leo Epist. 87. Expectanda sunt vota civium, testi-monia populorum, honoratorum arbitrium, Electio clericorum. Item: Teneatur honoratorum testimonium, subscriptio clericorum, ordinis consensus ac plebis; aliter fieri nulla ratio finit.
units.tr: What we have said of pastors, says Peter Martyr on 1 Sam. c. 8, is also to be understood of the calling of elders, saying that in this sense the institution of elders is by right from the magistrate. Here one should also observe what the learned Walaeus warns, p. 173: that the right of calling pastors pertains not only to the supreme magistrates, but that the subordinate or inferior magistrate must be acknowledged in this matter as the principal member of each Church, although he had not received authority for that matter by a special law of the supreme magistrate. Moreover, he approves, with many Reformed teachers, and especially with Calvin, Institutes IV, c. 4, §12, the opinion of Leo, Bishop of Rome, who says that the judgments and testimonies of other notable members and honoured men, as well as the desires of the citizens, are to be heeded, and their reasons taken into account in the election of pastors. For Leo, Epistle 87: The votes of the citizens are to be awaited, the testimonies of the peoples, the judgment of the honoured, the election of the clergy. Likewise: Let the testimony of the honoured, the signature of the clergy, and the consent of the order and of the common people be upheld; otherwise no reason permits it to be done.

units.la: Posterius membrum hujus propositionis est: Vocationem pastorum pertinere ad Magistratum etiam objectivè. Hæc doctrina etiam est Ecclesiarum Reformatarum; eamque Cl. Walæus p.174.dicit esse conformem verbo Dei, praxi Ecclesiæ primitivæ & Ecclesiarum, quæ quam optimè Reformatæ sunt. Et p. 173. dicit Supremos Magistratus tanquam nutricios Ecclesiæ & defensores constitutionum Jesu Christi, curam gerere debere, aut per se ipsos, aut per deputatos suos, ut secundùm ordinem suprà commemoratum personæ Ecclesiasticæ eligantur, idque sub ipsorum inspectione, seu direction; & paulò post addit, debere Magistratum curam gerere & operam dare, ne pastores abutantur[?] potestate istâ spirituali. Similiter p.175.184.189. docet Magistratum inspectionem debere habere in Electione & vocatione ministrorum, ne abusus in ea committantur. Et clarius ac significantius Cl. Proff. Leydenses in Synopsi purioris Theologiæ Disput. L th. 47. Magistratus ad conferenda Ecclesiæ munera, non solùm intercessione, sed etiam authoritate suâ uti potest. potest, & corruptelas impedire aut corri-gere §[?] quæ civili animadversione dignæ p.817. Etth.52. p.819. dicunt Magistratum tanquam quarti præcepti custodem procurare debere, ut viri idonei pcr presbyterium accedente tùm INPRIMIS ipsius, tùm totius quoque Ecclesiæ consensu ac suffragio ad munus pastorale legitimè vocentur, ac coram Ecclesia ordinentur ex more Apostolorum & Euangelistarum. Act.14.23. Tit 1.5. quem patres nostri sub piis viventes Magistratibus constanter observarunt. Summa: cura, ut omnia rectè fiant, in vocatione seu Electione pastorum pertinet ad Magistratum, ait rectissimè Amesius Cas. conscientiæ p.265. Cum hac curâ & potestate Magistratus circa Electionem, conjuncta est etiam potestas illius circa ordinationem pastorum. Constat Magistratus potestatem non versari circa eam formaliter; versatur tamen circa eam objectivè. Nam ut rectè idem vir Clarissimus ibidem ait: Ordinationem potest Magistratus imperare post legitimum personæ examen, sed eam non potest perse exercere.
units.tr: The latter member of this proposition is: The calling of pastors pertains to the magistrate also objectively. This doctrine too belongs to the Reformed Churches, and the learned Walaeus, p. 174, says it is in agreement with the Word of God, with the practice of the primitive Church, and of the Churches which are most purely Reformed. And on p. 173 he says that the supreme magistrates, as nursing fathers of the Church and defenders of the constitutions of Jesus Christ, ought to take care, either themselves or through their deputies, that ecclesiastical persons be elected according to the order mentioned above, and that under their oversight or direction; and shortly after he adds that the magistrate ought to take care and make an effort that the pastors do not abuse that spiritual power. Similarly, on pp. 175, 184 and 189, he teaches that the magistrate ought to have oversight in the election and calling of ministers, so that abuses are not committed in it. And more clearly and significantly, the distinguished professors of Leiden, in the Synopsis of Purer Theology, Disputation L, thesis 47: The magistrate can use, for conferring the offices of the Church, not only intercession but also his own authority, and can prevent or correct corruptions which are worthy of civil punishment. Also on p. 817, and in thesis 52, p. 819, they say that the magistrate, as guardian of the fourth commandment, must take care that men fit for the pastoral office are lawfully called to that office, by the presbytery, with the consent and vote both of himself in particular and of the whole Church, and are ordained before the Church after the manner of the Apostles and Evangelists, Acts 14:23, Titus 1:5, which our fathers, living under pious magistrates, constantly observed. In sum, the care that everything is done rightly in the calling or election of pastors pertains to the magistrate, as Amesius rightly says, Cases of Conscience, p. 265. Joined to this care and power of the magistrate concerning election is also his power concerning the ordination of pastors. It is clear that the magistrate's power does not concern ordination formally, yet it does concern it objectively. For, as the same most distinguished man rightly says there: The magistrate can command ordination after a lawful examination of the person, but he cannot exercise it himself.

units.la: Confirmatur hęc propositio quoad prius membrum: Quia jus vocationis pastorum ad totam Ecclesiam pertinet, Ergo etiam & insigniter ad Magistratum; tum quatenus est Ecclesiæ membrum, ratione personæ; cùm enim jus illud toti etiam populo competat, non potest excl[illegible, ~2 letters]i pius Magistratus; tum maximè ratione muneris, cùm populi sit caput. Hoc argumentum totidem verbis est Cl. Riveti p. 267. 2. Posterius membrum probatur ex eo; quia Magistratus est custos Quarti præcepti, quo sanctificatio sabbathi & consequenter procuratio cultus divini ipsi est commendata; quod est argumentum totidem verbis Cl. Walæi p. 173. & Cl. Proff. Leydens verbis paulo ante citatis ex th. 52. Accedit praxis piorum Regum ac Principum, tum in Ecclesia Veteris tum in Ecclesia N. Testamenti. Quæ pro suâ sententiâ affert Bellarminus refutata vide apud Junium, Wittakerum, Pareum, alios. Atque hæc quidem est ordinaria potestas quam Magistratus habet in Electione Ministrorum. Extraordinariè v. g. quando dissensio circa Electionem est inter personas Ecclesiasticas, Magistratus aliquando plus auctoritatis debet adhibere tanquam conservator Ecclesiæ ait Cl. Walæus p. 185. quemadmodum à Theodosio M. decretum[?], qui cum videret dissentire Episcopos illius provinciæ inter se circa Electionem Episcopi Constantinopolitani, nullius nominationem voluit ratam habere; sed cùm ipsi commendarus esset per Episcopum Antiochenum Nectarius, eum proposuit Imperator Ecclesiasticis & cupere se eum Episcopum habere exposuit. Resistebant multi Episcopi; permansit tamen Imperator in suâ sententiâ; tandem cesserunt ipsi omnes, & suffragio Imperatoris suum etiam calculum unanimi consensu addidêre. Quod exemplum etiam ex Sozomeno lib. 7. c. 8: refert Cl. Walæus ibidem.
units.tr: This proposition is confirmed as to its first member: because the right of calling pastors pertains to the whole Church, therefore it pertains also, and in a special way, to the magistrate; both as he is a member of the Church, by reason of his person (for since that right belongs also to the whole people, a godly magistrate cannot be excluded); and especially by reason of his office, since he is the head of the people. This argument is, in the same words, that of the distinguished Rivetus, p. 267, no. 2. The latter member is proved from this: the magistrate is guardian of the fourth commandment, in which the sanctification of the sabbath and consequently the maintenance of divine worship is committed to him; which is, in the same words, the argument of the distinguished Walaeus, p. 173, and of the professors of Leiden, in the words cited a little above from thesis 52. To this is added the practice of pious kings and princes, both in the Church of the Old Testament and in the Church of the New Testament. What Bellarmine brings forward in support of his opinion has been refuted; see Junius, Whitaker, Pareus, and others. And this is indeed the ordinary power which the magistrate has in the election of ministers. Extraordinarily, for example, when there is dissension about an election among ecclesiastical persons, the magistrate must sometimes apply more authority, as the preserver of the Church, says the distinguished Walaeus, p. 185. Thus the Great Theodosius decreed, who, seeing that the bishops of that province disagreed among themselves about the election of the bishop of Constantinople, would not allow anyone's nomination to stand valid. But when Nectarius was commended to him by the bishop of Antioch, the emperor proposed him to the churchmen and declared that he wished to have him as bishop. Many bishops resisted, but the emperor remained fixed in his opinion; at last they all yielded and, with unanimous consent, added their own votes to the emperor's suffrage. Walaeus relates this example from Sozomen, book 7, c. 8, in the same place.

units.la: Ad Quæst quartam.
units.tr: To the Fourth Question.

units.la: Si Magistratus jure divino potestatem habet vocandi Pastores Ecclesiæ, probari debet è verbo Dei ista potestas. In Vet. Testamento Magistratus non constituerunt sacerdotes, & ministros cultus divini, sed ipse Deus sibi selegit tribum Levi, Aaronemque, & ejus posteros, ipse constituit in sacerdotes. In Novo Test. Ipse Christus dedit Apostolos, Prophetas, Evangelistas, Pastores & Doctores: quæ deinceps, per Ecclesiæ suffragia, alios elegerunt, vocarunt, instituerunt. Ubi ergo jus illud divinum? Aliud est pastorem nen præfici Ecclesiæ, ubi illa in publico versatur, & à Magistratu defenditur, nisi conscio & consentiente Magistratu: quia Pastor ille in publico loqui debet: Aliud verò, Ius vocandi Pastores formaliter pertinere ad Magistratum.
units.tr: If the magistrate has the power of calling the ministers of the Church by divine right, this power ought to be proved from the Word of God. In the Old Testament the magistrates did not appoint the priests and ministers of the divine worship; God himself chose the tribe of Levi, and Aaron and his posterity, and himself appointed them as priests. In the New Testament Christ himself gave apostles, prophets, evangelists, pastors and teachers; afterwards these men, by the votes of the Church, chose, called and installed others. Where, then, is that divine right? It is one thing for a minister not to be set over the Church, where the Church lives in public and is defended by the magistrate, unless the magistrate is aware of it and consents, since that minister must speak in public; it is quite another thing for the right of calling ministers to belong formally to the magistrate.

units.la: Resp.
units.tr: Answer.

units.la: Quando dico Magistratui competere jus vocandi aut formaliter vocandi Pastores, non hoc volo, ac si Magistratus solus exclusâ Ecclesia, posset vocare Pastores. Nam contrarium expresse statuo saepissime & forte ad minimum tricies in hac disputatione; atque contendo Pastoribus ribus & Ecclesiæ jus suum integrum servari debere, tum in aliis rebus omnibus, tum in vocatione Ministrorum: speciatim in hac Q. IV. ubi explico meam thesin verbis aliorum Theologorum, dicens inter alia ex Synopsi DD. Proff. Leydd.eum debere procurare,ut Pastores per PRESBYTERIVM legitimè vocentur. Sed hæc est mens mea; quod quemadmodum Pastores habent suffragium suum in vocatione ministrorum; ita etiam Magistratus suffragium suum in vocatione eorum habent. Eam mentem meam esse & non aliam ex verbis meis est manifestum. Nam de Imperatore Theodosio sub finem Quæstionis loquens aliam potestatem formaliter vocandi ministros non tribuo quàm jus suffragii, sive suffragium in vocatione Nectarii. Et me ibidem interpretor verbis D. Proff. Leydd. ex Synop. disput. L. th. 51. ubi dicunt Magistratum tanquam Quarti præcepti custodem procurare debere, ut viri idonei per presbyterium accedente tum imprimis ipsius, tum totius quoq; Ecclesiæ consensu ac SVFFRAGIO ad munus pastorale legitimè vocentur. Summa; aliud nihil volo, quàm vult Synodus Dordracena Constitut. Eccles. art 4. 5. ad quam ibidem me conceptis verbis refero; quod etiam vult Praxis Ecclesiarum Reformatarum speciatim in Belgio, & quod denique volunt Theologi nostri, quos ibidem allego. Suffragium porrò illud Magistratus vocatur etiā consensus, prout non solùm in Consideratione vocatur, sed etiam à me ipso ex loco modo allegato Synopseos. Et certè consentire & suffragari συνψηφίζεσθαι[?] & ψηφίζεσθαι[?] sæpè pro eodem sumuntur apud auctores, quà prosanos, quà Ecclesiasticos, cujus rei varia exempla afferre possem. Quod non intelligunt Pontificii, qui ex eo, quod interdum Imperatores dicuntur consensisse Synodo, inferunt eos suffragii jus in Synodis non habere: Vocatur etiam Confirmatio ab aliis, ut Sibbrando cont. Grot. p. 172. item approbatio, ut in Canonibus citatis art. 4. §. [?] Iunius lib. de Cleric. c. 7. n. 31. vocat etiam approbationem, item Electionem n. 17. cùm inquit: Nec populi solius aut Magistratus est Electio, quod Concilium 2. Nicænum negat, nec solius Cleri, quod prisci Canones; sed conjunctim ad utrosque pertinet, ut Capitulari Caroli & Ludovici prudenter cautum. Hoc est quod ego volo & non aliud. Alii vocationem vocant, ut Pareus Comm. Rom. c. 13. p. 1086. Cl. Rivetus p. 267. & alii. Usus autem sum termino Scholastico convenienter & idoneè,quia natura seu forma vocationis non consistit vel in successione hereditariâ, ut in Vet. Testam. vel in electione per sortem, ut electio Matthiæ Apostoli Act.1. sed in electione per suffragia,&speciatim etiam in suffragio Magistratus, non tantùm in suffragio Pastorum & populi, ut rectè docetur etiam Constit. Dordrac. art.4. ubi Synodus his verbis inter alia utitur: Legitima eorum qui nondum functi sunt ministerio, hisce tribus vocatio continetur: primo Electione &c. Mihi alioquin perinde est, quo nomine suffragium Magistratus appelletur;modò de re constet & Magistratui non minus quam Pastoribus & reliquæ Ecclesiæ jus suum sartum tectum conservetur. Tale autem jus seu suffragium, sive consensum[?], sive confirmationem[?], sive vocationem, sive approbationem competere Magistratui, ex Scriptura uno verbo ibidem ostendi. Docet enim ea jus vocationis ministrorum pertinere ad totam Ecclesiam (prout speciatim patet ex Act. 14.23.) Ergo etiam docet illud ad Magistratum simul pertinere.
units.tr: When I say that the right of calling ministers, or of calling them formally, belongs to the magistrate, I do not mean that the magistrate alone, with the Church excluded, could call ministers. For I state the opposite expressly, and very often, perhaps thirty times at least, in this disputation; and I contend that the ministers and the Church must keep their whole right, both in all other matters and in the calling of ministers, and especially in this Fourth Question, where I explain my thesis in the words of other theologians, saying among other things, from the Synopsis of the Professors of Leiden, that the magistrate ought to take care that the ministers are lawfully called through the presbytery. But this is my view: just as the ministers have their vote in the calling of ministers, so the magistrate also has his vote in their calling. That this is my view, and not another, is clear from my own words. For when I speak of the Emperor Theodosius near the end of the Question, I do not attribute to him any other power of formally calling ministers than the right of voting, or the vote in the calling of Nectarius. And there I explain myself by the words of the Professors of Leiden from the Synopsis of Disputations on Common Places, disp. 51, where they say that the magistrate, as guardian of the fourth commandment, ought to take care that fit men are lawfully called to the pastoral office through the presbytery, with the consent and VOTE of the magistrate himself, as well as of the whole Church. In short, I want nothing other than what the Synod of Dort wants in its Church Order, art. 4 and 5, to which I expressly refer myself there; and what the practice of the Reformed Churches wants, especially in Belgium; and finally what our theologians want, whom I cite there. Moreover, that vote of the magistrate is also called consent, as not only in the Consideration but also by me myself from the passage of the Synopsis just cited. And indeed, to consent and to vote together [συνψηφίζεσθαι] and to vote [ψηφίζεσθαι] are often used by authors, both secular and ecclesiastical, for the same thing, and I could bring various examples of this. The Papists do not understand this; from the fact that emperors are sometimes said to have consented to a synod, they infer that they did not have the right of voting in synods. It is also called confirmation by others, as by Sibrandus against Grotius, p. 172; likewise approval, as in the Canons cited, art. 4. Junius, in his book on the clergy, ch. 7, n. 31, also calls it approval, and election at n. 17, when he says: Election belongs neither to the people alone nor to the magistrate alone, as the Second Council of Nicaea denies, nor to the clergy alone, as the ancient canons hold; but it pertains to both jointly, as was prudently provided in the capitulary of Charles and Louis. This is what I mean and nothing else. Others call it calling, as Pareus in his commentary on Romans, ch. 13, p. 1086, and Rivetus, p. 267, and others. I have used the scholastic term fittingly and suitably, because the nature or form of calling does not consist either in hereditary succession, as in the Old Testament, or in election by lot, as the election of the apostle Matthias in Acts 1, but in election by votes, and especially in the vote of the magistrate, not only in the vote of the ministers and the people; as is also rightly taught in the Church Order of Dort, art. 4, where the Synod uses these words among others: The lawful calling of those who have not yet entered the ministry consists of these three things: first, Election, etc. Otherwise it is all the same to me by what name the vote of the magistrate is called, provided the fact is established and the magistrate's right, no less than that of the ministers and the rest of the Church, is kept safe and sound. Moreover, that such a right or vote, whether we call it consent, confirmation, calling or approval, belongs to the magistrate, I showed from Scripture in a single word there. For it teaches that the right of calling ministers belongs to the whole Church (as is clear especially from Acts 14:23). Therefore it also teaches that this right belongs at the same time to the magistrate.

units.la: QUÆST. V. An ad Magistratum pertineat judicium de Religione & controversiis fidei & causis Ecclesiasticis?
units.tr: QUESTION 5. Does the judgment concerning religion, controversies of faith and ecclesiastical causes pertain to the magistrate?

units.la: Bellarminus negat cap. 17. lib. de Laicis lib. de Clericis cap. 28. lib. 1. de Pontifice cap. 7. unde etiam negat Magistratus esse convocare Concilia lib, 1. de Conciliis capp. 12. 13. Sed dicit c. 19. eum vocari ab Ecclesia ad Concilium; negat illius esse in iis præsidere capp. 19. 20. &c. & quando locum occupat supra Episcopos, attribuit id non juri summorum Magistratuum, sed tolerautiæ Ecclesiasticorum: quamvis, inquit, utcumque tolerabile sit Principes seculares in concilio sedere ante alios Episcopos, modo non ante summum Pontificem. ibid. Negat etiam Magistratui summo definitivum suffragium in Con-ciliis competere c. 15. Sed ait Principes vocari tum, ut Concilium defendant, tum ut testes & conscii decretorum Concilii, postea transgressores & contumaces poenis corporalibus puniant; Et sic cum Episcopi in conciliis subscribant definiendo, ut judices: Imperatores ait consentiendo subscripsisse, idque solum in paucis generalibus Conciliis cap. 15.
units.tr: Bellarmine denies it in ch. 17 of the book on laymen, in ch. 28 of the book on clergy, and in ch. 7 of book 1 on the Pope; hence he also denies that the magistrate is to convene councils (book 1 on councils, chs. 12 and 13). But he says in ch. 19 that the magistrate is called by the Church to a council. He denies that it is his place to preside in them (chs. 19, 20, etc.), and when he occupies a place above the bishops, he attributes this not to the right of supreme magistrates but to the tolerance of churchmen: "although," he says, "it is somehow tolerable for secular princes to sit in council before the other bishops, provided it is not before the supreme Pontiff" (ibid.). He also denies that the supreme magistrate has a decisive vote in councils (ch. 15). But he says princes are summoned partly to defend the council, partly as witnesses and parties to its decrees, and afterwards to punish transgressors and the contumacious with bodily penalties. And since bishops subscribe in councils by defining, as judges, he says emperors subscribed only by consenting, and that only in a few general councils (ch. 15).

units.la: Nos affirmamus & contra Bellarm. hanc propositionem formamus: Non solum ad Pastores & Doctores Ecclesiae, sed etiam ad Magistratum pertinet judicium de Religione seu rebus fidei & causis Ecclesiasticis, unicè ex verbo Dei instituendum: & quidem ad eum pertinet tum formaliter, tum objectivè. Haec etiam est doctrina totius Ecclesiae Reformatae. Vide speciatim Ivellum Episcopum Sarisburiensem Apolog. capp. 9.10. Item Antapolog. Cap. 9. 10. &c. Chamierum de Oecumenico Pontifice; Wittakerum, Junium cont. Bellarm. Sibbrandum, item Bogermannum cont. Grot. Cll. Proff. Leydens. in Synopsi Disput. XLIX. Cl. Rivetum in Decal, Cl. Walæum de-officio ministrorum. Amesium cont. Bell. Altstedii Supplem. in Chamierium & alios. Est autem hęc propositio bimembris, primò dicimus ad Magistratum pertinere judicium de religione &c. formaliter. Hoc membrum ut eo magis cum altero membro intelligatur, tenendum est judicium circa res Religionis & Ecclesiæ triplex esse, discretionis, definitionis, & executionis. Quantum attinet ad judicium discretionis, pertinet illud ad omnes homines, adeoque etiam consequenter, imò magis ad Magistratum, idq; omni tempore, speciatim ante Synodum, in Synodo post Synodum. Quantum ad judicií definitivum (quod ita vocatur ab orthodoxis per accidens, nim. respectu verbi Dei, cui per se unicè judicium definitivum competit) convenit illud Magistratui & in Synodo, ita ut habeat suffragium decisivum æquè ac Doctores Ecclesiæ, & post Synodum, quando aut à parte condemnatâ, querela defertur ad Magistratum, aut Ecclesia de errantibus vel Hæreticis apud ipsum conqueritur, ut, ut custodem ac vindicem legis divinę: Hæretici autem apud ipsum se defendere conantur. Et tunc recte fecerit, si in consilium adhibeat peritiores & pios Theologos; nisi forte rei gravitas postulet, ut de ipsius voluntate res in aliâ Synodo resumatur, prout nonnunquam à piis Impp. in vetere Ecclesiâ factum. Quantum ad judicium exequutionis, pertinet illud ad eum post Synodum, ita ut ipsius officii sit, per judicia publica exequi sententiam, quæ non solùm Ecclesiasticorum est; sed etiam primò & præcipuè ipsius Magistratus, ut nobilissimi membri & directoris totius Synodi.
units.tr: We affirm the contrary, and against Bellarmine we frame this proposition: "The judgment concerning religion, or matters of faith, and ecclesiastical causes, to be carried out solely from the Word of God, pertains not only to the ministers and teachers of the Church but also to the magistrate; and indeed it pertains to him both formally and objectively." This is also the doctrine of the whole Reformed Church. See especially Jewel, bishop of Salisbury, Apology chs. 9 and 10; likewise the Antapology, chs. 9, 10, etc.; Chamier on the Ecumenical Pope; Whitaker and Junius against Bellarmine; Sibrandus; likewise Bogerman against Grotius; the learned professors of Leiden in the Synopsis, Disputation XLIX; the learned Rivet on the Decalogue; the learned Walaeus on the office of ministers; Ames against Bellarmine; Alsted's Supplement against Chamier, and others. This proposition has two parts. First, we say that the judgment concerning religion etc. pertains to the magistrate formally. To understand this part more fully along with the other, it must be held that judgment concerning matters of religion and the Church is threefold: of discernment, of definition, and of execution. As far as the judgment of discernment is concerned, it pertains to all men, and consequently also, and even more so, to the magistrate, and at all times: before the synod, in the synod, and after the synod. As to the definitive judgment (which the orthodox so call by accident, namely with respect to the Word of God, to which definitive judgment belongs solely in its own right), it belongs to the magistrate both in the synod, so that he has a decisive vote equally with the teachers of the Church, and after the synod, when either a complaint is brought to the magistrate by the condemned party, or the Church complains to him about erring or heretical persons, as to the guardian and avenger of divine law, and heretics try to defend themselves before him. Then he will do rightly if he calls in more skilled and pious theologians as counsel; unless perhaps the gravity of the matter requires that, at his will, the matter be taken up again in another synod, as was sometimes done by pious emperors in the ancient Church. As to the judgment of execution, it belongs to him after the synod, so that it is his office to carry out the sentence by public judgments. This is not only the business of churchmen, but first and chiefly of the magistrate himself, as the most noble member and director of the whole synod.

units.la: Posterius membrum est, quòd judicium de Religione &c. pertinet ad Magistratum etiam objectivè, hoc est, ita ut ipsius officium sit dirigere quoad ordinem externum judicia publica Ecclesiasticorum de Reliligione &c. Cùm enim, quando controversia est aliqua fidei orta, seu quæstio de dogmate valdè dubio, sive cujus non notoria est veritas & falsitas ( nam notoriam veritatem non debet pati Magistratus in dubium vocari, nedum ad Synodum pertrahi, sed coërcere contradicentes potestate suâ coactivâ) ordinarius, & verbo Dei maximè conformis modus judicandi sit, qui à Synodis peragitur secundum verbum Dei; Magistratus est non vocari ad Synodum ab Ecclesiasticis, sed convocare Ecclesiasticos ad Synodum aut ipsis petentibus permittere Synodum. Et ubi Ecclesiæ deputatos nominârunt ipsarum est rem referre ad Magistratum, quo ita confirmentur à Magistratu, si is justas causas non videat eos reiiciendi, vide Sibb. p. 149. quemadmodum è contrario poterit excludere personas ab Ecclesiis deputatas, quæ ipsi ob veras & justissimas causas displicent, & mandare Ecclesiis, ut alios, qui idonei sunt, eligant, ait Sibrandus p. 149. Vide Cl. Walæum p. 214. 215. ubi inter alia ait eum accedente Ecclesiarum assensu posse excludere eos, qui notorie affectibus suis ducuntur, & magis studeant propriæ gloriæ, quam paci Ecclesiæ. Extraordinarie ipse etiam potest nominare personas, quas cupit interesse Synodo, maxime ubi Ecclesiæ turbatæ vehementer sunt, aut earum Reformatio instituitur, quo ultimo in casu potest uti Doctoribus, quos præsens opportunitas ipsi suppeditat. Vide eoldem[?] locis citatis. Vbi jam Synodi initium est faciendum, ipsius est comparere in ea aut per se, aut per Legatos suos sive Deputatos. Potest etiam adducere secum ad Synodum viros doctos, & in rebus Theologicis bene exercitatos, quorum consilio utatur, ut Cl. Walæus monet p. 216. Comparet autem in Synodo cum potestate directiva, quâ totum ordinem externum regit. Quare ipsius est præsidere in Synodo, ita ut quemadmodum minister aliquis Ecclesiæ electivus & ministerialis præses est, quia minister est; ita ipse ut Princeps sit præses jure suo & quidem principalis. Ibi moderabitur actionem ita, ut omnia fiant piè, decenter, graviter, quietè, ordine, ut affectus exulent; si qui sint pertinaces, aut immodesti vel contumeliosi eos reprimet; in summa operam dabit, ut ex verbo Dei lis decidatur. Quod ubi factum est, non potest Synodi judicium publicam auctoritatem habere, nisi ad Synodi petitionem illud à Magistratu Summo confirmetur. Hæc etiam est declaratio posterioris membri. Confirmationem Propositionis hujus ut & responsiones ad argumenta Bellarmini, quia hæc res valdè latè patet, vide apud diversos ex citatis Theologis.
units.tr: The second part is that the judgment concerning religion etc. pertains to the magistrate also objectively, that is, so that it is his office to direct, as regards external order, the public judgments of churchmen concerning religion etc. For when some controversy of faith has arisen, or a question about a very doubtful dogma, or one whose truth or falsity is not notorious (for the magistrate must not allow notorious truth to be called in doubt, much less draw it into a synod, but must restrain contradictors by his coercive power), the ordinary mode of judging, and the one most conformable to God's Word, is that which is carried out by synods according to the Word of God. The magistrate is not called to the synod by churchmen; rather he calls churchmen to the synod, or permits a synod at their request. And where they have named deputies of the Church, it is their business to refer the matter to the magistrate, so that they may be confirmed by him, if he does not see just causes for rejecting them; see Sibrandus, p. 149. Just as, on the contrary, he may exclude persons deputed by the churches who displease him for true and most just causes, and order the churches to choose others who are fit; so Sibrandus says, p. 149. See the learned Walaeus, p. 214, 215, where, among other things, he says that with the consent of the churches the magistrate can exclude those who are notoriously led by their passions and seek their own glory more than the peace of the Church. Extraordinarily, he himself may also name persons whom he wishes to attend the synod, especially where the churches are violently disturbed or their reformation is undertaken; in this last case he may use the teachers whom the present opportunity supplies. See the same places cited. When the synod is about to begin, it is his business to appear in it, either in person or through his legates or deputies. He may also bring with him to the synod learned men well practised in theological matters, whose counsel he may use, as the learned Walaeus advises, p. 216.
