He appears in the synod, however, with directive power, by which he governs the whole external order. Hence it is his to preside in the synod, so that just as some elected and ministerial minister of the Church is president because he is a minister, so he himself, as prince, is president by his own right, and indeed the principal one. There he will moderate the proceedings so that everything is done piously, decently, gravely, quietly and in order, and passions are banished. If there are any who are obstinate, immodest or abusive, he will restrain them. In sum, he will take care that the dispute is decided from the Word of God. When this has been done, the judgment of the synod cannot have public authority unless, at the petition of the synod, it is confirmed by the supreme magistrate. This is also the declaration of the second part. As for the confirmation of this proposition, and the replies to Bellarmine's arguments, since this matter extends very widely, see the various theologians cited above.

units.la: Ad Quæst. quintam.
units.tr: To the fifth question.

units.la: An non ad thesis illius limitationem & explicationem, addi deberet, ut ad tutorem & defensorem fenforem Ecclesiæ, ut certò sciat se veram Religionem & veram Ecclesiam defendere? Nam cum judicium de Religione, & controversiis fidei, & causis Ecclesiasticis pertineat ad Pastores & Inspectores Ecclesiæ, an non considerandum & explicandum, quo modo & sensu ad illos pertineat: an ut ad delegatos à Magistratu: an vero ut cum Magistratu collaterales, in eâdem potestate cum illis positos: an denique ut ad Christi ministros? Quantum præjudicium poterit hinc creari Ecclesiæ Dei, ejusque ministris, nisi hæc rite explicentur?
units.tr: Should it not be added, to qualify and explain this thesis, that the magistrate is the guardian and defender of the Church, so that he may know for certain that he is defending the true religion and the true Church? For since judgment concerning religion, the controversies of faith, and ecclesiastical causes belongs to the pastors and overseers of the Church, should it not be considered and explained in what manner and sense it belongs to them: whether as delegates of the magistrate, or as colleagues placed with the magistrate in the same power, or finally as ministers of Christ? How great a prejudice could be created from this for the Church of God and its ministers, unless these matters are rightly explained?

units.la: Resp.
units.tr: Answer.

units.la: Ista limitatio seu explicatio argumentum continet, ex quo evincitur Magistratum debere judicare de rebus fidei. Quam explicationem seu argumentum haud obscurè expressi, quando in responsione ad Q. illam ibidem dico Magistratui competere judicium de rebus fidei, quando Ecclesia de errantibus vel Hæreticis apud Magistratum conqueritur, ut custodem ac vindicem legis divinæ; quæ verba ἐμφανίζω[?] & sunt, & includunt consequenter id, quod in Consideratione dicitur. Nam si judicat ut custos ac vindex legis divinæ: Ergo etiam ut defensor Ecclesiæ, quæ est στῦλος[?] & ἑδραίωμα[?] τῆς ἀληθείας[?]
units.tr: This qualification or explanation contains an argument from which it is shown that the magistrate ought to judge matters of faith. I have not obscurely expressed this explanation or argument when, in my answer to that question, I say there that the magistrate has the right to judge matters of faith when the Church complains before the magistrate about erring persons or heretics, as the guardian and avenger of the divine law. These words are emphatic [ἐμφανίζω] and consequently include what is said in the Consideration. For if he judges as guardian and avenger of the divine law, then he also judges as defender of the Church, which is the pillar and ground of the truth [στῦλος ... ἑδραίωμα ... τῆς ἀληθείας].

units.la: Quod quæritur, quomodo igitur judicent Pastores? Respondeo hanc quæstionem pertinere ad discrimina officii Pastorum & Magistratuum in gubernatione Ecclesiæ, quæ octodecim esse dixi in Conclusione, brevitatis autem causâ non potui enumerare. Inter alia enim discrimina utriusque officii est, quod etiamsi & Magistratus & Pastores judicent de rebus fidei; tamen in eo differunt; quod Magistratus judicat ut judex, qui custos est utriusque tabulæ legis gladio corporali armatus & potestate coactivâ externâ, adeòque ut rectè dicitur in Consideratione ut defensor Ecclesiæ: Pastores autem ut ministri Christi atque Ecclesiæ vocati ad docendum in Ecclesiâ; seu ut custodes utriusque tabulæ legis gladio ministeriali ac spirituali verbi divini, & potestate coactivâ spirituali nomine Christi instructi. Adeoque non judicant ut delegati à Magistratu, quam sententiam Arminianorum expresse & procul rejeci in Proœmio;neque etiam judicant nomine & titulo invidioso collateralitatis quo illi Ecclesias nostras odiosas reddunt; quamvis si adversarii collateralitatem vocent, quod & Pastores & Magistratus in Regimine Ecclesiæ Dei quoad ordinem externum suo modo conveniunt, id ferre cogimur prout prudenter D. Walęus alicubi loquitur. Unde patet hanc meam Thesin & doctrinam nullum afferre præjudicium Ecclesię aut ejus ministris: idque eo minus, quia expressè ibi dixi judicium de rebus fidei non ad Solum Magistratum pertinere, nec debere Pastoribus eripi jus suum de rebus fidei judicandi; sed pertinere illud etiam ad Pastores & Doctores Ecclesiæ: item ordinarium & verbo Dei maximè conformem modum judicandi esse,qui à Synodis peragitur, secundùm verbum Dei &c
units.tr: As to the question, how then do the pastors judge? I answer that this question belongs to the differences between the office of the pastors and the office of the magistrates in the government of the Church, which I said in the Conclusion are eighteen in number, but for the sake of brevity I could not enumerate. Among other differences between the two offices is this: even though both the magistrate and the pastors judge concerning matters of faith, yet they differ in this, that the magistrate judges as a judge, who is the guardian of both tables of the law, armed with the bodily sword and with external coercive power; and so he is rightly said in the Consideration to judge as defender of the Church. The pastors, however, judge as ministers called by Christ and the Church to teach in the Church, or as guardians of both tables of the law, armed with the ministerial and spiritual sword of the divine Word and with spiritual coercive power in the name of Christ. Therefore they do not judge as delegates of the magistrate, a view of the Arminians which I expressly and firmly rejected in the Preface. Nor do they judge under the name and odious title of collaterality, by which those men make our Churches hateful; although, if the opponents want to call it collaterality, in that both the pastors and the magistrates agree in their own way in the government of the Church of God as regards external order, we are compelled to bear it, as the prudent D. Walaeus says somewhere. From this it is clear that my thesis and doctrine bring no prejudice to the Church or its ministers; and all the less so because I there expressly said that judgment concerning matters of faith does not belong to the magistrate alone, nor should the right of judging matters of faith be snatched from the pastors; but that it belongs also to the pastors and teachers of the Church. Likewise, the ordinary mode of judging, and the one most conformable to the Word of God, is that carried out by Synods, according to the Word of God, etc.

units.la: QUÆST. VI. An Magistratus circa res Eccle- siasticas habeat potestatem cum impe- rio conjunctam & coactivam in Pasto- res Ecclesiæ?
units.tr: QUESTION VI. Does the magistrate, in ecclesiastical affairs, have a power joined with command and coercive over the pastors of the Church?

units.la: Bellarminus non permittit Magistratui, ut in rebus Ecclesiasticis ullam potestatem exerceat in personas Ecclesiasticas, & contendit eas liberas esse de jure divino in causis Ecclesiasticis à secularium Principum potestate. lib. de Cleric. c. 28. & propositione 3. ait omnino absurdum esse, ut ovis[?] Pastorem suum quocunque modo judicare præsumat. Et sic etiam non permittit Magistratui, ut deponat ministros Ecclesiæ, quemadmodum etiam lib. 2. de Pontif. cap. 26. negat imperatorem aut ullum Principem habere jus deponendi Papam. Atq; hanc esse mentem ipsius quoque, cùm negat lib. 1. de Pontif. cap. 7. & lib. de Laicis c. 17. ad magistratum ullo modo pertinere regimen Ecclesiæ, aut judicium de Religione, per se patet. Nos affirmativam tenemus, & contra eum hanc propositionem formamus: Magistratus circa res Ecclesiasticas habet potestatem cum imperio conjunctam & coactivam in Pastores Ecclesiæ & quasi personas Ecclesiasticas. Hoc est, Magistratus est non tantum monere & hortari pastores ad officium suum & quidem recte atque secundum præscriptum verbi divini faciendum; sed etiam id ipsis cum imperio præcipere, & si obedire nolint, potest eos in ordinem redigere, & cogere, ut officium rectè, vigilanter, impigrè, fideliter faciant, atque à malis & scandalosis actionibus abstineant. Adeoque pro delicti ratione potest in eos animadverrere civiliter, efficere seu mandare, ut suspendantur aut removeantur ab officio; speciatim si seditiosè concionentur, in[?] populum contra Magistratum concitare conentur, si in Magistratum contumeliosi sint, & in eum convitiis ac probris debacchentur (quod est unum ex gravissimis delictis, quorum in Scriptura falsi Doctores rei peraguntur 2. Pet. 2. 10. Jud. v. 8. veri autem Doctores ajunt hoc grave crimen esse & non serendum in Republicâ bene constitutâ: Sibbrandus cont. Grot. p. 1.) si errores aut hereses doceant; si denique alioquin flagitiosi sint. Hæc propositio etiam est totius Reformatæ Ecclesiæ.
units.tr: Bellarmine does not allow the magistrate to exercise any power over ecclesiastical persons in ecclesiastical affairs, and he contends that by divine law they are free from the power of secular princes in ecclesiastical causes (De Clericis, ch. 28). And in proposition 3 he says it is altogether absurd for a sheep to presume to judge its shepherd in any way. And so too he does not allow the magistrate to depose the ministers of the Church, just as in Book 2 of De Pontificibus, ch. 26, he denies that the emperor or any prince has the right to depose the Pope. That this is also his own mind, when in Book 1 of De Pontificibus, ch. 7, and in De Laicis, ch. 17, he denies that the government of the Church, or judgment concerning religion, belongs to the magistrate in any way, is plain in itself. We hold the affirmative, and against him we form this proposition: The magistrate, in ecclesiastical affairs, has a power joined with command and coercive over the pastors of the Church and over persons who are, as it were, ecclesiastical. That is, the magistrate is not only to admonish and exhort the pastors to their duty, and indeed to do it rightly and according to the prescription of the divine Word; but also to command them in authority to do it, and if they are unwilling to obey, he can bring them into order and compel them to perform their office rightly, watchfully, diligently and faithfully, and to abstain from evil and scandalous actions. Accordingly, in proportion to the offence, he can take civil action against them, bring it about or order that they be suspended or removed from office; especially if they preach seditiously, try to stir up the people against the magistrate, if they are insolent toward the magistrate and rage against him with insults and abuse (which is one of the most serious offences for which false teachers are called to account in Scripture: 2 Pet. 2:10; Jude v. 8; and true teachers say that this is a grave crime and is not to be tolerated in a well-ordered commonwealth: Sibrandus against Grotius, p. 1); if they teach errors or heresies; and finally if they are otherwise flagitious. This proposition is also held by the whole Reformed Church.

units.la: Confess. Anglic. artic. 37. ait: Magistratibus summis hanc prærogativam competere, quam in sacris scripturis à Deo ipso, omnibus piis Principibus videmus semper fuisse attributam: hoc est, ut omnes status atque ordines fidei suae à Deo commissos, sive illi Ecclesiastici sint, sive civiles in officio contineant, & contumaces & delinquentes gladio civili coërceant.
units.tr: The Confession of the English Church, Article 37, says: That the chief magistrates have this prerogative, which we see in the sacred Scriptures has always been ascribed by God himself to all godly princes: that is, that they keep all the orders and estates committed to them by God in their duty, whether these are ecclesiastical or civil, and restrain the contumacious and offenders with the civil sword.

units.la: Petrus Martyr in 1. Sam. 8. pag. 50.
units.tr: Peter Martyr, on 1 Samuel 8, p. 50.

units.la: Quid ergo? inquies: an imperabit Magistratus ministris & concionatoribus? Respondeo, verbum Dei & sacramenta nulli potestati subjiciuntur: ministri autem subjiciuntur bifariam, & quoad mores & quoad functionem attinet. Nam si aut perdite vivant, aut officium non faciant, possunt corripi à Magistratu & summoveri &c. Bullingerus de Episcoporum institut.
units.tr: What then? you will say: will the magistrate command the ministers and preachers? I answer: the Word of God and the sacraments are subject to no power; but ministers are subject in two respects, both as regards morals and as regards their function. For if they live wickedly or do not perform their office, they can be rebuked by the magistrate and removed, etc. Bullinger, On the Institution of Bishops.

units.la: In illis ipsis libris (Regum) proditum est, à sanctis Regibus etiam summos Sacerdotes, ab officio fuisse amotos, & alios in locum constitutos. Cœterum non praeter meritum ejus abjiciebatur, neque quicquam hic actum est contra leges Dei. Et paulò post dicit. In V. Testamento datam fuisse Principi potestatem agendi, quae pertine-bant ad incolumitatem & Religionis & Reipub. conservandam, etiam contra sacerdotes, si modo pergerent esse nebulones c. 3. s. 72. Zanchius Loco de Magistratu art.7. ait: Omnes homines, nemine excepto, ita Magistratui subjectos esse, ut si officium facere recusent, in eos animadvertere & omnes in officio retinere possit. Ivellus in Apolog. item in Antapolog. dicit Principes facere illud, quod possunt, quod jubentur, quod debent, quodque & Davidem & Salomonem & alios Principes fecisse scimus, ut ipsis (Sacerdotibus) aut dormientibus aut nefariè resistentibus, Sacerdotum libidinem coërceant, eosque ad officium faclendum adigant, & in officio contineant c. 9. s. 2. Sic Beza cont. Erastum ait: Magistratum habere potestatem puniendi observato bono ordine. Doctores obstinatos, fideliter non exequentes officium, item falsos; & debere operam dare, ut alii secundum praxin Apostolicam sufficiantur in locum eorum. Quem locum Bezæ Cl. Walæus etiam laudat & probat p. 57. vide etiam Pareum in c. 13. Roman. p. 1098. item in Aphorism. Artic. 11. §. 19. Bucanum loco de Magistratu Q. 52. ubi ait, Magistratus officium esse cogere quemlibet in suo ordine & statu Ecclesiastico sive Politico, ut officium faciant, & punire eos, qui contumaces inveniuntur. Sibbrandus cont. Grot. p. 21. de Magistratu summo ait: Defendit & tuetur ministros quàm diu suo munere rectè funguntur, eosdem severe coërcet, si vel verbum falsâ doctrinâ adulterant, aut sacramenta idololatricis ritibus contaminant, aut disciplinam in Tyrannidem aut conscientiarum carnificinam commutant. Hoc modo pii Imperatores Ecclesiam gubernârunt &c. Similiter etiam p. 119. dicit: Magistratus esse adducere & cogere ministros ad officium faciendum. Idem docet Cl Walæus p. 57. 58, 129. 130. 144. 167. Et Bogermannus cont. Grot. p. 234. ex suâ & Junii mente ait Magistratus officium esse ministros limites tabularum mandati divini excedentes aut aberrantes legitimè & secundum Deum in viam revocare & coërcere. Cl. Rivetus in Decalog. Si non faciunt ministri ea, quæ ipsorum sunt, tunc Magistratus gravitate & imperio eos monet, & injungit ut fiant atque rectè fiant; vindicatque si secus p. 265. a. ibidem dicit, quod quemadmodum Magistratus pascuntur ministerio Pastorum, ita ipsi Magistratus pascant ministros imperio. Et p. 262. Constitutos dicimus esse Principes in iis, quæ ad Deum spectant, quia pœnis scitisque civilibus providere debet, ut suo Ecclesiæ ministri perfungantur in rebus divinis officio. Et p. 267. ostendit quis sit modus ordinarius observandus à Magistratu in depositione ministrorum flagitiosorum, aut Hæreticorum, nimirum via Ecclesiastica, seu ut ipse loquitur, vocatis & consultis, qui jus eligendi habuerunt. Rex autem, inquit, sive alius Magistratus, ut non ordinat, sic nec deponit formaliter, ut ita loquamur, vel administratoriè per se ipsum: id tamen facit non solum consilio, MANDATO ET AUCTORITATE, quia iis MANDARE potest, ubi subest justa causa de ministro exautorando, penes quos hæc potestas in Ecclesiâ viget: qui quidem in hoc casu, ubi nempe justa causa subest, NISI PARENT ET QUOD JUBET FACIUNT, obnoxii sunt non solùm iræ, sed etiam divino judicio. Ubi per iram intelligitur pœna infligenda à Magistratu, ut Roman. c. 13. 9. ad quem locum Cl. vir respicit. Alioquin orthodoxi Theologi docent Magistratum extraordinariè etiam seu absque præcedaneo judicio Ecclesiæ in Pastores animadvertere posse, quando manifesta flagitia aut scelera commiserunt. Sic Cll. Proff. Leydd. Disput. de Magistratu th. 54. p. 819. Si pastor sit seditiosus ac manifestus pacis publicæ violator, summus Magistratus eum interveniente subordinatorum procerum consilio potest eodem jure exautorare, quo Rex Salomon Abiatharum deposuit. Et Cl. Walæus p. 178. Quis unquam negavit propter notoria delicta, quæ simpliciter civilia sunt, speciatim ob proditionem contra summum Magistratum & bonum Reip. Pastorem posse neci dari, aut exilio multari, & consequenter etiam deponi suo ministerio à magistratu: Etiam absque præcedaneo judicio Ecclesiastico, quandoquidem omnia judicia Ecclesiastica in eo conveniunt. Hæc est sententia Hierarchiæ Antichristianæ, non autem Ecclesiarum Reformatarum; quasi tales primò degradandi essent à suis spiritualibus, quos vocant, & postea tradendi Magistratibus secularibus, ut puniantur. Et Junius ultra delicta capitalia illam potestatem extraordinariam extendit, quando Ecclesia ab officio suo deficit. Statuit enim deficiente Ecclesiâ ab officio posse Magistratum extra ordinem procurare, ut Ecclesia redeat ad officium: extraordinariis malis extraordinaria adhiberi remedia &c. Quam sententiam Junii laudat Bogermannus. cont. Grot. p. 193. & dicit pag. 92. Hanc esse communem Ecclesiarum no-strarum sententiam. Similiter etiam Bucerus lib 1. de regno Christi tribuit hanc potestatem extraordinariam Magistratui, quando ministerium corrupt-um est. Cujus verba laudat Cl. Walaeus p. 148.
units.tr: In those very books (Kings) it is recorded that by the holy kings even high priests were removed from office and others put in their place. Yet he was not dismissed without merit, and nothing was done here contrary to the laws of God. And a little later he says: In the Old Testament the prince was given power to act in whatever pertained to preserving the safety both of religion and of the commonwealth, even against priests, provided they persisted in being scoundrels (c. 3, s. 72). Zanchius, in the locus on the magistrate, art. 7, says: All men, no one excepted, are so subject to the magistrate that if they refuse to do their duty, he can punish them and keep all of them in their duty. Jewel, in the Apology and likewise in the Antapology, says: Princes do what they can, what they are commanded, and what they ought to do, as we know David, Solomon and other princes did: when the priests either sleep or wickedly resist, they restrain the priests' lust and compel them to perform their duty and keep them in it (c. 9, s. 2). So Beza, against Erastus, says: The magistrate has the power to punish, provided good order is observed: obstinate teachers who do not faithfully carry out their office, likewise false ones; and he should take care that others be substituted in their place according to apostolic practice. The distinguished Walaeus also praises and approves this passage of Beza (p. 57). See also Pareus on Romans 13, p. 1098, and in the Aphorisms, art. 11, §19. Bucanus, locus on the magistrate, Q. 52, where he says: The office of the magistrate is to compel each person in his order and ecclesiastical or political state to perform his duty, and to punish those who are found contumacious. Sibrandus, against Grotius, p. 21, says of the supreme magistrate: He defends and protects the ministers as long as they discharge their office rightly; he severely restrains them if they either adulterate the word with false doctrine, or contaminate the sacraments with idolatrous rites, or turn discipline into tyranny or into the torture of consciences. In this way pious emperors governed the Church, etc. Likewise he says on p. 119: It is the office of the magistrate to bring ministers and compel them to perform their duty. The distinguished Walaeus teaches the same at pp. 57, 58, 129, 130, 144 and 167. And Bogermann, against Grotius, p. 234, in his own view and that of Junius, says: The office of the magistrate is to lawfully and according to God lead back into the way, and restrain, ministers who exceed or stray from the limits of the divine commandment. The distinguished Rivetus, on the Decalogue: If ministers do not do what is their task, then the magistrate, with gravity and authority, admonishes them and enjoins that it be done, and done rightly; and he avenges it if otherwise (p. 265a). In the same place he says that just as magistrates are fed by the ministry of pastors, so the magistrates in turn should feed the ministers by their command. And at p. 262: We say that princes are set over those things which concern God, because they must provide by penalties and civil decrees that the ministers of the Church carry out their office in divine matters. And at p. 267 he shows what ordinary method the magistrate should observe in deposing flagitious or heretical ministers, namely the ecclesiastical way, or, as he himself puts it, by calling and consulting those who had the right to elect. The king, however, he says, or another magistrate, as he does not ordain, so neither does he depose formally, so to speak, or administratively by himself: yet he does this not only by counsel, BY COMMAND AND AUTHORITY, because he can COMMAND those in whom this power resides in the Church, where a just cause exists for removing the minister; who indeed in this case, where a just cause exists, UNLESS THEY OBEY AND DO WHAT IS COMMANDED, are liable not only to wrath but also to divine judgment. Here by wrath is understood the punishment to be inflicted by the magistrate, as in Romans 13, to which passage that distinguished man refers. Otherwise, orthodox theologians teach that the magistrate can, extraordinarily and even without a preceding judgment of the Church, punish pastors when they have committed manifest crimes or wickedness. So the distinguished professors of Leiden, in the disputation on the magistrate, thesis 54, p. 819: If a pastor is seditious and a manifest violator of public peace, the supreme magistrate, with the advice of the subordinate nobles intervening, can remove him by the same right by which King Solomon deposed Abiathar. And the distinguished Walaeus, p. 178: Who has ever denied that, on account of notorious offences which are simply civil, specifically treason against the supreme magistrate and the good of the commonwealth, a pastor can be put to death or punished with exile, and consequently also deposed from his ministry by the magistrate, even without a preceding ecclesiastical judgment, since all ecclesiastical judgments agree on this? This is the opinion of the Antichristian hierarchy, not of the Reformed Churches, as if such men were first to be degraded by their so-called spiritual authorities and only afterwards handed over to the secular magistrates to be punished. And Junius extends that extraordinary power beyond capital crimes to the case where the Church falls away from its office. For he lays down that when the Church has failed in its office, the magistrate can extraordinarily take care that the Church return to its office: extraordinary evils call for extraordinary remedies, etc. Bogermann approves this opinion of Junius, against Grotius, p. 193, and says at p. 92: This is the common opinion of our Churches. Likewise Bucer, in book 1 of On the Kingdom of Christ, attributes this extraordinary power to the magistrate when the ministry has become corrupt. The distinguished Walaeus, p. 148, quotes his words.

units.la: Confirmatur hæc propositio inter alia iis argumentis, quæ in modò laudatorum Theologorum quorundam verbis allegatis reperire est, qui etiam ad argumenta Bellarmini & sociorum ipsius respondent.
units.tr: This proposition is confirmed, among other arguments, by those found in the words of the aforementioned theologians cited above, who also answer the arguments of Bellarmine and his associates.

units.la: Ad Quaest. sextam.
units.tr: To Question Six.

units.la: Quamvis non sit assentiendum sententia Bellarmini, cogitandum tamen, an sexta illa Antithesis tam absolute poni debeat. Nam an non subditus in iis omnibus, in quibus Magistratus potestatem habet in ipsum cum imperio conjunctam, & coactivam, Magistratui morem gerere debet, & nisi fecerit, seditiosus habetur? An Magistratus Hierofolymitanus [?] in Apo-stolos habebat potestatem cum imperio conjunctam & coactivam? An Apostoli igitur seditionis rei fuerunt, contra mandatum illius Magistratus, annunciando Euangelium Iesu Christi? Nullâ ratione. An ergo discrimen non est statuendum inter causas religionis & politicas, sive merè civiles?
units.tr: Although one should not assent to Bellarmine's opinion, we must still consider whether that sixth antithesis ought to be stated so absolutely. For is not a subject bound to obey the magistrate in all those matters in which the magistrate holds power over him joined with command and coercive force, and if he does not, is he not regarded as seditious? Did the magistrate of Jerusalem [?] have power over the Apostles joined with command and coercive force? Were the Apostles therefore guilty of sedition against that magistrate's command by proclaiming the Gospel of Jesus Christ? By no reasoning. Therefore is no distinction to be drawn between causes of religion and political or merely civil causes?

units.la: Resp.
units.tr: Response.

units.la: Thesis illa quomodo intelligenda sit, ex immediate subsequentibus verbis patet, quibus explicatur & limitatur: nimirum quod Magistratus habeat potestatem non quidvis imperandi personis Ecclesiasticis & ni pareant eas puniendi; sed quod habeat potestatem imperandi iis, ut officium suum & quidem recte atque secundum præscriptum verbi divini faciant, & ni faciant officium suum rectè, impigrè, vigilanter, eas puniendi.
units.tr: How that thesis is to be understood is clear from the words that immediately follow, which explain and limit it: namely, that the magistrate has power not to command ecclesiastical persons in anything at all, and to punish them if they do not obey; but that he has power to command them to do their office, and indeed to do it rightly and according to the prescription of the Word of God, and, if they do not do their office rightly, diligently and vigilantly, to punish them.

units.la: Item quòd potestatem habeat Pastores cogendi, non ut à bonis actionibus, sed ut à malis & scandalosis actionibus abstineant. Atque huc faciunt omnia testimonia nostrorum Theologorum ibi à me allegata. Patet igitur me non attribuere ipsi potestatem absolutam, sed restringere eam & limitare ita, ut Magistratus non possit imperare ministris & eos cogere ut faciant quæ contra eorum officium sunt, sed quæ officium ipsorum postulat; non quæ ad destructionem Religionis, sed ad conservandam incolumitatem Religio[?]nis faciunt, ut Bullingerus loquitur à me citatus. Idem etiam patet ex Thesi X & hinc inde ex totâ Disputatione. Unde facile respondere est ad exemplum Magistratus Hierosolymitani. Is enim præcipiebat Apostolis illicita & impia, cujus jussu consequenter illi non tenebantur obedire, sed mandato Dei, qui contrarium ipsis præceperat Act.[?]4.5.capp. Cui accedit quòd ego loquor per totam Disputationem, ut expressè protestatus sum in Proœmio, non de quovis Magistratu summo, sed de Orthodoxo, qualis certè Magistratus ille non erat; quemadmodum stultè quidam Pontificii sentiunt, qui existimant Ecclesiam illam, quæ Christum & Apostolos condemnavit, ac persecuta est, veram Ecclesiam fuisse. Atque hoc est illud ipsum discrimen, quòd inter potestatem Magistratus circa res Religionis & circa merè civiles in Consideratione rectè statuitur.
units.tr: Likewise, that the magistrate has power to compel ministers, not to good actions, but to abstain from evil and scandalous actions. To this point bear all the testimonies of our theologians which I cited there. It is therefore plain that I do not attribute to the magistrate an absolute power, but restrict and limit it, so that the magistrate cannot command ministers and compel them to do what is contrary to their office, but only what their office requires; not what tends to the destruction of religion, but what tends to preserve its soundness, as Bullinger, whom I cited, puts it. The same is plain from Thesis X and from the whole of the Disputation here and there. Hence it is easy to answer the example of the magistrate of Jerusalem. For he ordered the Apostles what was unlawful and impious, and consequently they were not bound to obey his command, but the command of God, who had ordered the opposite (Acts 4–5). To this must be added that I speak throughout the whole Disputation, as I expressly declared in the Preface, not of any supreme magistrate whatever, but of an orthodox one, which that magistrate certainly was not. Just as some Papists foolishly think, who suppose that that Church which condemned and persecuted Christ and the Apostles was the true Church. And this is precisely the distinction, that between the power of the magistrate in matters of religion and in merely civil matters, which is rightly laid down in the Consideration.

units.la: QUÆST. VII. An Magistratus curam gerere debeat, ne ministri Ecclesiæ disciplina Ecclesiastica abutantur, & alicui injuriam faciant?
units.tr: QUESTION VII. Whether the magistrate ought to take care that the ministers of the Church do not abuse ecclesiastical discipline and do injury to anyone?

units.la: BEllarminum negativam tueri per se ex praecedentibus manifestum est. Nam quia statuit ad Magistratum non pertinere cognitionem causarum ullarum Ecclesiasticarum: certè patet eum etiam pati non posse ut Magistratus curam gerat conservandæ disciplinæ Ecclesiasticæ in puritate suâ: & sic non permittere ulli, ut, si sentiat sibi per censuram Ecclesiasticam injuriam fieri, conqueri possit apud Magistratum, nec etiam Magistratui concedere, ut causæ cognitionem suscipiat,& conquerenti prospiciat. Unde fluit, quod ex Gelasii Papæ epistolâ ad Faustum statuit Bellarminus, non licere ulli mor-talium (adeoq; ne Principi quidem) appellare à judicio Papæ de Pontif. lib. 2. c. 21. Item, quod volunt acquiescendum censuræ Ecclesiasticæ utut injustę, imò etiam contra Principem ipsum latæ, & non conquerendum aut judicandum esse de sententia injusta Episcopi: Si fortè spiritus, inquit, indiscretis laboribus mentis ut nimis orando vel meditando laedat corporis sanitatem, peccabit quidem spiritus, sed non ideo poterit caro in spiritum imperium sumere; sed gemendo & fatiscendo faciet, ut spiritus remittat aliquid de nimio fervore suo. Sic etiam si forte Princeps spiritualis abutatur potestate sua injuste excommunicando temporalem Principem, vel ejus subditos sine justa causa ab obedientia ejus absolvendo, & eo modo perturbet statum Reip. Temporalis: peccabit princeps spiritualis; sed non poterit tamen Princeps Temporalis judicium sibi sumere de spiritualibus rebus, aut spiritualem Principem judicare, & multo minus de sede sua deponere cont. Bar. clajum c. 17. p. 922. (ubi observetur, quis spiritualis Princeps Bellarmino sit; nimirum non tantum Papa, sed etiam quivis Sacerdos. Nam ipsos etiam Diaconos ait Principes & praesules esse, si comparentur ad plebem lib. de Cleric. cap. 11.) Et c. 31. p. 961. contendit excommunicationi etiam injustæ acquiescendum esse à Magistratibus & subditis. Unde etiam Concilium Tridentinum statuit non licere Magistratui prospicere conquerentibus de injuriâ sibi facta per censuram Ecclesiasticam. Nefas autem sit, inquit, seculari cuilibet Magistratui prohibere Ecclesiastico judici, ne quem excommunicet, aut mandare ut latam excommunicationem revocet sub prætextu, quod contenta in præsenti decreto non sint observata, cum non ad seculares sed ad Ecclesiasticos hæc cognitio pertineat. Session. 25. cap. 3. Eam doctrinam etiam praxi confirmant Pontificii, ut notum est; & Pontifex Bullâ Cœnæ Domini horribiliter ratam esse jubet; cùm singulis annis die Jovis ante Paschatis festum excommunicationis fulmen vibrat contra Reges & Magistratus, qui ullam cognitionem causarum Ecclesiasticarum ausint suscipere. Et inquisitio Hispanica peculiariter hoc privilegio gaudet, quod Eymericus Inquisitor mortuus anno millesimo trecentesimo nonagesimo tertio, postquam officio illo per 37. annos functus esset, his verbis exprimit: Nemo potest liberare eos, qui ab inquisitione sunt apprehensi. Hæc igitur Bellarm. & aliorum Pontificiorum sententia est. Nos è contrario affirmativam tuemur, & contra Bellarm. hanc propositionē formamus: Quemadmodum Magistratus officium est operam dare, ut disciplina Ecclesiastica à Christo instituta conservetur: ita etiam ipsius est curare, ut illa legitimè à Pastoribus in consistoriis & aliis judiciis Ecclesiasticis exerceatur; efficere ne abusus circa eam committantur; impedire ne cuipiam injuria fiat in ejus administratione; & si quidem injuria alicui fiat aut facta sit à Pastoribus per exercitium seu potius abusum disciplinae Ecclesiasticae, sive in Consistorio sive in Synodo; licet ei apud Magistratum conqueri, ut Custodem ac vindicem externi ordinis in Ecclesiâ à Christo instituti: & tunc tenetur setetur[?] Magistratus ex officio prospicere conquerenti. Ubi observetur, nos non dicere licere alicui, cui injuria facta est per abusum potestatis clavium, provocare ad Magistratum seu appellare ut ad judicem superiorem; sed tantum conqueri apud eum, ut custodem & vindicem utriusque Tabulae legis. Nam non potest proprie loquendo provocari ad Magistratum à sententia potestatis clavium. Etenim disciplina Ecclesiastica non exercetur à ministris nomine Magistratus, sed Christi, qui illius author est, & à quo immediatè potestas clavium est commissa Ecclesiæ.
units.tr: That Bellarmine defends the negative is plain in itself from what has gone before. For since he holds that the magistrate has no concern with the cognizance of any ecclesiastical causes, it is clear that he cannot allow the magistrate to take care of preserving ecclesiastical discipline in its purity; and so he does not permit anyone, if he feels that an injury has been done him through ecclesiastical censure, to complain before the magistrate, nor does he grant the magistrate the right to take up the cause and provide for the complainant. Hence it follows that, from Pope Gelasius's letter to Faustus, Bellarmine determines that it is not lawful for any mortal (and so not even for a prince) to appeal from the judgment of the Pope (On the Pontiff, bk. 2, ch. 21). Likewise, they want one to submit to ecclesiastical censure however unjust, even if it is imposed against the prince himself, and that one must not complain of or judge an unjust sentence of a bishop: If perhaps the spirit, he says, through indiscreet labours of the mind, as by praying or meditating too much, harms the health of the body, the spirit will indeed sin, but the flesh cannot on that account assume command over the spirit; rather by groaning and fainting it will make the spirit give up something of its excessive fervour. So too, if perhaps a spiritual prince abuses his power by unjustly excommunicating a temporal prince, or by absolving his subjects from obedience to him without just cause, and in that way disturbs the state of the commonwealth: the spiritual prince will sin; but the temporal prince cannot on that account take upon himself judgment in spiritual matters, or judge the spiritual prince, and much less depose him from his see (Against Barclay, ch. 17, p. 922; where it should be noted who the spiritual prince is for Bellarmine: not only the Pope, but any priest whatever. For he says that even deacons are princes and prelates, if compared with the people (On Clerics, bk. ch. 11)). And in ch. 31, p. 961, he contends that magistrates and subjects must submit even to unjust excommunication. Hence the Council of Trent also laid down that the magistrate may not provide for those complaining of injury done them through ecclesiastical censure. It would be wrong, it says, for any secular magistrate to forbid an ecclesiastical judge to excommunicate anyone, or to order him to revoke an excommunication already pronounced, on the pretext that the matters contained in the present decree have not been observed, since this cognizance pertains not to secular but to ecclesiastical judges. (Session 25, ch. 3.) The Papists also confirm that doctrine in practice, as is well known; and the Pontiff in the Bull of the Lord's Supper orders it to be ratified under terrible penalties, since every year on the Thursday before Easter he hurls the thunderbolt of excommunication against kings and magistrates who dare to take up any cognizance of ecclesiastical causes. And the Spanish Inquisition enjoys this privilege in particular, which the Inquisitor Eymericus, who died in the year 1393, after he had discharged that office for thirty-seven years, expresses in these words: No one can free those who have been apprehended by the Inquisition. This, then, is the opinion of Bellarmine and the other Papists. We, on the contrary, defend the affirmative, and against Bellarmine we formulate this proposition: Just as it is the office of the magistrate to see to it that the ecclesiastical discipline instituted by Christ is preserved, so it is also his to see that it is legitimately exercised by ministers in consistories and other ecclesiastical courts; to bring it about that abuses are not committed in connection with it; to prevent any injury being done to anyone in its administration; and if indeed any injury is done, or has been done, to anyone by ministers through the exercise or rather the abuse of ecclesiastical discipline, whether in consistory or in synod, it is lawful for him to complain before the magistrate, as to the guardian and avenger of the external order instituted by Christ in the Church; and then the magistrate is bound by his office to provide for the complainant. Here it should be noted that we do not say that anyone who has been wronged through the abuse of the power of the keys may appeal to the magistrate, or appeal to him as to a superior judge; but only that he may complain before him, as guardian and avenger of both tables of the law. For, properly speaking, one cannot appeal to the magistrate from a sentence of the power of the keys. For ecclesiastical discipline is not exercised by ministers in the name of the magistrate, but of Christ, who is its author, and from whom the power of the keys was committed to the Church immediately.

units.la: Est autem hæc propositio omnium orthodoxorum Theologorum, qui hanc quæstionem tractarunt, P. Martyr. Loc. commun. class. IV. c. 13. §. 12. Addendum prætereà est, non solùm quoad ista, quæ recensui, ministros Magistratui subjici, sed etiam, ut innui superius quoad functionem. Quia si non rectè docent, nec ex ordine admiadministrent sacramenta, Magistratus est eos in ordinem redigere ac videre, ne impurè doceant, neve fabulas admisceant, neve SACRAMENTIS ABUTANTUR aut aliter ea tradant, quam Dominus jusserit. Piscator explicatione Aphorismi de Magistratu ait, Magistratus officium esse, ut operam det, quo legitimè exerceatur disciplina Ecclesiastica. Iuellus in Antapolog. post quam dixisset sacerdotum officium interalia consistere in excommunicando, absolvendo, addit Magistratus officium in eo versari, ut ab Episcopis & fieri haec curet & vero recte ac fideliter fieri c. 9. p. 488. Sibbrandus ait, Magistratus esse, efficere ut pastores disciplinam Ecclesiasticam juxta Dei verbum stringant; & addit: Magistratus defendit & tuetur eos, quàm diu eo munere recte funguntur; eosdem severè coërcet, si vel verbum falsâ Doctrinâ adulterant, aut sacramenta idololatricis ritibus contaminant, aut denique disciplinam in tyrannidem aut conscientiarum carnifici-nam nam commutant. Hoc modo prisci Imperatores Ecclesiam gubernarunt. cont. Grot. p. 121. Cl. Rivetus in Decal. p. 262. dicit, etsi Magistratus non sit praedicare verbum, administrare sacramenta, Ecclesiasticam disciplinam exercere, tamen debere eum curare, ut isthaec fiant, sicut oportet ab iis, quos ad eadem Deus vocavit. Omnium apertissime Beza magnum illud lumen Ecclesiae, & summus assertor consistoriorum contra Thomam Erastum Professorem Heidelbergensem scribit: Cùm etiam à recte constituto consistorio possit reis delatis injuria fieri; in angustioribus territoriis citra ullam ordinis Ecclesiastici violationem Christianus Magistratus, ut tabulae utriusque & Ecclesiasticae εὐλαξίας custos & vindex prospicere potest conquerentibus. Cll. Proff. Leydenses in eadem sunt sententia & approbant illam ingenuam confessionem Bezae. Nam disputat. 48. th. 16. dicunt de disciplinâ Ecclesiasticâ: Hanc spiritualem potestatem à Christiani Magigistratus inspectione tanquam utriusque tabulæ custode non eximimus. Et postquam dixissent, hanc potestatem per provocationem aut appellationem proprie dictam non posse ad Magistratus aut Principum tribunal deferri, addunt: interim tamen non diffitemur verum esse, quod Bezæ adversum Erastum fatetur; cum etiam a recte constituto consistorio possit reis delatis injuria fieri; in angustioribus territoriis citra ullam &c. & allegant omnia illa verba Bezæ modo a nobis citata. Item disputat. de Magistratu th. 47. proprie jus est penes Pastores disciplinam Ecclesiasticam, unà cum suo presbyterio ex fidei & sacræ doctrinæ analogia decernendi: Magistratus vero penes quem est summa imperii potestas disciplinam illam aut præsens approbare, aut absens examinare potest, & si quid in eâ jure desideretur, à Pastoribus exigere, ut illud ex verbi Dei analogia addatur vel emendetur. Cl. Walæus p. 48. etiam allegat & approbat sententiam ac verba Bezæ modo à nobis allegata. Et p. 23. libenter inquit, fatemur summum Ma-gistratum curam gerere debere, ne disciplina Ecclesiastica in abusum trahatur, quemadmodum in Papatu contigit: & p. 43. diximus superius & patebit etiam in sequentibus satis ex verbo Dei; officium supremorum Magistratuum esse curam gerere totius cultus divini & consequenter quoque operam dare, ut haec potestas spiritualis, (censura Ecclesiastica) non in abusum trahatur, quemadmodum notorie in Papatu contigit. Et. p.44. ait inter caetera, in talibus casibus (quos ipse extraordinarios recte vocat si cogitetur, quando alicui injuria fit per disciplinam Ecclesiasticam, id extra seu potius contra ordinem à Christo in-stitutum fieri) Magistratus tanquam nutricios Ecclesiæ posse cognitionem suscipere causarum & rationum excommunicationis, aut antequam ea sit instituta, aut postquam facta sit, nec posse eos, qui Ecclesiæ præsunt recusare iis redditionem rationis facti sui; & confirmat id ex
units.tr: This proposition is held by all the orthodox theologians who have treated this question, P. Martyr, Loc. commun. class. IV, c. 13, §12. It must moreover be added that ministers are subject to the magistrate not only in those matters I have listed, but also, as I hinted above, in respect of their function. For if they do not teach rightly, or do not administer the sacraments in good order, the magistrate must bring them into order and see that they do not teach impurely, nor mix in fables, nor abuse the SACRAMENTS, nor hand them on otherwise than the Lord has commanded. Piscator, in his explanation of the Aphorism on the Magistrate, says that the office of the magistrate is to take care that ecclesiastical discipline is lawfully exercised. Jewel, in the Apologia, after saying that the office of priests consists among other things in excommunicating and absolving, adds: the office of the magistrate lies in seeing to it that these things are done by the bishops, and done rightly and faithfully, c. 9, p. 488. Sibbrandus says that the magistrate is to ensure that the ministers enforce ecclesiastical discipline according to the Word of God; and he adds: the magistrate defends and protects them as long as they discharge that office rightly; he severely restrains them if they corrupt the Word with false doctrine, or contaminate the sacraments with idolatrous rites, or finally turn discipline into tyranny or a torturer of consciences. In this way the ancient emperors governed the Church. Against Grotius, p. 121. The distinguished Rivetus, in the Decalogue, p. 262, says: although it is not the magistrate's task to preach the Word, administer the sacraments, or exercise ecclesiastical discipline, nevertheless he must take care that these things are done as they ought to be by those whom God has called to them. Most openly of all, Beza, that great light of the Church and chief champion of consistories against Thomas Erastus, professor at Heidelberg, writes: Since injustice can also be done to accused persons by a rightly constituted consistory, in smaller territories, without any violation of ecclesiastical order, the Christian magistrate, as guardian and avenger of both tables and of ecclesiastical good order, can provide for those who complain. The distinguished professors of Leiden are of the same opinion and approve that frank confession of Beza. For in Disputation 48, thesis 16, they say of ecclesiastical discipline: We do not exempt this spiritual power from the oversight of the Christian magistrate as guardian of both tables. And after saying that this power cannot be referred to the tribunal of magistrates or princes by provocation or appeal properly so called, they add: Meanwhile, however, we do not deny that what Beza affirms against Erastus is true, since injustice can also be done to accused persons by a rightly constituted consistory, and so on, and they cite all those words of Beza just quoted. Likewise, in the Disputation on the Magistrate, thesis 47: Properly, the right to decree ecclesiastical discipline, together with their presbytery, from the analogy of faith and sacred doctrine lies with the pastors. The magistrate, in whose hands is the supreme power of rule, can either approve that discipline when present or examine it when absent, and if anything in it is lacking in law, he can require the pastors to add or amend it according to the analogy of God's Word. The distinguished Walaeus, p. 48, also cites and approves the opinion and words of Beza just quoted. And on p. 23 he says: We gladly confess that the supreme magistrate ought to take care that ecclesiastical discipline is not drawn into abuse, as happened in Papacy. And on p. 43: We have said above, and it will be clear enough from what follows from the Word of God, that the office of supreme magistrates is to take care of the whole of divine worship and consequently also to see to it that this spiritual power (ecclesiastical censure) is not drawn into abuse, as notoriously happened in Papacy. And on p. 44 he says, among other things, that in such cases (which he rightly calls extraordinary, when someone is wronged by ecclesiastical discipline, which happens outside or rather against the order instituted by Christ), magistrates, as nursing fathers of the Church, may take up the cognizance of the causes and grounds of excommunication, either before it has been instituted or after it has been carried out, and those who preside over the Church cannot refuse them an account of their action; and he confirms this from

units.la: 1. Pet. 3. Quod si superiores videant, inquit, actum esse contra ordinem: ipsorum officium est efficere, ut resumatur negotium in conventibus Ecclesiasticis, imò etiam impedire exequutionem; quemadmodum Constantinus & alii boni Imperatores interdum ita egerunt, qui essecerunt ut causæ Athanasii & aliorum Orthodoxorum Doctorum, injustè condemnatorum à Concilio, resumerentur, & in integrum restituerentur per alias Synodos, vide Socrat. lib. 2. Quemadmodum etiam Principes Christiani post cognitionem causæ tuiti sunt (prout hodieque faciunt) primos reformatores Ecclesiæ Christi contra excommunicationem Papæ & Concilii Tridentini. Et p. 37. ait. in tali casu Magistratui competere tantum illam judicaturam, quam verbum Dei ipsi attribuit, ad impediendam talem punitionem spiritualem, si impertinens sit & verbo Dei repugnet &c. & Magistratus Christianus nunquam secundum ordinem aliud jus sibi attribuit. Quod amplius est cum Beza territoriorum exigui distridistrictus[?] tantùm mentionem sece-rit; Cl. Walæus id extendit ad Magistratus supremos majorum etiamterritoriorum ac regionum; item quod Beza dixerat de Consistoriis, ipse extendit ad conventus Ecclesiasticos etiam majores imò supremos, seu Synodos: Eadem ratio, inquit, locum debet habere etiam respectu Magistratuum supremorum, qui majoribus territoriis & regionibus imperant, nec non respectu maximorum seu supremorum conventuum Ecclesiasticorum, qui in illis quoq; regionibus sunt. Nam etiamsi co-gnitio & judicium talium conventuum majorum minus suspectum esse debeat, quàm minorum congregationum; nihilominus tamen similes errores ab iis committi possunt, quemadmodum experientia Synodorü & Conciliorum monstravit, quorum injustis actionibus possunt ac debent resistere supremi Magistratus ex obligatione officii sui. Idem vir Clarissimus p. 141. citat pro suæ sententiæ declaratione Robertum Burhillum
units.tr: 1 Pet. 3. If superiors see, he says, that something has been done contrary to order, it is their office to bring it about that the matter is taken up again in ecclesiastical assemblies, or even to prevent its execution; as Constantine and other good emperors sometimes did, who saw to it that the causes of Athanasius and other orthodox teachers, unjustly condemned by a council, were taken up again and restored in full by other synods; see Socrates, book 2. Likewise Christian princes, after examining the case, have defended (as they do even today) the first reformers of the Church of Christ against the excommunication of the Pope and the Council of Trent. And on p. 37 he says that in such a case the magistrate has only that jurisdiction which the Word of God gives him, to prevent such spiritual punishment if it is irrelevant and repugnant to the Word of God, etc.; and a Christian magistrate never claims for himself any other right according to the order. What is more, whereas Beza mentioned only small territories, the distinguished Walaeus extends this to the supreme magistrates of larger territories and regions; and what Beza said of consistories he himself extends to ecclesiastical assemblies, even the larger and indeed the supreme ones, that is, synods: The same reasoning, he says, must hold also with respect to the supreme magistrates who rule over larger territories and regions, and likewise with respect to the greatest or supreme ecclesiastical assemblies which exist in those regions too. For even if the examination and judgment of such larger assemblies ought to be less suspect than those of smaller congregations, nevertheless similar errors can be committed by them, as the experience of synods and councils has shown, and the supreme magistrates can and ought to resist their unjust actions from the obligation of their office. The same most distinguished man, on p. 141, cites in support of his opinion Robert Burhill,

units.la: Q[?] marks the opening of the quaestio title in the running head; the first word of the page is cut at the top edge and only partly legible. Theologum Anglum & probat quod dicit cont. Becanum &c. c. 10. Magistratum supremum non debere auctoritatem suam commodare vanis, intolerabilibus, noxiis decretis Ecclesiæ, & cogere quenquam ad iis obediendum: nec etiam debere permittere ut innocentia cujusquam opprimatur, si aliquis, penes quem Ecclesiasticæ censuræ sunt, convertat suam potestatem non ad ædificationem, sed ad destructionem. Similiter Sibbrandus Lubbertus dicit à Synodi sententiâ ad supremum Magistratum provocari (ita enim loquitur) posse: Si tamen, inquit, p. 151. quod est humanum in judicando erraverunt Patres in Synodi congregatione, video tres vias quas in hoc casu sequi possumus. Una est provocatio à Synodo ad summum Magistratum. Hanc tenuit (ait quidem Sibbrandus) Apostolus Act. 25.6. Ad tribunal Cæsaris sto, ibi me oportet judicari. Altera est, ut Iesus petat à supremo Magistratu, ut omnia ad tempus eo loco relinquere vellit, quo ante latam sententiam erant. Hanc tenuit Leo Epist. 35. &c. Tertia est, ut quis injuriam sibi factam patienter ferat. Ubi quicquid sit de exemplo Pauli (ex quo non posse inferri appellationem proprie sic dictam ad Magistratum a Censura Ecclesiastica inter alia monet Cl. Walæus p. 46. 47.) constat Sibbrandum cum praecedentib. Theologis omnibus in re consentire. Professus autem erat p. 12. se sincere Ecclesiarum Reformatarum sententiam explicaturum. Theologis Reformatis calculum suum addit-Sapientissimus Rex Jacobus M. Britan. cujus verba ex scripto ipsius ultimo contra Cardinalem Perronium Cl. Walæus hæc laudat p. 153. quibus Rex dicit Imperatores pios cognitionem decretorum & canonum Conciliorum ac disciplinæ Ecclesiasticæ suscipere solitos fuisse &c. ut viderent an in consultationibus Episcoporum (qui æquè, inquit, obnoxii [?] sunt ambitioni atque alii homines) nihil esset contra fidelitatem Imperatori debitam, nec contra Reip. tranquillitatem, nec contra Decreta Conciliorum præcedentium. Cæterū quemadmodum in omnibus aliis negotiis Ecclesiasticis, ita etiam in hoc nihil iniquè, temerè, leviter, malitiosè, imprudenter à quoquam est agen-dum, prout rectè etiam monet Cl. Walæus p. 44. ne fraus fiat ordini à Christo instituto, & disciplinæ Ecclesiasticæ sub prætextu injuriæ acceptæ illudatur. Quod qua ratione caveri & quomodo in eum finem Magistratus prospicere secundum doctrinam verbi divini receptam in Ecclesiis Reformatis debeat conquerentibus, jam exponere possemus. Scd hæ paucæ pagellæ id non patiuntur.
units.tr: English theologian, and proves by what he says against Becanus, etc., c. 10, that the supreme magistrate ought not to lend his authority to vain, intolerable, and hurtful decrees of the Church, nor compel anyone to obey them; nor should he permit the innocence of anyone to be oppressed if someone who holds ecclesiastical censures turns his power not to edification but to destruction. Similarly, Sibbrandus Lubbertus says that an appeal (for so he puts it) can be made from the sentence of a synod to the supreme magistrate: If, however, the fathers in the assembly of the synod have erred in judging, as is human, I see three ways we may follow in this case. One is appeal from the synod to the supreme magistrate. This was followed by the Apostle (Act. 25.6), "I stand at Caesar's tribunal; there I must be judged." The second is that one should ask the supreme magistrate to have everything left, for the time being, in the state it was in before the sentence was passed. This was followed by Leo, Epist. 35, etc. The third is that someone bear the injury done to him with patience. Whatever the case with Paul's example (from which, as Walaeus, p. 46–47, among other things warns, no appeal properly so called to the magistrate from ecclesiastical censure can be inferred), it is clear that Sibbrandus agrees on the matter with all the theologians before him. He had professed on p. 12 that he would set out sincerely the opinion of the Reformed Churches. He adds his vote to the Reformed theologians: the most wise King James of Great Britain, whose words Walaeus praises from the King's last writing against Cardinal Perron, p. 153, in which the King says that pious emperors were accustomed to take up the cognizance of the decrees and canons of councils and of ecclesiastical discipline, so that they might see whether in the deliberations of bishops (who, he says, are as liable to ambition as other men) there was anything against the fidelity owed to the emperor, or against the tranquillity of the commonwealth, or against the decrees of earlier councils. But just as in all other ecclesiastical matters, so in this one nothing is to be done by anyone unjustly, rashly, lightly, maliciously, or imprudently, as Walaeus rightly warns on p. 44, lest fraud be done to the order instituted by Christ and ecclesiastical discipline be mocked under the pretext of an injury received. How this is to be guarded against, and in what way the magistrate ought, according to the doctrine of God's Word received in the Reformed Churches, to provide for those who complain, we could now set forth. But these few pages do not allow it.

units.la: Confirmationem hujus propositionis quod attinet; nobis argumenta non panca ex verbo Dei & praxi Ecclesiæ veteris suppetunt: Sed inpræsentiarum ob instituti nostri brevitatem sufficiet argumentum Bezæ & Cll. Prof. Leydens. quod in eo consistit, quòd Magistratus sit custos & vindex utriusque tabulæ & σὺλαξίας Ecclesiasticæ. Accedat exemplum commendatum à Spiritu Sancto, Principum scilicet Judæ, qui Jeremiam è manibus & violentiâ Sacerdotum eripuerunt Jerem. 26.16. &c. quod est argumentum Cl. Walæi p. 46. Denique si impunè liceret ministris abuti disciplinâ Ecclesiasticâ, ita ut non coërcerentur à Magistratu; certè nec Magistratus ipse, nec alius honestus vir tutus esse posset & securus officiorum & honorum suorum; maximè si velint imitari praxin Papatus, in quo privatio jurisdictionis & officiorum eorum etiam, quæ non pendent ab Electione Ecclesiæ, pari passu ambulant. Confirmat hoc argumentum praxis ejusdem papatus. Si quis dicat non esse metuendum, ne orthodoxi pastores alicui injuriam faciant: is meminerit Bezam & alios Theologos, quos modo laudavimus fateri, alicui injuriam etiam à legitimè constituto consistorio fieri posse. Meminerit etiam, ut Pareus recte observat Rom. 13. p. 1088. nō discipulorum Christi, sed Iudæorum vocem esse: Nisi hic maleficus esset, nō tibi tradidissemus eum. Nec puto quenquam Reformatum Theologum hoc bonâ conscientiâ dicere posse: cum nec ipse Pontifex Romanus, qui tamen sibi infallibilitatem in judicio de rebus fidei tribuit, adeo impudens sit, ut audeat dicere se in quæstionibus facti errare non posse.
units.tr: As for the confirmation of this proposition, we have no small number of arguments from the Word of God and the practice of the ancient Church. For the sake of brevity in our present purpose, the argument of Beza and of the learned professors of Leiden will suffice, namely that the magistrate is the guardian and defender of both tables of the law and of ecclesiastical discipline [σύλαξις]. Let the example commended by the Holy Spirit be added, that of the princes of Judah, who snatched Jeremiah from the hands and violence of the priests (Jer. 26:16 ff.), which is the argument of the learned Walaeus, p. 46. Finally, if ministers could abuse ecclesiastical discipline with impunity and were not restrained by the magistrate, then neither the magistrate himself nor any other honest man could be safe and secure in his office and honours. This is especially so if they wished to imitate the practice of the Papacy, in which the removal of jurisdiction and of offices, even of those that do not depend on the election of the Church, goes hand in hand. The practice of that same Papacy confirms this argument. If anyone says that there is no need to fear that orthodox ministers will do injury to anyone, let him remember that Beza and the other theologians we have just cited admit that an injury can also be done to someone by a lawfully constituted consistory. Let him remember too, as Pareus rightly observes on Romans 13 (p. 1088), that these are not the words of the disciples of Christ but of the Jews: "Unless this man were an evildoer, we would not have delivered him to you." Nor do I think any Reformed theologian can say this with a good conscience, since even the Roman Pontiff, who nonetheless ascribes to himself infallibility in judging matters of faith, is not so shameless as to dare to say that he cannot err in questions of fact.

units.la: Nec potest objicere aliquis: sic violari disciplinam Ecclesiasticam; Nam ut modo vidimus, Beza. Cll. Proff. Leydd. Cl. Walæus dicunt id fieri citra ullam violationem ordinis Ecclesiastici. At censura Ecclesiastica, inquiet aliquis, à Christo est instituta immediatè Matth. 16. & 18 Respondeo cum Hieronymo in Matth. 16. Istum locum Episcopi & Presbyteri non intelligentes, aliquid sibi de Pharisæorum assumunt superciliio, ut vel damnent innocentes; tes; vel solvere se noxios arbitrentur, cùm apud Deum non sententia sacerdotum, sed reorum vita quæratur. Quem locum citat Sibbrandus p. 152. & tanquam scitè dictum ab Hieronymo laudat, postquam premisisset: Si judicium est de persona ut vel aliquē ligent, vel ligatum solvant, sciendum est Ecclesiæ judicium habere momentum, si cum veritate congruit, neque esse pertimescendum, si ab illa discrepet. Ita Sibbrandus. Ratio est: quia tantum usus disciplinæ non autem abusus à Christo est institutus, de quo hic quæstio est. Deinde ita arguere est nihil aliud quam Magistratum à gubernatione & curâ rerum Ecclesiasticarum planè velle excludere, & dicere eas ad illum non pertinere aliter, quàm ut defensor & exequutor Ecclesiæ sit. Nam prædicatio verbi & administratio Sacramentorum etiam est immediate à Christo instituta. Si igitur non licet Magistratui curam gerere, ut disciplina Ecclesiastica rectè & non malè exerceatur; ideò quod immediatè à Christo sit; certè nec licebit Magistratui curam gerere, & imperare ministris ut officio rectè fungantur circa prædicationem verbi & administrationem Sacramentorum, nec eoscoërcere, quando officium suum non faciunt, aut non rectè faciunt. Denique ex inde aliud nihil sequitur, quàm Magistratum ipsum non posse exercere disciplinam Ecclesiasticam, seu ligare & solvere, retinere vel dimittere peccata: item ad eum non posse instituì[?] appellationem propriè sic dictam à potestate clavium: non autem sequitur ad Magistratum non pertinere curam & directionem ordinis externi circa eam, ut ea rectè & sine abusu exerceatur.
units.tr: Nor can anyone object: "In this way ecclesiastical discipline is violated." For, as we have just seen, Beza, the learned professors of Leiden and Walaeus say that this happens without any violation of the ecclesiastical order. But ecclesiastical censure, someone will say, was instituted immediately by Christ (Matt. 16 and 18). I answer with Jerome on Matthew 16: "Bishops and presbyters, not understanding this passage, assume for themselves something of Pharisaic haughtiness, so that they either condemn the innocent or think that they release the guilty, whereas before God the judgement of priests is not what is sought, but the life of the accused." Sibrandus cites this passage on p. 152 and praises it as a saying well put by Jerome, after first setting out: "If the judgement concerns a person, so that they bind someone or release one who is bound, it must be understood that the judgement of the Church has weight if it agrees with the truth, and that it is not to be feared if it departs from it." So Sibrandus. The reason is this: it is only the use of discipline, not its abuse, that Christ instituted, and that is what is at issue here. Furthermore, to argue thus is nothing other than to wish to exclude the magistrate entirely from the government and care of ecclesiastical affairs, and to say that they pertain to him only in the sense that he is the defender and executor of the Church. For the preaching of the Word and the administration of the sacraments are also instituted immediately by Christ. If therefore the magistrate may not take care that ecclesiastical discipline is exercised rightly and not wrongly, on the ground that it is immediately from Christ, then certainly the magistrate may not take care to direct ministers to fulfil their office rightly in preaching the Word and administering the sacraments, nor restrain them when they do not, or do not rightly, perform their duty. Finally, nothing else follows from this except that the magistrate himself cannot exercise ecclesiastical discipline, that is, bind and loose, retain or remit sins, and that an appeal, properly so called, cannot be instituted to him by the power of the keys. But it does not follow that the magistrate has no concern for and direction of the external order connected with that discipline, so that it is exercised rightly and without abuse.

units.la: Nec etiam potest obiici[?]: per hanc doctrinam enervari aut everti auctoritatem consistoriorum. Nam si id locum habet, certè Magistratui abstinendum erit etiam à cæteris partibus officii sui circa res Ecclesiæ, quò ita auctoritas Ecclesiasticorum non evertatur. Et verò auctoritas Episcoporum & ministrorum Ecclesiæ non in eo consistit, ut impunè nocere, possint & contra officium suum praevaricari vel in disciplinâ Ecclesiasticâ, vel in aliis actionibus sacris: sed potius male agendo ipsi evertunt, prostituunt ac perdunt auctoritatem suam, ac res suas; ut testatur experientia Papatus. Tertiò tantum abest, ut hac doctrina labefactetur authoritas Pastorum, ut potius revera stabiliatur.
units.tr: Nor can it be objected that by this doctrine the authority of the consistories is weakened or overthrown. For if that objection held, the magistrate would certainly have to abstain also from the other parts of his office concerning the affairs of the Church, so that the authority of the ecclesiastics would not be overthrown. Indeed, the authority of bishops and ministers of the Church does not consist in their being able to do harm with impunity and to act contrary to their office, either in ecclesiastical discipline or in other sacred actions. Rather, by acting badly they themselves overthrow, prostitute and destroy their own authority and their own affairs, as the experience of the Papacy bears witness. Thirdly, the authority of the pastors is so far from being weakened by this doctrine that it is, in truth, rather established.

units.la: Nam primo videntes hac ratione se Magistratum habere, qui de jure divino inspector & judex sit actionum suarum, etiam in hac parte prudenter agent & cavebunt sibi ne cuiquam injuriam faciant, praetextu disciplinæ Ecclesiasticæ. Dubium autem non est, quin authoritas mini-sterii integra maneat quando pastores officio suo recte funguntur. Quem-admodum è contrario contemptum sibi attrahunt, quando secus faciunt. Quâ de re incomparabilis servus Dei Calvinus in aureo tractatu de Scandalis graviter conqueritur p. 92.
units.tr: For, first, seeing that by this arrangement they have a magistrate who, by divine right, oversees and judges their actions, they will act prudently even in this part and will take care not to do injury to anyone under the pretext of ecclesiastical discipline. There is no doubt that the authority of the ministry remains whole when pastors perform their office rightly, just as, on the contrary, they bring contempt upon themselves when they act otherwise. On this matter the incomparable servant of God, Calvin, complains earnestly in his golden treatise On Scandals, p. 92.

units.la: Sed aliud est, inquit, Ecclesiæ ulcus magis deplorandum, quòd Pastores, ipsi, inquam Pastores, qui suggestum, h.e. sacrum Christi tribunal eâ lege conscendunt, ut vitæ puritate præ aliis omnibus excellant; interdum sunt turpissima vel nequitiæ, vel malorum aliorum exempla. Ita fit ut nihilo plus fidei ac gravitatis obtineant eorum conciones, quàm[?] si fabulam in scenâ ageret histrio. Et tales scilicet contemtui se esse apud plebem, aut etiam ludibrii causâ digito se monstrari conqueruntur.
units.tr: "But there is another ulcer of the Church, more to be deplored," he says, "namely that the pastors themselves, yes, the pastors, who mount the pulpit, that is, the sacred tribunal of Christ, on the condition that they excel all others in purity of life, are sometimes the most disgraceful examples either of wickedness or of other vices. So it comes about that their sermons carry no more faith or weight than if an actor were performing a play on the stage. And such men, of course, complain that they are despised by the common people, or even that they are pointed at with the finger for mockery."

units.la: Ego autem potiùs vulgi miror patientiam, quòd non eos luto & stercoribus mulieres & pueri operiunt. Ministerii dignitatem extollunt plenis buccis; at illis non venit in mentem non haberi suum ministerio honorem, quia ipsum suâ turpitudine conspurcant. Nam sicuti vere olim à quodam dictum est: ut ameris amabilis esto; ita morum gravitate & san-
units.tr: "But I rather marvel at the patience of the common people, that women and children do not cover them with mud and dung. They extol the dignity of the ministry with full cheeks, but it does not occur to them that the honour of their ministry is not held in regard, because they defile it by their own baseness. For, as was truly said long ago by someone: 'Be lovable, that you may be loved'; so those who wish to be held in esteem must acquire reverence for themselves by the gravity and holiness of their morals.

units.la: ctimoniâ[?] moniâ reverentiam sibi acquirant oportet, qui in precio haberi volunt. Atque utinam tali hominum colluvie exonerari purgarique posset Ecclesia &c. Ita Calvinus, qui inter alia scandala, quae impediunt cursum verae Religionis; hoc vel maximum esse contendit.
units.tr: And would that the Church could be unburdened and purged of such a rabble of men, etc." So Calvin, who contends that among the other scandals which hinder the course of true religion, this is the greatest of all.

units.la: Deinde etiam aliâ ratione stabilitur auctoritas ministrorum per hanc doctrinam. Nam ad quam potestatem pertinet cura defendendi eos, quibus injuria facta est per abusum disciplinae Ecclesiasticę; monendi ministros, ut ab injuriâ desistant, ac si nolint, utendi potestare [?] suâ coercitivâ adversum ipsos: ad eandem potestatem pertinet etiam cura defendendi disciplinae Ecclesiasticae verum & legitimum usum. Quae si quis malitiosè & superbè se opponat disciplinae Ecclesiasticę juste & sine abusu exercitae; & adeò temerarius sit, ut apud Magistratum conqueri audeat; Magistratus est re bene co-gnitâ mandare [?] ipsi, ut pareat consi[?]storio, & hortari ministros ut pergant procedere contra eum. Si necdum parere velit, Magistratus est pro exigentia rei, & qualitate delicti etiam civili animadversione vindicare non solùm violationem ordinis à Christo instituti, sed etiam inobedientiam, quâ adversus Magistratus mandatum usus est.
units.tr: Next, the authority of ministers is also established by this doctrine on another ground. For the power to which belongs the care of defending those who have been wronged through the abuse of ecclesiastical discipline, of admonishing ministers to desist from injury, and, if they will not, of using its coercive power against them, is the same power to which belongs also the care of defending the true and lawful use of ecclesiastical discipline. If anyone maliciously and arrogantly opposes ecclesiastical discipline exercised justly and without abuse, and is so rash that he dares to complain before the magistrate, the magistrate, once the matter is well understood, is to order him to obey the consistory, and to exhort the ministers to proceed against him. If he still refuses to obey, the magistrate, according to the demands of the case and the nature of the offence, is to punish with civil penalty not only the violation of the order instituted by Christ but also the disobedience by which he has defied the magistrate's command.

units.la: Ad Quaest. septimam.
units.tr: To the seventh question.

units.la: Etiamsi is cui notoria ab Ecclesiastico judicio fit injuria, vel qui ab illo tyrannidem patitur, implorare possit Magistratus opem, cujus est quemlibet à quâlibet injuriâ vindicare, consi-derandum tamen, an ad quaestionem illam, sine limitatione & explicatione, affirmative respondere debeat. Hoc enim si fiat, jam statuendum erit Magistratum debere adsidere omnibus conventibus Ecclesiasticis, ibique observare num ministri Ecclesiae disciplinâ Ecclesiasticâ ritè utantur, quemadmodum vel Domini famulis, vel parentes liberis suis adsident ut eorum facta observent. Ubinam hoc docet verbum Dei, aut permittit praxis Ecclesiae?
units.tr: Even if the one to whom an injury is manifestly done by an ecclesiastical judgment, or who suffers tyranny from it, can implore the help of the magistrate, whose duty it is to defend anyone from any injury, we must consider whether he ought to answer that question affirmatively, without limitation or explanation. For if this be done, it will have to be decided that the magistrate must sit in on all ecclesiastical assemblies and there observe whether the ministers of the Church properly use ecclesiastical discipline, just as masters sit in on their servants, or parents on their children, to watch what they do. Where does the Word of God teach this, or where does the practice of the Church permit it?

units.la: Alia est ratio conciliorum, in quibus causa religionis, & doctrina publica tractatur, quam Magistratus tueri debet & conservare, & quae, vel vel tranquillitatem, vel commorationem Reip. secum trahit: alia vero privatorum consistoriorum, in quibus causa & delicta privata tractatur, ad singulorum conscientias instruendas.
units.tr: The purpose of councils is one thing, in which the cause of religion and public doctrine is treated, and which the magistrate ought to protect and preserve, and which brings with it either the tranquillity or the disturbance of the commonwealth; but the purpose of private consistories is another, in which private causes and offences are treated, in order to instruct the consciences of individuals.

units.la: Resp.
units.tr: Answer.

units.la: Explicavi illam Quæstionem, quantum quidem brevitas permittebat & ratio instituti postulabat. Quò inter alia facit, quod (ut cætera quæ ad illius theseos explicationem protuli omittam) dixi in hoc negotio nihil iniquè, temerè, leviter, maliciosè, à quoquam (& sic nec à Magistratu) esse faciendum, ne fraus fiat ordini à Christo institu-to, & disciplinæ Ecclesiasticæ illudatur &c.
units.tr: I have explained that question as far as brevity allowed and the plan of this work required. Among other things it bears on this, that (to omit the rest of what I brought forward to explain that thesis) I said that in this business nothing is to be done unjustly, rashly, lightly, maliciously by anyone (and so not by the magistrate either), lest a fraud be committed against the order instituted by Christ, and church discipline be mocked, and so on.

units.la: Nec ex meathesi id quod in consideratione ponitur, sequitur magis, quàm exthesi eadem sine ulteriore declaratione à Cl. Proff. Leyd. in Synopsi, & à cæteris Theologis omnibus à me ibi adductis id sequitur. Nam non est necessum, ut ob eam causam Magistratus conventibus omnibus Ecclesiasticis adsideat. Ratio est: potest enim disciplinam Ecclesiasticam etiam absens examinare, & si quid in eâ jure desideretur, à Pastoribus exigere, ut illud ex verbi Dei analogiâ addatur vel emendetur, ut loquuntur DD. Proff de hac re verbis à me citatis, quorum ipsorum verborum allega-tio sufficere debebat ad explicationem, &c. & ad solutionem objectionis & Quaestionis illius. Adeoq; si injuria palpabilis & planè notoria alicui illata sit, ut in Quaestionibus facti item vitae & morum evidentior esse res solet, quàm in Quaestionibus fidei, Magistratus immediatè potest prospicere conquerenti, ut factum à Principibus Iudæ;si autem injuria non sit adeò notoria, ut in Quaestionibus fidei contingere solet; debet Maigstratus operam dare, ut à majore conventu Ecclesiastico seu Synodo legitimâ res decidatur, prout in vetere Ecclesiâ secundum verbum Dei pii imperatores fecere, & Reformati Doctores semper contra Ex-communicationem Papalem contenderunt ac petierunt. Hæc omnia perspicuè & solidè pluribus deducere & ostendere possem. Ceterùm an Magistratui liceat adsidere Consistorio, videatur Synod. Dord. Constit. Eccles. art. 37. & D. D. Proff, Leydd. loco citato.
units.tr: Nor does what is put forward in the consideration follow from my thesis any more than it follows from the same thesis set out (exthesis) without further explanation by the distinguished professors of Leiden in the Synopsis, and from all the other theologians I cited there. For it is not necessary that, for this reason, the magistrate sit in on all ecclesiastical assemblies. The reason is this: for he can examine ecclesiastical discipline even when absent, and if anything is rightly lacking in it, he can require the ministers to add or amend it according to the analogy of the Word of God, as the learned professors put it in the words I cited on this matter. The citation of those very words ought to have been enough for the explanation, and for the solution of the objection and of that question. Therefore, if a palpable and plainly notorious injury has been done to someone, as the matter is usually more evident in questions of fact, of life and of morals than in questions of faith, the magistrate can immediately come to the aid of the complainant, as the princes of Judah did. But if the injury is not so notorious, as usually happens in questions of faith, the magistrate ought to take care that the matter be decided by a larger ecclesiastical assembly or a lawful synod, just as in the ancient Church the pious emperors did according to the Word of God, and the Reformed doctors always contended and sought against the Papal excommunication. I could set out and demonstrate all of this more fully, clearly and soundly. As for whether the magistrate may sit in on the consistory, let the Synod of Dort, Church Constitution, art. 37, and the learned professors of Leiden, in the place cited, be consulted.

units.la: QUÆST. VIII. An Magistratus habeat potestatem leges ferendi Ecclesiasticas?
units.tr: QUESTION VIII. Whether the magistrate has the power to enact ecclesiastical laws?

units.la: BEllarminus negat, & Magistratui tantum tribuit potestatem leges ferendi civiles, solis autem Ecclesiasticis tribuit potestatem leges ferendi Ecclesiasticas. Sicut, inquit, inter alia, Reges possunt condere leges civiles; ita Pontifex seu Episcopus potest condere leges Ecclesiasticas lib. 4. de Pontif. c. 15. p. 857. vide & c. 16. 17. 18. 19. 20. 21. Nos affirmamus & contra Bellarminum hanc propositionem formamus: Magistratus habet potestatem leges ferendi Ecclesiasticas verbo Dei non repugnantes, tam circa personas, quam circa res Ecclesiasticas. Haec propositio etiam est doctrina Ecclesiae Reformatae. Vide inter alios P. Martyrem in 1. Sam. 14. Wittackerum cont. IV. Q. 7. Junium controvers. III. lib. 4. & controv. V. lib. 3. Pareum Comment. Rom. Dub. 5. CII[?]. Prof Leydd. Cens. Confess. Remonstr- c. 25. §. 34.
