Eosdem in Synopsi Disput. de Magistratu th. 46. ubi dicunt Magistratum circa res Ecclesiasticas suo quoque imperio praescribere nonnulla posse: loquuntur autem de rebus de quibus præceptum speciale divinum nullum est,nimirum de ritibus in se indifferentibus, seu iis, quæ ad externum Ecclesiæ ordinem pertinent Cl. Rivetum in decal: p. 267. 168. Alsted. in Supplem. Chamierii, Amesium Medull. lib. 2. c. 17. Ubi observandum 1. ne ferat leges circa ceremonias, quę cum periculo Idololatriæ sint conjunctæ,item ne multitudine rituum talium obruat Ecclesiam Christianam, ut in Papatu factum. Deinde tenendum; Magistratum leges Ecclesiasticas ferre posse, non tantùm ut ministrum Dei, sed etiam respectu hominum cum imperio proprio ac potestate coactiuâ temporali; nec pendere eum in illis ferendis à potestate aliquâ humanâ superiore; consequenter etiam non opus habere confirmatione aliena (quamvis consilium prudentiû, piorum & peritorum Doctorum Ecclesiæ recte adhibeat) & denique obligari conscientias illis legibus et-iam iam extra casum scandali & contemptus ob mandatum generale Dei de obedientiâ debita Magistratui Rom. 13. & alibi. Ex quibus per se sequitur eas esse propriè sic dictas leges, quæ in Ecclesiasticis à Magistratu feruntur. Denique observandum est quod Cl. Rivetus monet, circa leges quæ ipsos Ecclesiasticos spectant: Hæ, inquit, ita à Principibus[?] pendent, ut sæpe etiam INVITIS ipsis ministris Ecclesiæ obtrudantur; quæ si iniquæ sint & onerosæ, conscientiam tamen non lædunt, obligant nihilominus: si justæ & necessariæ, iis etiam est obtemperandum, etiamsi aliquam notam inurant, sed quam mali mores, quibus obviam eundum fuit, attraxerint: p. 268. Et exempli loco affert illam legem, cujus Hieronymus alicubi meminit, quâ Christiani Imperatores caverunt, ne Testamenta caperent Ecclesiastici; ubi dicit se de lege non conqueri tanquam injustâ, sed de eo tantum, quod eam suis factis meruissent. Hæc & similes leges quin latæ fuerint invitis & dolentibus Ecclesiasticis dubium non est vel ex iis verbis Hieronymi; Nam mali dolent ob cohibitam malitiam; boni ob scandalum datum & ob notam aspersam ministerio per malas aliorum actiones. Quas quidem in causa fuisse tot legum ab Impp. latarum citca personas Ecclesiasticas, recte observat Parœus Comment. Rom. c. 13. p. 1097 ex Novell. 137. ubi Imperator præfatur se cogi ad leges ferendas de Ordinatione Episcoporum & Clericorum per varias querimonias, quæ ad se deferrentur contra eos, ut qui secundum canones divinos minime viverent, adeo ut etiam flagitiosè rudes essent.
units.tr: Bellarmine denies it, and grants to the magistrate only the power to enact civil laws, while he grants the power to enact ecclesiastical laws to the clergy alone. Just as, he says among other things, kings can enact civil laws, so the Pope or bishop can enact ecclesiastical laws (book 4 on the Pontiff, ch. 15, p. 857; see also chs. 16, 17, 18, 19, 20, 21). We affirm, and against Bellarmine we frame this proposition: The magistrate has the power to enact ecclesiastical laws that do not contradict the Word of God, both concerning persons and concerning ecclesiastical things. This proposition is also the doctrine of the Reformed Church. See among others Peter Martyr on 1 Samuel 14; Wittaker, Controversy IV, Q. 7; Junius, Controversy III, book 4, and Controversy V, book 3; Pareus, Commentary on Romans, Dub. 5; the professors of Leiden, Censure of the Remonstrant Confession, ch. 25, §34; the same in the Synopsis, Disputation on the Magistrate, thesis 46, where they say that the magistrate can also prescribe some things by his own authority concerning ecclesiastical matters. They speak, however, of matters on which there is no special divine precept, namely of rites indifferent in themselves, or those which pertain to the external order of the Church. See the learned Rivetus on the Decalogue, pp. 267, 168; Alsted in the Supplement to Chamier; Amesius, Medulla, book 2, ch. 17. Where it must be observed: first, that he should not enact laws concerning ceremonies which are joined with the danger of idolatry, nor overwhelm the Christian Church with a multitude of such rites, as was done in the Papacy. Next, it must be held that the magistrate can enact ecclesiastical laws not only as a minister of God, but also with respect to men, with his own authority and temporal coercive power; and that in enacting them he does not depend on any superior human power, and consequently does not need another's confirmation (although he rightly makes use of the counsel of prudent, pious and skilled teachers of the Church); and finally that consciences are bound by those laws even outside the case of scandal and contempt, by the general command of God concerning the due obedience owed to the magistrate, Romans 13 and elsewhere. From these things it follows in itself that they are properly so called laws, which are enacted by the magistrate in ecclesiastical matters. Finally, it must be observed what the learned Rivetus warns concerning laws which concern the ecclesiastics themselves: These, he says, depend so much on the princes that they are often imposed even AGAINST THE WISHES of the ministers of the Church; which, if they are unjust and burdensome, nevertheless do not harm the conscience, yet they bind all the same; if they are just and necessary, they are to be obeyed even if they leave some mark of disgrace, which evil morals, which had to be opposed, have brought about (p. 268). And by way of example he brings forward that law of which Jerome somewhere makes mention, by which the Christian emperors provided that ecclesiastics should not take inheritances; where he says that he does not complain about the law as unjust, but only that they had deserved it by their own deeds. That these and similar laws were enacted against the wishes and grief of the ecclesiastics there is no doubt, even from those very words of Jerome; for the wicked grieve because their malice is restrained, the good because of the scandal given and the stain cast on the ministry by the wicked actions of others. That the many laws enacted by the emperors concerning ecclesiastical persons had this cause, Parœus rightly observes (Commentary on Romans, ch. 13, p. 1097), from Novel 137, where the emperor states that he is compelled to enact laws concerning the ordination of bishops and clergy by the various complaints brought to him against them, because they did not live according to the divine canons at all, so that they were even shamefully ignorant.

units.la: Confirmationem hujus propositionis & responsionis ad Argumenta Bellarm. vide apud citatos Theologos.
units.tr: For the confirmation of this proposition and the answer to Bellarmine's arguments, see the theologians cited above.

units.la: Ad Quæst. octavam.
units.tr: On the Eighth Question.

units.la: An Magistratus potestatem illam exercere potest, etiam ineonsulta & invita Ecclesia, & quidem quidem orthodoxâ & bene ordinatâ? Si non: An non ergo thesis illa periculosè asseritur? An Magistratus potestatem illam leges ferendi habet, ut Dominus Ecclesiæ in Ecclesiâ existens, uti in Repub. suâ potestatem habet ut supremus in terris Dominus? Item, An nullæ hic sunt partes ministrorum & inspectorum Ecclesiæ? Dices: Sequitur in thesi nonâ. Sed an non æque explicandum, Vtrum Magistratus potestate illâ architectonicâ, quâ in Repub: leges fert, etiam ferre eas potest in Ecclesiâ, an secus? Et quo pacto Magistratus suâ illâ potestate uti debeat, ut illi Ecclesiæ potestati & ministrorum ejus damnum non inferat?
units.tr: Can the Magistrate exercise that power even without the consent of the Church and against its will, and that even when the Church is orthodox and well ordered? If not, is that thesis not dangerously asserted? Does the Magistrate hold the power of making laws in the Church as the Lord of the Church present within it, just as he holds power in his commonwealth as the supreme lord on earth? Likewise, are there no parts here for the ministers and overseers of the Church? You will say: this follows from the ninth thesis. But should it not equally be explained whether the Magistrate, by that architectonic power by which he makes laws in the commonwealth, can also make them in the Church, or not? And in what way ought the Magistrate to use that power, so that he does no harm to the Church's power and to its ministers?

units.la: Resp.
units.tr: Answer.

units.la: Quinque hic quæruntur, ad quæ uno verbo præter ea, quæ ante in genere dicta sunt, respondere possem: In quæstione meâ quæri de jure, quod sufficit contra thesin Bellarmini, in Considerationibus autem agi ferè de exercitio juris, seu modo exercendi illam potestatem. Tamen breviter ad singula respondebo. primo quæritur: An Magistratus potestatem leges ferendi exercere possit etiam inconsultâ & invitâ Ecclesiâ, & quidem Orthodoxa & bene ordinata? Si non; An non Ergò thesis illa periculosè asseritur? Respondeo: 1. PericuloIosa[?] igitur est doctrina Ecclesiarum Reformatarum; & periculosè asseritur illa thesis ab omnibus Theologis Reformatis illis, quos ego citavi, adeoque nominatim à DD. Proff. Leydd. Nemo enim ex illis limitationem eam expressit.
units.tr: Five questions are raised here, to which I could reply in one word, apart from what has been said earlier in general terms. My question concerned the right, which is enough against Bellarmine's thesis, whereas the Considerations deal mostly with the exercise of that right, or the manner of exercising that power. Still, I will answer each point briefly. First, it is asked: Can the magistrate exercise the power of making laws even without the consent of the Church, and indeed of an orthodox and well-ordered Church? If not, is that thesis not therefore asserted dangerously? I answer: 1. Is the doctrine of the Reformed Churches therefore dangerous? And is that thesis dangerously asserted by all those Reformed theologians whom I cited, and so by name by the Reverend Professors of Leiden? For none of them expressed that limitation.

units.la: 2. In Resp. ad Q. illam dixi, Magistratum recte adhibere in eâ re consilium prudentium piorum & peritorum Doctorum Ecclesiæ. Et sic etiam non impedio quo minus adhibeat in consilium totam Ecclesiam seu Consistorium; imò laudo illud & probo; modò non existimetur eum in illâ re pendere ab Ecclesiâ ut potestate superiore, hoc enim repugnat doctrinæ Ecclesiarum Reformatarum, imò verbo Dei, ut facilè ostendere possem: Maximè autem ubi consuetudo aut constitutio Ecclesiastica alicujus regni, provinciæ, civitatis illud postulat, non repugno; quemadmodum expressè protestatus sum in Conclusione me nullius loci consuetudinibus aut Constitutionibus Ecclesiasticis quicquam derogare velle. 3. Ecclesia Orthodoxa & benè ordinata vel officium suum facit secundùm ordinem sibi à Deo præscriptum, vel non. Si officium facit, nunquam eâ invitâ legem feret Ecclesiasticam pius Magistratus atque observans [?] conditiones, quas partim in thesi, partim in Exegesi illius & alibi expressi. Nam ex unâ parte semper studere debet concordiae cum Ecclesiâ; ex alterâ parte ipsa Ecclesia novit officii sui partem esse obedire Magistratui Rom. 13. 1. Tit. 3. II. [?] 1. Pet. 2. 13. Si autem Ecclesiastici non faciunt officium, Magistratus eos cogere, adeoque vel invitos compellere debet ad officium secundum verbum Dei faciendum; ad quam potestatem coactivam νομοθετικὴν [?] etiâ pertinet. Hinc dixi, aliquando invitus Pastoribus MALE docentibus aut viventibus leges à Magistratu ferri posse, quibus coerceantur. Sed aliud est dicere invitis Pastoribus male agentibus aut docentibus, adeoque invitâ parte Ecclesiae leges ferre; aliud est, eas invitâ totâ Ecclesiâ ferre; quod quidem non fit, quando mali Pastores coercentur. Nam Ecclesia reliqua aut saltem sanior pars potius optat coerceri tales, quàm ut se opponat Magistratui eos legibus justis coërcenti.
units.tr: 2. In my answer to that question I said that the magistrate rightly takes in this matter the counsel of prudent, pious and skilled teachers of the Church. So I do not forbid him to take the whole Church, or the consistory, into counsel; indeed I praise and approve it, provided it is not thought that he depends on the Church in that matter as on a superior power, for this contradicts the doctrine of the Reformed Churches, and indeed the Word of God, as I could easily show. Especially where the custom or ecclesiastical constitution of some kingdom, province or city requires it, I do not object; just as I expressly declared in my Conclusion that I wish to take nothing away from the customs or ecclesiastical constitutions of any place. 3. A Church that is orthodox and well ordered either performs its office according to the order prescribed to it by God, or it does not. If it performs its office, a pious magistrate will never make an ecclesiastical law against its will, provided he observes the conditions that I have set out partly in the thesis, partly in its explanation, and elsewhere. For on the one hand he must always strive for harmony with the Church; on the other hand the Church itself knows that it is part of its duty to obey the magistrate (Rom. 13. 1; Tit. 3. 1; 1 Pet. 2. 13). If, however, the ecclesiastical persons do not perform their office, the magistrate must compel them, and so must force them, even against their will, to perform their office according to the Word of God; and this coercive power also belongs to the legislative [nomothetikēn] power. Hence I said that sometimes laws may be enacted by the magistrate against the will of the ministers who teach or live badly, by which they may be restrained. But it is one thing to say that laws are made against the will of ministers who act or teach badly, and so against the will of part of the Church; it is another to make them against the will of the whole Church. The latter is not done when wicked ministers are restrained. For the rest of the Church, or at least the sounder part, would rather wish such men to be restrained than set itself against the magistrate who restrains them by just laws.

units.la: Secundò quaeritur: An Magistratus habeat potestatem illam ut Dominus Ecclesiae? Respondeo: habet illam potestatem, ut custos utriusque tabulae legis gladio corporali armatus, & sic ut director ordinis externi in Ecclesiâ, qui habet potestatem [?]νομοθετικὴν secundùm verbum Dei circa omne bonum subditorum suorum, adeoque etiam circa bonum spirituale, ut Pareus rectè loquitur in Com. Rom. c. 13. p. 1085. |
units.tr: Secondly it is asked: Does the magistrate have that power as lord of the Church? I answer: he has that power as guardian of both tables of the law, armed with the bodily sword, and thus as director of the external order in the Church, who has legislative [nomothetikēn] power according to the Word of God over all the good of his subjects, and so also over their spiritual good, as Pareus rightly says in his Commentary on Romans, chapter 13, p. 1085.

units.la: Tertiò Quæritur: An nulla hîc sint partes ministrorum & inspectorum Ecclesiæ? Respondeo 1. ipsorum est consulere Magistratui in talibus, ut in Exegesi ibidem dixi, 2. ipsi etiam possunt leges seu constitutiones Ecclesiasticas ferre, ut doceo Q. 9.
units.tr: Thirdly, it is asked: Is there no part here for the ministers and overseers of the Church? I answer: 1. It is their task to advise the magistrate in such matters, as I said in the explanation there. 2. They themselves can also enact ecclesiastical laws or constitutions, as I teach in Question 9.

units.la: Quarto quæritur: An Magistratus potestate architectonicâ leges possit ferre in Ecclesiâ? Respondeo cum DD. Proff. Leyd. in Censurâ Confessionis Remonstr. c. 25. §. 3. 4. p. 330. 331. Christus ministris utitur ad regiminis sui administrationem; Ecclesiæ & ministerio ejus in rebus indifferentibus tribuens quandam dispositionem seu dispensationem: Magistratui vero secundùm sublimem ejus vocationem, ut utrisque tabulæ custodi divini cultus, omnisque publici ordinis tutori hæc eadem potestas convenit, sed suo modo; nempe Politicè, dum pro [illegible, ~9 letters] & ἀρχι[?]πνευματικῶν sua potestate pietatem & ordinem Ecclesiæ legibus sancit ad vigorem publicæ observantiæ. Quo neque Ecclesiæ suam, neque Magistratui suam potestatem detrahimus, sed trisque quod suum est tribuimus, & amicè in uno Christi opere conjungimus.
units.tr: Fourthly, it is asked: Can the magistrate make laws in the Church by his architectonic power? I answer with the Reverend Professors of Leiden in their Censure of the Remonstrant Confession, chapter 25, §§ 3–4, pp. 330–331: Christ uses ministers for the administration of his government, granting to the Church and its ministry a certain disposition or dispensation in indifferent matters. But to the magistrate, according to his lofty calling, as guardian of both tables of the law, protector of divine worship and of all public order, this same power belongs, yet in his own way, namely politically; for by his power over [illegible] and archipneumatic [archipneumatikōn] matters he sanctions piety and order in the Church by laws, so that they may have force of public observance. By this we take away neither the Church's power nor the magistrate's power, but we give each what is its own, and join them in friendly fashion in the one work of Christ.

units.la: Unde etiam facilè ad Quintam Quæ-stionem responderi potest; nimirum: Quo pacto Magistratus suâ illa potestate uti debeat, ut ille Ecclesiæ potestati & ministrorum ejus damnum non inferant? Responsionem suppeditant primò ea, quæ modò ex D. D. Pross. Leydd. verbis protuli. Magistratus enim semper cogitare debet, sibi non licere ullo modo infringere libertatem & potestatem, quam Christus Ecclesiæ suæ etiam in hac parte dedit: Sed amicè in uno opere & quantum omnino fieri potest conjunctis consiliis conspirare cum ea debet. Adeoque ubi Ecclesia legem vult ferre verbo Dei non repugnantem, sed utiliter, piè, prudenter aut necessario, pro temporis aut aliarum circumstantiarum ratione conceptam, debet eam suâ auctoritate confirmare. Deinde meminisse semper debet regulæ generalis à me propositæ Q. VII. in omnibus negociis Ecclesiasticis nihil iniquè, temerè, leviter, malitiosè, imprudenter à se agendum esse.
units.tr: Hence the Fifth Question can also be answered easily, namely: In what way ought the magistrate to use that power, so that they do no harm to the power of the Church and its ministers? The answer is supplied first by what I have just quoted from the words of the Reverend Professors of Leiden. For the magistrate must always bear in mind that it is not lawful for him in any way to infringe the liberty and power that Christ has given to his Church, even in this respect; but he must conspire with it in friendly fashion in one work, and join counsels as far as this can at all be done. Accordingly, when the Church wishes to make a law that does not contradict the Word of God, but is useful, pious, prudent or necessary, conceived according to the circumstances of the time or of other matters, he ought to confirm it by his authority. Then he must always remember the general rule I proposed in Question 7: that in all ecclesiastical business nothing is to be done by him unjustly, rashly, lightly, maliciously or imprudently.

units.la: QUÆST. IX.
units.tr: QUESTION IX.

units.la: An Ecclesiastici habeant pote- statem leges proprie sic dictas ferendi?
units.tr: Do ecclesiastics have the power of making laws properly so called?

units.la: BEllarminus affirmat locis citatis quæstione præcedente & contendit inter alia leges Ecclesiasticorum non opus habere confirmatione aut etiam consensu Magistratus, sed ipsos Episcopos in suis diœcesibus & Romanum Pontificem in totâ Ecclesiâ esse veros Principes Ecclesiasticos, qui possunt suâ authoritate etiam sine consensu aliorum leges ferre, quæ in conscientiâ obligent etiam extra casum scandali & contemptus, & sic eos habere veram potestatem in omnes fideles in spiritualibus, ut habent reges in temporalibus &c. Nos negamus & contra Bellarm. hanc propositionem formamus: Ecclesiastici non habent potestatem leges condendi proprie sic dictas, sed tantum διατάξεις seu ordinationes & constitutiones, quæ non obligant conscientias extra casum scandali seu contemptus, atq; ut vim legum accipiant, opus habent auctoritate & confirmatione Magistratus, quae ubi accessit, obligant respectu non ministrorum, sed Magistratus etiam extra casum scandali sive contemptus. Haec etiam est doctrina Ecclesiarum Reformatarum specia-rim Calvini lib. IV. Instit. c. 10. 11. 12. F. Junii lib. 4. de Pontif. capp. 15. 16. &c. Wittackeri controvers. IV. Q. 7. P. Martyris, qui in 1. Sam. 14. recte dicit, leges Politicas Principum multo plus obligare, quam Ecclesia-sticae Episcoporum constitutiones obli-gant. Vrsini in Catech. explicat. Q. 56. Sibbrandi cont. Grot. p. 151. 152. Bogermanni contra eundem p. 193. DD. Proff. Leyd. Synopf. Disput. 50.th. 46. Cl. Walaei p. 126. Cl. Riveti Decal. p. 267. Amesii in Bellarm. Enervato ad Q. illam. Probatur haec propositio. I. Quia ministri Ecclesiae nihil nisi alieno, hoc est, Christi imperio praescribunt. Gubernatio enim Ecclesiastica est omnino ὑ-πηρετικὴ[?] seu ministerialis; sunt verba DD. Proff. Lyd. loc. cit. th. 46. Et sunt in se considerati mandatarii meri, qui proprii nihil habent, quod est argumentum Amesii. Et ut F. Junius loquitur de hac re lib.4.c.16. Potestas Ecclesiastica est ministerii potius, quàm potestatis, nec citra rationem decori & honestatis quicquam in Ecclesia potest. Item ibid. Ecclesiastica potestas est ministerium non potestas αὐτοκρατορικὴ[?] ut Magistratus. II. Quia consequenter etiam ministris non competit potestas coactiva externa. Unde non possunt judicium ferre, quando quæstio est de incarceratione, exilio, multâ pecuniariâ aut ullâ pœna corporali. Vide P. Martyrem Loc. communib. Cl. IV. c, 13. §. 9. & Cl. Walæum p. 53. 54. 55. ubi hanc doctrinam contra Concil. Trident. Sess. 25. 3. & contra praxin Episcoporum in Papatu defendit ex verbo Dei, atque inter alia ait p. 54. Ministros ne quidem acceptare debere hanc potestatem à Magistratu, sive vel magumen-[?] ximè ipsis deferretur ab illis. Plura argumenta ut & solutionem objectionum Bellarm. vide apud citatos Theologos, maximè Junium & Wittakerum.
units.tr: Bellarminus affirms, in the places cited under the previous question, and contends among other things that the laws of ecclesiastics need no confirmation or even consent from the magistrate. Rather, the bishops themselves in their dioceses, and the Roman Pontiff in the whole Church, are the true ecclesiastical princes, who can by their own authority, even without the consent of others, make laws that bind the conscience even outside the case of scandal and contempt, and so have true power over all the faithful in spiritual matters, as kings have in temporal matters, and so on. We deny this, and set against Bellarmine this proposition: Ecclesiastics do not have the power to enact laws properly so called, but only διατάξεις, that is, ordinances and constitutions, which do not bind consciences outside the case of scandal or contempt. In order to take on the force of laws they need the authority and confirmation of the magistrate, and once this is added they bind not only the ministers but also the magistrate, even outside the case of scandal or contempt. This is also the teaching of the Reformed Churches, especially Calvin, Institutes book 4, chapters 10, 11, 12; F. Junius, book 4 on the Pontiffs, chapters 15, 16, etc.; Wittaker, Controversy 4, question 7; P. Martyr, who rightly says on 1 Samuel 14 that the political laws of princes bind far more than the ecclesiastical constitutions of bishops bind; Ursinus in the Catechism explained, question 56; Sibrand against Grotius, pp. 151–152; Bogerman against the same, p. 193; the professors of Leiden in the Synopsis of Disputations, disputation 50, thesis 46; the learned Walaeus, p. 126; the learned Rivet on the Decalogue, p. 267; Amesius in his refutation of Bellarmine on that question. This proposition is proved as follows. (1) Because ministers of the Church prescribe nothing except by another's command, that is, by the command of Christ. Ecclesiastical government is wholly ministerial [ὑπηρετικὴ]; these are the words of the professors of Leiden, loc. cit., thesis 46. And considered in themselves they are mere agents, who have nothing of their own, which is the argument of Amesius. As F. Junius puts it on this matter in book 4, chapter 16: Ecclesiastical power is a power of ministry rather than of authority, and nothing can be done in the Church apart from the reasons of decency and honesty. Likewise in the same place: Ecclesiastical power is a ministry, not an autocratic [αὐτοκρατορικὴ] power like that of the magistrate. (2) Because consequently ministers do not possess outward coercive power. Hence they cannot pass judgment when the question concerns imprisonment, exile, a fine, or any corporal punishment. See P. Martyr, Common Places, class 4, chapter 13, section 9, and the learned Walaeus, pp. 53–55, where he defends this doctrine against the Council of Trent, session 25, chapter 3, and against the practice of the bishops under the Papacy, from the Word of God; among other things he says on p. 54: Ministers ought not even to accept this power from the magistrate, even if it were offered to them by him in the greatest measure. For further arguments, and the answer to Bellarmine's objections, see the Theologians cited, especially Junius and Wittaker.

units.la: QUÆST. X. An ullus homo in terris habeat potestatem absolutam in rebus Ecclesiasticis?
units.tr: QUESTION X. Does any human being on earth have absolute power in ecclesiastical matters?

units.la: BEllarm. affirmat, & quidem eum hominem Papam esse contendit, cui summam & absolutam potestatem ac Monarchiam spiritualem in Ecclesiâ & rebus Ecclesiasticis tribuit, tum quoad directionem ordinis externi, tum quoad dogmata fidei, ac præcepta morum. Vide lib. 1. & 2. de Pontif. Rom. lib 3. de verbo Dei cap. 3. 4. 5. &c. Item de Pontif. lib. 4. c. 1. 3. 5. 2. 22. 23. 15. 16. lib. 3. c. 5. Nos negamus & asserimus contra eum: Nullus homo quicunque tandem ille sit, sive Episcopus sive Magistratus, potestatem in rebus Ecclesiasticis absolutam habet; ita ut pro arbitrio quidlibet statuere, vel decernere possit aut debeat circa Religionem & res Ecclesiasticas; sed perpetuo meminisse debet se Dei ministrum esse, adeoque ad ejus jussa ac voluntatem in verbo Dei contentam se in omnibus componere, & contra eam nihil decernere aut facere. Hæc propositio etiam est totius Ecclesię Reformatæ. Vide illius confirmationem, & confutationem doctrinæ Pontificię, speciatim apud eos Theologos, qui contra Bellarm. scripsère. Hîc operæ pretium esset ostendere quomodo quidam Orthodoxi Theologi, qui tamen inter[?] se nequaquam pugnant, potestatem Magistratus circa res Ecclesiasticas vocent architectonicam, quo sensu rursus alii id negent. Item quo sensu quidam dicant præcipuam curam Religionis penes Magistratum esse: alii penes ministros: sed de hac re forte in ipsa disputatione dabitur dicendi locus. Nobis hîc ad finem est properandum. Tantùm addemus ex hac propositione facile patere; nos non in locum unius Papæ Romani tot numero constituere, quot summi Magistratus sunt.
units.tr: Bellarmine affirms it, and indeed contends that the man in question is the Pope, to whom he grants supreme and absolute power and spiritual monarchy in the Church and in ecclesiastical matters, both as to the direction of external order and as to the doctrines of faith and the precepts of morals. See his books 1 and 2 on the Roman Pontiff, book 3 on the Word of God, chapters 3, 4, 5, etc.; likewise on the Pontiff, book 4, chapters 1, 3, 5, 2, 22, 23, 15, 16, and book 3, chapter 5. We deny this and assert against him: No human being, whoever he may be, whether bishop or magistrate, has absolute power in ecclesiastical matters, so that he may decree or determine whatever he pleases, or ought to, concerning religion and ecclesiastical affairs. Rather he must always remember that he is a minister of God, and therefore must conform himself in all things to his commands and will as contained in the Word of God, and decree or do nothing against it. This proposition is also that of the whole Reformed Church. See its confirmation and the refutation of the Papist doctrine, especially in those theologians who wrote against Bellarmine. It would be worthwhile here to show how certain orthodox theologians, who nonetheless by no means quarrel among themselves, call the power of the magistrate in ecclesiastical matters "architectonic," and in what sense others deny this; likewise in what sense some say that the chief care of religion lies with the magistrate, and others with the ministers. But perhaps there will be an opportunity to speak of this matter in the disputation itself. For now we must hasten to an end. We will only add that from this proposition it can easily be seen that we do not set up as many persons in the place of the one Roman Pope as there are supreme magistrates.

units.la: QUÆST. XI. An Magistratus in rebus Eccle-siasticis subjectus sit ministris Eccle-siæ?
units.tr: QUESTION XI. Is the magistrate in ecclesiastical matters subject to the ministers of the Church?

units.la: Bellarm. affirmat. lib. 1. de Pontif, c. 7. lib. 5. c. 7. De Cleric. lib. 1. c. 28. Item in tract. de officio Principis Christiani lib. 1. c. 5. Nos contra cum hanc propositionem for-mamus: Magistratus summus in rebus Ecclesiasticis, ministris subjectus seu subditus sensu Pontificio nequaquam est, & non nisi falsò ab illis dicitur: ab orthodo-xis autem quibusdam tantum Catachresticè[?] seu abusivè Magistratus ministris Ecclesiæ subditus esse dicitur. Hæc propositio bimembris est. Pars prior est: Magistratum in rebus Ecclesiasticis sensu Pontificio falsò dici subjectum seu subditum esse Pastoribus. Hæc est doctrina omnium Theologorum Reformato-rum. Et patet veritas illius exinde: Quia Pontificii Doctores ita subditum faciunt Magistratum Ecclesiae & ministris illius, ut ei omnem jurisdictionem Ecclesiasticam, omnem potestatem in rebus fidei ac Religionis eripiant; atque ex eo mancipium pastorum, imò carnificem faciunt, qui teneatur gladium stringere ad nutum sacerdotis: quod certè improbè & contra verbum Dei fit. Alterum membrum est: quid [?] quando orthodoxi quidam dicunt Magistratum esse subditum ministris in rebus Ecclesiasticis: id accipiendum sit non proprie, sed improprie, non per se, sed per accidens; adeoque catachresticè, nimirum respectu Christi & verbi illius, cujus illi sunt ministri, præcones & nuncii. Hanc esse doctrinam & mentem orthodoxorū Theologorum patet ex ipsorum declaratione, quâ phrasin illam explicant. Ita enim omnes declarant, speciatim Fr. Iunius lib. 5. de Pontif. c. 7. P. Mar-
units.tr: Bellarmine affirms it: book 1 On the Pope, ch. 7; book 5, ch. 7; On the Clergy, book 1, ch. 28. Likewise in his treatise On the Duty of a Christian Prince, book 1, ch. 5. We, on the contrary, state the proposition thus: The highest magistrate in ecclesiastical matters is in no way subject or subordinate to the ministers in the Papists' sense, and it is said of him by them only falsely; but some orthodox writers say that the magistrate is subject to the ministers of the Church only catachrestically, or in an improper sense. This proposition has two parts. The first part is: In the Papists' sense it is falsely said that the magistrate in ecclesiastical matters is subject or subordinate to the pastors. This is the teaching of all the Reformed theologians. The truth of this is plain from the following: the Papist doctors make the magistrate of the Church, and its ministers, so subject to them that they strip him of all ecclesiastical jurisdiction and all power in matters of faith and religion; and so they make him the bondsman of the pastors, or even their executioner, bound to draw the sword at the nod of the priest. This is certainly done wrongly and against the Word of God. The second part is: when some orthodox writers say that the magistrate is subject to the ministers in ecclesiastical matters, this must be taken not properly but improperly, not in itself but incidentally, and so catachrestically, namely with respect to Christ and his Word, whose ministers, heralds and messengers they are. That this is the teaching and mind of the orthodox theologians is clear from their own explanation of that phrase. For all of them explain it so, especially Franciscus Junius, book 5 On the Pope, ch. 7, and P. Mar-

units.la: &c. qui hanc quæstionem solidè & ex professo decidit; & inter alia ait: Talis est parendi ratio, quâ senatui Ecclesiastico Magistratus paret. Non enim hoc facit obedientia civili, quæ collegium Ecclesiasticum respiciat: sed obedientiâ religiosâ, quæ Deum respicit: ut qui apparitori à Senatu misso parebat, Senatui proprie parebat, non apparitori: vel etiam judicio rationis, quia judicat unicuique in suâ arte perito credendum esse, & rationibus ducitur, quibus id utile esse ipsi persuadeatur, ita tamen, ut si in talibus non pareat (quod ei liberum manet) non habeat, quod pœnam temporalem metuat, qui non est subjectus ratione talis pœnæ, & subjicere se debeat rationi & veritati.
units.tr: &c., who settles this question solidly and at length, and among other things says: Such is the manner of obedience by which the magistrate obeys the ecclesiastical senate. It is not obedience of a civil kind, which looks to the ecclesiastical college, but religious obedience, which looks to God: just as one who obeyed a messenger sent by the Senate was really obeying the Senate, not the messenger. Or it is obedience of reasoned judgement, because one must believe a man skilled in his own craft, and one is led by reasons by which it is persuaded to be useful to oneself; yet in such things, if he does not obey (which is left free to him), he has no reason to fear a temporal penalty, since he is not subject to such a penalty, and he ought to submit himself to reason and truth.

units.la: Hinc etiam orthodoxi Theologi interdum expresse negant Magistratum subjectum esse Ecclesiæ. Ut F. Junius lib. 5. de Pontif. c. 7. n. 3. Ubi negat quod Bellarm. dixerat, Tem-
units.tr: Hence the orthodox theologians sometimes also expressly deny that the magistrate is subject to the Church. So Franciscus Junius, book 5 On the Pope, ch. 7, n. 3, where he denies what Bellarmine had said, that the temporal

units.la: P. Martyr loc. Commun. Cl 4. c. 13. §. 10. Pareus comment. Rom. 13. p. 1081. Cl. Rivetus in Decal. p. 258. &c. poralem potestatem subjectam esse spirituali: si enim dicamus, ut subordina-tæ sunt facultates, ita & fines communiter: Ergo potestas civilis subordinata est spirituali communiter, nempe prout Dei potestas cum legatione servorum ejus conjuncta est: hæc sententia verissima est. Sed si dixeris ergo subordinata atque subje-cta est spirituali ministrorum potestati, negatur argumentatio. Et cap. 6. n.2. dispar omnino ratio est politicæ potestatis & Ecclesiasticæ; illa absoluta & principalis est; hæc limitata & ministratoria solum. Rex enim Deo subjectus est, quia nulla est potestas nisi a Deo; at non subjectus præconi illius est, etsi præconem propter mittentem audit.
units.tr: power is subject to the spiritual; P. Martyr, Common Places, class 4, ch. 13, §10; Pareus, commentary on Romans 13, p. 1081; Rivetus on the Decalogue, p. 258, etc. "For if we say that the powers are subordinated, so are their ends, generally speaking: therefore civil power is subordinate to spiritual power in general, namely insofar as God's power is joined with the embassy of his servants; this statement is most true. But if you say, therefore it is subordinate and subject to the spiritual power of the ministers, the argument is denied." And ch. 6, n. 2: "The reason of political power and of ecclesiastical power is wholly unlike; the former is absolute and principal, the latter limited and merely ministerial. For the king is subject to God, because there is no power except from God; but he is not subject to God's herald, although he hears the herald on account of the one who sent him."

units.la: Confirmatur autem [?] hoc membrum inter alia. 1. Ex eo, quia obedientia, quæ debetur ministerio, non terminatur ad ipsos ministros, sed ad Christum, cujus præcones illi sunt. 2. Quia nullus etiam minimus fidelis per se & proprie loquendo subditus est ministris in rebus Ecclesiasticis. Ergo multò minus Magistratus, cujus officium etiam in illis rebus in imperio consistit. Antecedens patet ex eo, quod proprie subditum seu subjectum esse correlatum est illius, qui Dominus est sive imperium habet. Atqui ministri nullum imperium habent teste Christo Matth.20. 25.26.27.28. Marc. 10. 42.43.44. 45. Luc.22.25.26.27. & Petro 1. Epist.c.5.3. Sed tota eorum officii ratio ministerialis est, ut scriptura testatur, non solum respectu Christi 1. Cor.3.5.c.4.1. 2.Cor.1.34.c.4.1. sed etiam Ecclesiæ. v. 5. ut adeò recte Cl. Rivetus de potestate Magistratus circa res Ecclesiasticas loquens p.264. dicat: Nos nullum superiorem eo in terris agnoscimus à quo dependeat, & hæc est summa authoritas, quam ei vendicamus. Dicimus autem, inquit, à nullo pendere in talibus, ita ut non excludamus consilium, sed imperium; aliud est enim consilio uti, aliud se imperio subjicere. Ex dictis jam facile est re-jicere. spondere ad argumenta, quae Bellarm. affert.
units.tr: This member is confirmed, among other things, as follows. First, because the obedience owed to the ministry does not terminate on the ministers themselves but on Christ, whose heralds they are. Second, because not even the very least believer is, properly and strictly speaking, subject to the ministers in ecclesiastical matters. Therefore much less is the magistrate subject to them, whose office in those matters also consists in authority. The antecedent is plain, because to be properly subject or subordinate is correlative to being one who is lord or has authority. But the ministers have no authority, as Christ testifies, Matt. 20:25–28; Mark 10:42–45; Luke 22:25–27; and 1 Peter 5:3. Yet the whole reason of their office is ministerial, as Scripture testifies, not only with respect to Christ, 1 Cor. 3:5; 4:1; 2 Cor. 1:24; 4:1, but also with respect to the Church, v. 5. So the learned Rivetus, speaking of the power of the magistrate over ecclesiastical matters, rightly says on p. 264: "We acknowledge no superior on earth on whom it depends, and this is the sum of the authority we claim for him. We say, he says, that it depends on no one in such matters, so that we do not exclude counsel, but command; for it is one thing to use counsel, another to subject oneself to command." From what has been said it is now easy to reject the arguments which Bellarmine brings forward.

units.la: Ad Quaest undecimam.
units.tr: To the Eleventh Question.

units.la: An non Magistratus, etiam summus, non catachrestice, sed proprie, subsit verbo Dei: An non Pastores & ministri Ecclesiae totum Dei verbum debeant pradicare omnibus cujuscunq; status hominibus, idque omnium conscientiis sine exceptione applicare, non catachrestice, sed proprie? Et si hoc ita sit, an non illa thesis ad hoc negandum commodè adhiberi possit?
units.tr: Does not the magistrate, even the highest, be subject to the Word of God not catachrestically but properly? Do not the ministers and pastors of the Church have to preach the whole Word of God to all men of every rank, and apply it without exception to the consciences of all, not catachrestically but properly? And if this is so, can that thesis not be conveniently brought in to deny this?

units.la: Resp.
units.tr: Response.

units.la: Responsio ex Exegesi manifesta est. Nam ex eo, quòd Magistratus Catachrestice tantùm seu improprie loquendo & per accidens subditus est Pastoribus, id nequaquam sequitur. Ratio, cur non sequatur, in eo consistit; quod verbum Dei seu Christus habet imperium proprium in Magistratum & omnes homines, eorumque Dominus est; & sic illi proprie loquendo subditus est omnis homo, etiam summus Magistratus. At alia ratio est ministrorum; ut qui imperium proprium non habent; sed tantùm ministerium verum, & proprie sic dictum quo imperium alienum n. Christi verbumque ejus annunciant. Ut igitur non valet consequentia: Titius non est subjectus præconi propriè & per se. Ergo nec Regi, cujus jussum præco annunciat; ita non sequitur: Magistratus non est propriè & per se loquendo subditus Præconibus Christi & verbi ejus: Ergo nec Christo & verbo ejus propriè & per se subjectus est.
units.tr: The answer is plain from the exegesis. For it does not follow from the fact that the magistrate is subject to the pastors only catachrestically, or improperly speaking and by accident, that he is not subject to the Word of God in the proper sense. The reason it does not follow is this: the Word of God, that is Christ, has a proper dominion over the magistrate and over all men, and he is their Lord. Thus every man, even the highest magistrate, is properly speaking subject to him. But the ministers are in a different position, since they do not have a dominion of their own, but only a true ministry, properly so called, by which they announce the command of Christ and his Word, which is another's. So, just as the inference is invalid, "Titius is not subject to the herald properly and in himself; therefore neither is he subject to the king whose command the herald announces," so it does not follow: "The magistrate is not properly and in himself subject to the heralds of Christ and of his Word; therefore neither is he properly and in himself subject to Christ and his Word."

units.la: QUÆST. XII. An ministri Ecclesiæ aliquo mo- do pendeant à Magistratu in rebus Ecclesiasticis, & eatenus illi subjecti sint?
units.tr: QUESTION XII. Whether the ministers of the Church depend in some way on the magistrate in ecclesiastical matters, and are subject to him in so far?

units.la: Bellarm. negat. lib. de Laic. c. 17. de Cleric. c. 28. nos affirmamus & contra Bellarm. hanc propositionem formamus: Ministri Ecclesiæ aliquo modo pendent à Magistratu in rebus Ecclesiasticis, & eatenus eis subjecti in illis sunt. Hæc etiam est doctrina Ecclesiarum Reformatarum. P. Martyr loc. commun. Cl. IV. c. 13. §. 12. postquam dixisset, ministros subjectos esse Magistratui, quatenus homines sunt & cives, &c. subjungit: Addendum praeterea est non solùm quoad ista quae recensui ministros Magistratui subjici, sed etiam, ut innui superius, quoad functionem. Quia si non rectè docent, nec ex ordine administrent sacramenta, Magistratus est, eos in ordinem cogere, &c. Polanus Syst. lib. 7. c. 19. Secundò subjecti esse debent Ecclesiastici omnes Magistratui in omnibus, quae Reges in Ecclesiastico ordine constituunt secundum voluntatem Dei, sive ceremonias, sive decorum externum, sive res indifferentes spectemus, sicut Sacerdotes & Levitae fuerunt subjecti ordini illi, quem David constituerat & postea confirmavit Salomon, revocavit in usum Ezechias & Josias. Talis primatus in Ecclesia datus est à Deo piis Regibus & Principibus ac Magistratibus, ac proinde primatum habet in suis ditionibus, tum quoad regimen corporale, tum quoad curam Religionis & cultus Dei, &c. Similiter etiam Pareus Comment. Rom. dub. 1. p. 1024. ubi ait, pastores non solùm ut cives, sed etiam ex parte, quatenus ministri sunt potestati civili subjectos esse debere. Et dub. V. p. 1085. 1086. probat ex Rom. 13. cap. Ecclesiasticos circa bonum spirituale debere Magistratui subjectos esse; & ad exceptionem Stapletoni dicentis Ecclesiasticos quatenus tales, hoc est, quatenus potestatem spiritualem habent, non subjici Regi, sed tantum ut homines & cives Reipub. respondet; Licet Ecclesiastici ut sunt tales, non pendeant à civili potestate suprema simpliciter, quantum ad genus doctrinae & sacramentorum peragendum, tamen pendent ab eâ secundum quid, ratione vocationis, directionis & censurae ut mox patebit. Sic igitur etiam verba Chrysostomi intelligenda, &c. Et Cl Rivetus in Decal. p. 265. postquam dixisset Magistratus quidem pasci ministerio Pastorum, sed tamen vicissim ipsum pascere eos imperio addit: Minister enim cùm doctrinae radiis illuminat, cum Baptismo tingit, cùm salutari Sacramento alit, cum censurae aculeos in contumaces exerit, hæc omnia facit facit Magistratui subjectus, ab eo dependens, tutus illo Euangelii vindice ac custode gladio, &c. & illustrat similI exemplo Aristotelis, Magistri Alexandri, cùm inquit: Potuit eodem tempore & regnum quoddam in artibus apud suum alumnum obtinere eique de totâ scientiarum ratione praecipere, & interim vel ipsius juvenis vel Philippi Patris altiori gubernationi subjici: sic etiam qui ipsos Magistratus docent res sacras, iisdem subjiciuntur & ab eorum auctoritate in exercitio pendent. Cl. Walæus ex professo totâ parte secundâ libri sui p. 51. &c. tractat hanc rem, & ostendit, quousque (sunt verba illius) officium ministrorum subjectum sit officio Magistratus; Et p. 64. dicit se quando ait ministrum non esse subditum aut servum Magistratus, loqui de partibus essentialibus, & substantia ministerii ipsorum, non autem de circumstantiis administrationis aut ministerii. Et p.67. ait: Reformatos Theologos non contradicere, si quis dicat ministros certo modo subordinatos dinatos dinatos esse Magistratui, ut & p.128. Et probat Augustini sententiam super hac re. Atque ex verbis citatis Theologorum Orthodoxorum patet, tum quomodo intelligi velint, quod dicunt ministros in Ecclesiasticis rebus subjectos esse Magistratui; nimirum non quoad substantiam officii, sed quoad exercitii directionem, ordinem externum & circumstantias: tum etiam ex parte apparet, quibus argumentis sententiam suam confirment. Ad objectiones Bellarm. respondent tum alii, tum Cl. Rivetus pag. 165.
units.tr: Bellarmine denies this (book on laymen, ch. 17; on clerics, ch. 28); we affirm it, and against Bellarmine we frame this proposition: The ministers of the Church depend in some way on the magistrate in ecclesiastical matters, and in so far are subject to him in those matters. This is also the teaching of the Reformed Churches. Peter Martyr (Common Places, class IV, ch. 13, §12), after saying that ministers are subject to the magistrate in so far as they are men and citizens, etc., adds: It must further be added that ministers are subject to the magistrate not only in those matters which I have listed, but also, as I hinted above, in their function. For if they do not teach rightly, or do not administer the sacraments in good order, it is the magistrate's business to bring them into order, etc. Polanus (System, book 7, ch. 19): Secondly, all ecclesiastics ought to be subject to the magistrate in all those things which kings establish in the ecclesiastical order according to the will of God, whether we look at ceremonies, external decency, or indifferent matters, just as the priests and Levites were subject to that order which David had established and which Solomon afterwards confirmed, and which Hezekiah and Josiah restored to use. Such a primacy in the Church has been given by God to pious kings, princes and magistrates, and therefore they hold the primacy in their own domains, both as to bodily government and as to the care of religion and the worship of God, etc. Pareus likewise (Commentary on Romans, dub. 1, p. 1024), where he says that pastors ought to be subject to civil power not only as citizens, but also in part, in so far as they are ministers. And (dub. 5, pp. 1085–1086) he proves from Romans 13 that ecclesiastics ought to be subject to the magistrate in what concerns the spiritual good; and in answer to the objection of Stapleton, who says that ecclesiastics as such, that is, in so far as they have spiritual power, are not subject to the king, but only as men and citizens of the commonwealth, he replies: Although ecclesiastics, as such, do not depend simply on the supreme civil power as to the kind of teaching and the carrying out of the sacraments, yet they depend on it in a certain respect, by reason of vocation, direction and censure, as will soon be made clear. In this way, then, the words of Chrysostom too must be understood, etc. And the learned Rivetus (on the Decalogue, p. 265), after saying that the magistrate is indeed fed by the ministry of the pastors, but in turn feeds them by his authority, adds: For the minister, when he illumines with the rays of doctrine, when he washes with baptism, when he nourishes with the saving sacrament, when he brings the sting of censure against the stubborn, does all this as one subject to the magistrate, dependent on him, safe under the sword of that guardian and protector of the Gospel, etc. He illustrates this with a similar example of Aristotle, the tutor of Alexander: He could at the same time hold a kind of kingship over his pupil in the arts and instruct him on the whole system of the sciences, and yet at the same time be subject to the higher government of the young man himself or of his father Philip; so too those who teach the magistrates themselves sacred things are subject to them and depend on their authority in the exercise of their office. The learned Walaeus, in the whole second part of his book (p. 51 and following), treats this matter expressly and shows how far (these are his words) the office of ministers is subject to the office of the magistrate; and on p. 64 he says that when he says the minister is not subject or a slave of the magistrate, he speaks of the essential parts and the substance of their ministry, and not of the circumstances of its administration or of its office. And on p. 67 he says: The Reformed theologians do not contradict if someone says that the ministers are in a certain way subordinated to the magistrate, as also on p. 128, and he proves Augustine's opinion on this matter. From the cited words of the orthodox theologians it is clear both how they wish their statement to be understood, that ministers are subject to the magistrate in ecclesiastical matters (namely not as to the substance of their office, but as to the direction of its exercise, external order and circumstances), and in part also what arguments they use to confirm their view. Both others and the learned Rivetus (p. 165) answer the objections of Bellarmine.

units.la: Ad Quæst. duodecimam.
units.tr: To the Twelfth Question.

units.la: An non necesse sit explicari, quo modo ministri Ecclesiæ in rebus Ecclesiasticis pendeant à Magistratu, eique subjecti sint? Nam hoc ita generaliter & indefinitè positum facile in malam partem sumi posset. An non debebit ostendi, Ministros non pendere à Magistratu, ut servi pendent à dominis, aut ut ministri delegati à suis principibus, ut planum maneat, Pastores & ministros Ecclesiæ, non Magistratus, sed Dei & Christi ministros esse, quod D. VValæus totâ secundâ parte libri sui evidenter & solidè demonstravit.
units.tr: Is it not necessary to explain in what way the ministers of the Church depend on the magistrate in ecclesiastical matters, and are subject to him? For if this is stated so generally and indefinitely, it could easily be taken in a bad sense. Ought it not to be shown that ministers do not depend on the magistrate as servants depend on their masters, or as delegated ministers depend on their principals, so that it stays plain that the pastors and ministers of the Church are ministers not of the magistrates but of God and Christ? This Walaeus demonstrated clearly and solidly throughout the second part of his book.

units.la: Resp.
units.tr: Answer.

units.la: Satis explicatum est tùm verbis aliorum Orthodoxorum Theologorum, quæ citavi; nimirùm Pastores non simpliciter pendere à suprema potestate seu quantum ad genus doctrinæ & Sacramentorum; sed secundùm quid ratione vocationis, directionis & censuræ, ut Pareus loquitur; seu ut clarius Dn. Walæus ait: non in partibus essentialibus & substantia ministerii ipsorum, sed in circumstantiis administrationis:tum verbis meis propriis, quando dixi, eos subjectos esse Magistratui non quoad substantiam officii, sed quoad exercitii directionem, ordinem externum & circumstantias. Et in ipso proœmio rejeci doctrinam Arminianorum, quam Cl. V. Valqus[?] solidè refutavit in secunda parte tractatus sui; nimirum Ministros pendere à Magistratu, ut delegati pendent â suis principalibus, quorum servi seu vicarii sunt. Summa: Satis indicavi hoc non esse intelligendum de potestate ipsâ ordinis & jurisdictionis, quasi eam & quidem omnem non à Christo immediatè accepissent; sed esse intelligendum de circumstantiis ministerii in exercitio potestatis illius.
units.tr: It has been explained sufficiently, both by the words of the other orthodox theologians that I have quoted, namely that pastors do not depend simply on the supreme power, that is, as regards the kind of doctrine and the sacraments; but depend in a qualified way, in respect of their calling, direction and censure, as Pareus puts it. Or, as Walaeus says more clearly, not in the essential parts and substance of their ministry, but in the circumstances of its administration; and by my own words, when I said that they are subject to the magistrate not as regards the substance of their office, but as regards the direction of its exercise, external order and circumstances. Moreover, in the very preface I rejected the doctrine of the Arminians, which the learned Walaeus solidly refuted in the second part of his treatise: namely, that ministers depend on the magistrate as delegates depend on their principals, of whom they are servants or agents. In sum, I have sufficiently indicated that this is not to be understood of the power of office and jurisdiction itself, as though they had not received that power, and indeed all of it, immediately from Christ; but that it is to be understood of the circumstances of the ministry in the exercise of that power.

units.la: QUÆST. XIII. An Magistratus honore & dignitate inferior sit personis Ecclesiasticis?
units.tr: QUESTION XIII. Is the magistrate inferior to ecclesiastical persons in honour and dignity?

units.la: Bellarm. affirmat lib. de Laic. c. 17. Reges, Principes, & quosvis Magistratus summos, ut membra Ecclesiæ sunt, dignitate & honore inferiores esse Ecclesiasticis: Sic enim, inquit, primum locum habent Episcopi præcipuè Pontifex summus, secundum Presbyteri, tertium Diaconi, aliique ministri Ecclesiastici, ultimam Laici, inter quos etiam Reges & Principes numerantur. Vide & lib. 1. de Pontif. c. 7. Et lib. 1. de Concil. c. 19. ait, quando Reges & Principes in conventibus Ecclesiasticis sedent ante Episcopos, id tantum per tolerantiam Episcoporum fieri: utcunque tolerabile est inquit.
units.tr: Bellarmine affirms, in the book on laymen, chapter 17, that kings, princes, and any supreme magistrates, as members of the Church, are inferior to ecclesiastical persons in dignity and honour. For, he says, the first place belongs to the bishops, especially the supreme Pontiff; the second to the presbyters; the third to the deacons and other ecclesiastical ministers; the last to the laity, among whom kings and princes are also counted. See also book 1 on the Pontiff, chapter 7. And in book 1 on councils, chapter 19, he says that when kings and princes sit before the bishops in ecclesiastical assemblies, this is done only by the tolerance of the bishops: it is tolerable to that extent, he says.

units.la: Nos contra eum hanc propositionem formamus: Magistratus summus in Ecclesia Christianâ primum locum ob-tinet. tinet. Hæc propositio est etiam doctrina totius Ecclesiæ Reformatæ; speciatim Ecclesiæ orthodoxæ Anglicanæ, ut constat: & omnium eorum Theologorum, qui potestatem Magistratus in rebus Ecclesiasticis primatum Regium vocant, item Bullingeri de Episcoporum Institut. cap 3. f. 71. b. f. 82 a. ubi ex verbo Dei ostendit: Episcopum non debere præferre se Magistratui, ut loquitur. Pareus comment. Rom. p. 1112 [?] pro ridicula petitione principii habet, quod Bel-larm. dixerat, Magistratum in Ecclesiâ non esse primum, sed posteriorem Ecclesiasticis. vide & Fr. Junium lib. 1. de Pontif. c. 7. Cll. Proff. Leyd. in Synopsi. disputat. 5o. th. 46. docent, ministris Ecclesiæ non deberi æqualem honorem cum Magistratu, tantum abest, ut concedant ipsis plus honoris deberi. Itidem th. 48. vide & Cl. Rivetum, qui p. 256. ait hanc esse doctrinam omnium Ecclesiarum & Theologorum Reformatorum, & inter alia ait: sacrum ministerium externos honores non affectat, delatos temerè, rejicit humiliter &c. Cl. Walæus par. II. p. 53. docet etiam ministris Ecclesiæ non solùm majorem honorem non competere, quàm Magistratui, sed ne quidem æqualem; & dicit omnes Doctores Reformatos perpetuo hoc contra Papistas docuisse. Et probat illud ex praxi Veteris Testamenti; item ex N. Testamento. Et pag. 129. dicit ministros subordinatos esse Magistratui inter alia quoad honorem. Et ideò ait p. 53 Magistratus capita populi vocari. Adeoque manifestè indicat, ministros Ecclesiæ non esse capita populi, prout in Papatu eum honorem & appellationem superbè sibi tribuunt. Atque hanc quidem esse sententiam Ecclesiarum Reformatarum, patet etiam ex praxi illarum in Synodis & aliis conventibus Ecclesiasticis; item ex eo, quod in administratione rituum sacrorum, speciatim S. Cœnæ (ubi certè omnis ambitio quàm maximè procul esse debet ) hunc debitum honorem deferre solent Pastores Reformati Magistratibus summis, ut ii ministri, qui sacram coenam non ipsi administrant, non ante ad mensam Domini accedant, quam Magistratus accesserit: quod conforme est præcepto Spiritus S. jubenti per Paulum, ut omnia bono ordine in Ecclesia fiant, quod quidem præceptum perpetuo à ministris repetitur, quando sacra Coena celebratur.
units.tr: Against him we frame this proposition: The supreme magistrate holds the first place in the Christian Church. This proposition is also the doctrine of the whole Reformed Church, specifically of the orthodox Anglican Church, as is well known; and of all those theologians who call the power of the magistrate in ecclesiastical matters royal primacy; likewise of Bullinger, on the institution of bishops, chapter 3, fols. 71b and 82a, where from the word of God he shows that a bishop ought not to place himself before the magistrate, as he puts it. Pareus, in his commentary on Romans, p. 1112, calls it a ridiculous begging of the question that Bellarmine had said the magistrate in the Church is not first, but comes after the ecclesiastical persons. See also Francis Junius, book 1 on the Pontiff, chapter 7. The learned professors of Leiden, in the Synopsis of Disputations, disputation 50, thesis 46, teach that ministers of the Church are not owed equal honour with the magistrate; so far are they from conceding that more honour is due to them. Likewise thesis 48; see also the learned Rivetus, who at p. 256 says this is the doctrine of all the Reformed Churches and theologians, and among other things says: the holy ministry does not aspire to external honours, and rejects humbly those offered rashly, etc. The learned Walaeus, part II, p. 53, also teaches that not only is no greater honour due to the ministers of the Church than to the magistrate, but not even an equal one; and he says that all the Reformed teachers have constantly taught this against the Papists. He proves it from the practice of the Old Testament and likewise from the New. And at p. 129 he says that the ministers are subordinated to the magistrate, among other things as regards honour. And for this reason he says at p. 53 that magistrates are called the heads of the people. Thus he clearly indicates that the ministers of the Church are not the heads of the people, as in the Papacy they proudly claim that honour and title for themselves. That this is indeed the view of the Reformed Churches is also evident from their practice in synods and other ecclesiastical gatherings; and from the fact that in the administration of the sacred rites, especially the Lord's Supper (where surely all ambition ought to be as far away as possible), the Reformed pastors are accustomed to pay this due honour to the supreme magistrates: the ministers who do not themselves administer the holy supper do not approach the Lord's table until the magistrate has arrived. This accords with the command of the Holy Spirit, who through Paul bids that all things be done decently and in order in the Church; and this command is constantly repeated by the ministers whenever the holy Supper is celebrated.

units.la: Confirmationem hujus propositionis & responsionem ad argumenta contraria vide apud modò laudatos Theologos. Posset forte objici Theologos quosdam orthodoxos dicere Ministerium Ecclesiæ suo modo dignius esse officio civili, ut Pareus loquitur p. 1113. item Cl. Rivetus p. 256. sed illi loquuntur de Potestate, quæ tantum civilis est; h. e. de Magistratu inferiore, penes quem non est gubernatio Ecclesiæ, non autem de potestate civili architecto-nica; nica; item loquuntur de eo, quod ministriis non per se, sed per accidens competit, nimirum respectu Christi, cujus sunt Legati: quamvis & ipsi Magistratus ministri Dei sint, & quidem ita ut Dii vocentur, qui appellationis honor ministris Ecclesiæ in Scripturâ non tribuitur.
units.tr: For confirmation of this proposition and the reply to the contrary arguments, see the theologians just cited. Perhaps it could be objected that some orthodox theologians say the ministry of the Church is in its own way more worthy than the civil office, as Pareus says at p. 1113, and likewise the learned Rivetus at p. 256. But they speak of a power that is merely civil, that is, of the lower magistracy, in which the government of the Church does not lie, and not of the architectonic civil power; likewise they speak of what belongs to the ministers not in themselves but by accident, namely with respect to Christ, whose ambassadors they are. Although the magistrates themselves are also ministers of God, and indeed are called gods, an honour of title which is not given to the ministers of the Church in Scripture.

units.la: Conclusio interrogatorum.
units.tr: Conclusion of the questions.

units.la: Certè Magistratus non est in Ecclesia. Qui Magistratu funguntur, si sunt fideles, & Ecclesiæ membra, sunt in Ecclesiâ cum reliquis fidelibus: At Magistratus, quâ Magistratus, in Ecclesiâ non est. Alioqui nemo posset Magistratus munere fungi nisi fidelis; neminemque pro subdito agnoscere posset Magistratus præter fidelem, ut Pastor Ecclesiæ.
units.tr: Certainly the magistrate is not in the Church. Those who hold the magistracy, if they are faithful and members of the Church, are in the Church together with the other faithful; but the magistrate, as magistrate, is not in the Church. Otherwise no one could discharge the office of magistrate unless he were faithful, and the magistrate could acknowledge as his subject only a faithful person, as the minister of the Church does.

units.la: Discrimen hîc agnoscendum inter regnum Dei universale, quod, tanquam creator & conservator, habet in universo mundo, in, & inter omnes homines, quibus imperat lege suâ, & quos gubernat potestate suâ absolutâ: & inter regnum Dei speciale, quod regnum est gratia, comprehenditque omnes fideles, quos gratiosè gubernat verbo suo & Spiritu, in quo filium suum, electorum & fidelium mediatorem & redemtorem, speciatim in regem constituit, Psal. 2. In primo illo regno universali Magistratus à Deo constitutus est, ut ipsius Vicarius. Hinc dicitur potestas à Deo ordinata Rom. 13. & qui illo munere funguntur Deorum nomine in S. Literis insigniti sunt Psal. 82. Unde etiam omnes ejusdem ditionis incolæ illos qui ibi rerum potiuntur pro Magistratibus agnoscere debent, sive fideles, sive infideles, sivepios, sive impios. Hujus potestatis est in illo regno universali, nomine Dei, custodire, & authoritate suâ coactivâ tueri, utramque legis tabulam, id est, subditos suos dirigere & legis divinæ observantiam. Verum, quia regnum illud universale rebellionis est regnum, utpote quod totum à Deo defecit, per inobedientiam universalem totius humani generis, nil nisi externum hominem coercere, & aliquo modo in ordinem cogere potest Magistratus. At in regno Christi mediatoris, sive in regno hoc posteriori, sive regno gratiæ, quod est Ecclesia, in quo Deus electos suos & fideles, è potestate illâ tenebrarum, & universali defectione, erutos, sibi morigeros verbo & spiritu suo efficit, Christus ordinavit Pastores & Inspectores Ecclesiæ suæ, quorum operâ hoc regnum erigit, promovet, & gubernat spirituali ratione. Eph. 4.
units.tr: Here a distinction must be recognised between the universal kingdom of God, which he has over the whole world, as creator and preserver, in and among all men, whom he rules by his law and governs by his absolute power; and the special kingdom of God, which is the kingdom of grace and embraces all the faithful, whom he governs graciously by his word and Spirit, and in which he has appointed his Son, the mediator and redeemer of the elect and faithful, specifically as king, Ps. 2. In that first, universal kingdom the magistrate has been appointed by God as his vicar. Hence the power is said to be ordained by God, Rom. 13, and those who discharge that office are in Scripture called by the name of gods, Ps. 82. Whence also all the inhabitants of the same dominion ought to acknowledge as magistrates those who hold power there, whether they are faithful or unfaithful, pious or impious. It is the power of the magistrate in that universal kingdom, in the name of God, to guard, and by his coercive authority to protect, both tables of the law; that is, to direct his subjects and to enforce observance of the divine law. But since that universal kingdom is a kingdom of rebellion, inasmuch as it has wholly fallen away from God through the universal disobedience of the whole human race, the magistrate can only restrain the outward man and in some way bring him into order. But in the kingdom of Christ the mediator, that is, in this latter kingdom, the kingdom of grace, which is the Church, in which God makes his elect and faithful, rescued from that power of darkness and universal defection, obedient to himself by his word and Spirit, Christ has ordained ministers and overseers of his Church, by whose work he raises up, advances and governs this kingdom in a spiritual manner. Eph. 4.

units.la: Pastorum, Doctorum, & Inspectorum Ecclesiæ hujus est, omnes cujuscunque ordinis hominis, pro ratione muneris & vocationis sua, docere, instruere, & monere, ut è regno Satanæ & tenebrarum, in hoc regnum Christi & lucis sese recipiant: & omnes, qui se eò receperunt, nomenque suum Ecclesiæ, ut regno illi Christi, dederunt, ministeriali sua potestate, sive clavibus regni cælorum, à Christo sibi traditis, in obedientia debitâ continere, & prudenter gubernare, refractarios verò excludere.
units.tr: It is the task of the ministers, teachers and overseers of this Church, according to the nature of their office and calling, to teach, instruct and admonish men of every rank, that they may withdraw from the kingdom of Satan and of darkness into this kingdom of Christ and of light; and to hold in due obedience, and govern prudently, by their ministerial power, or by the keys of the kingdom of heaven given to them by Christ, all those who have withdrawn there and given their name to the Church as to that kingdom of Christ, while excluding the refractory.

units.la: Viceversâ, Quia hoc regnum eo fine à Deo erectum & stabilitum est, ut in illo debitè colatur, justumque, quod in regno universali ipsi negatur, recipiat obsequium; tenentur omnes, quotquot sunt, vocationi illi divinæ parere, ministerialem illam Pastorum Ecclesiæ potestatem, sive claves regni cælorum, agnoscere, eis sese humiliter, cum spirituali obedientia subjicere, sed ex verbo Dei rite edocti: & quamcunque in regno universali habent potestatem, quascunque ibi possident dotes, ad promotionem regni illius spiritualis, ejusque defensionem, & malorum omnium ab eo aversionem ex veræ regni illius cognitione, impendere.
units.tr: Conversely, because this kingdom has been established and set up by God for this end, that he may be duly worshipped in it and may receive the obedience that is rightly denied him in the universal kingdom, all men, whoever they are, are bound to obey that divine calling, to acknowledge that ministerial power of the ministers of the Church, or the keys of the kingdom of heaven, to submit themselves to them humbly and with spiritual obedience, provided they are rightly taught from the word of God; and to devote to the advancement of that spiritual kingdom, to its defence and to the turning away of all evils from it, whatever power they have in the universal kingdom and whatever gifts they possess there, drawing on the true knowledge of that kingdom.

units.la: Sic Christus dominatur in medio inimicorum suorum. Sic osculantur cum Principes & Judices terræ.
units.tr: So Christ rules in the midst of his enemies. So do the princes and judges of the earth kiss him.

units.la: Resp.
units.tr: Reply.

units.la: Corollarii loco subjungitur in Annot. tionibus, quod Magistratus ut talis non sit in Ecclesiâ, sed ut Orthodoxus & fidelis; atque additur distinctio Regni Dei in universale & speciale, &c. In quibus omnibus facile acquiesco; quia puto non afferri eas distinctiones sensu & scopo illo, quem Anabaptistæ habent; qui iis utuntur, ut evincant Magistratum nullam potestatem habere in rebus Ecclesiasticis; sed potestatem omnem circa eas pertinere ad ministros Ecclesiæ solos, & sic Magistratum volunt nullâ ratione esse in Ecclesiâ; ut patet ex Confessionibus ipsorum, & Colloquio Embdano, aliisque scriptis eorum. Sed è contrario statuitur in distinctione illâ : Magistratus officium esse in regno illo universali nomine Dei custodire & auctoritate suâ coactivâ tueri utramque legis tabulam, hoc est, subditos suos dirigere ad legis divinæ observantiam; item, eum externum hominem coërcere & aliquo modo in ordinem cogere posse. Et ex altera parte statuitur etiam, Magistratum, quatenus membrum Ecclesiæ est, debere potestatem illam, quam in regno universali habet ad promotionem regni illius Spiritualis ejusque defensionem & malorum omnium ab eo aversionem impendere. Quæ omnia redeunt ad ea, quæ DD. Prosit. in Cens. Confess. Remonstr. c. 25. §. 3.4. dicunt: Magistratum suâ potestate circa res Ecclesiasticas uti debere non tantùm, quod boni publicique ordinis sit tuitor, qualiter & Ethnicus Magistratus modò Ecclesiam ferat, eamque foveat, Ecclesia statum tutari potest, sed etiam quod membrum Ecclesiae Christi sit, cujus est quoque externam suam potestatem (qualiter omnia membra pro modulo quaeque suo facere debent) conferre ad Ecclesiae bonum, & se ejus nutricium prebere ac prestare. Summa: modò illa distinctiè non adhibeatur ad potestatem Magistratui eripiendam, quam verbum Dei illi tribuit, eam non rejicio: nec plus tribuo Magistratui, quàm in eâ ipsi defertur. Et hæc breviter dicta sunto ad interrogata proposita. Nunc ego vicissim jure possem proponere varias Quæstiones & responsionem ad eas postulare; quandoquidem Considerationes illæ propriam mentem Dn. Auctoris earum non exhibent circa quædam, quæ ex me quæruntur; quò ita apparere posset, an consensus inter Auctorem earum & Ecclesiarum Reformatarum reliquos Doctores sit speciatim illos, quos allegavi, an verò peculiares opiniones habeat circa materiâ illâ. Spiritus enim prophetarum prophetis subjiciuntur. Sed finio; quia spero in re ipsâ consensum inter nos omnes esse; & tantùm diversitatem in modo explicandi quantum hactenus quidem potui intelligere, aut vehementer fallor.
units.tr: By way of a corollary it is added in the Annotations that the magistrate, as such, is not in the Church, but as orthodox and faithful; and the distinction between the universal and the special kingdom of God is added, and so on. I readily assent to all these points, because I think these distinctions are not advanced in the sense and with the aim that the Anabaptists have, who use them to prove that the magistrate has no power in ecclesiastical affairs, but that all power over them belongs to the ministers of the Church alone, and so they wish the magistrate to be in the Church in no way at all; as is clear from their Confessions, the Colloquy of Emden, and their other writings. On the contrary, it is laid down in that distinction that the office of the magistrate in that universal kingdom is to guard in the name of God, and by his coercive authority to protect, both tables of the law, that is, to direct his subjects to the observance of the divine law; likewise that he can restrain the outward man and in some way bring him into order. And on the other side it is also laid down that the magistrate, insofar as he is a member of the Church, ought to devote the power he has in the universal kingdom to the advancement of that spiritual kingdom, to its defence, and to the turning away of all evils from it. All these points come back to what the Doctors Prosit. say in Censura Confessionis Remonstrantium, ch. 25, §§ 3–4: that the magistrate ought to use his power in ecclesiastical matters not only in that he is a guardian of the public good and order, in the way that even a heathen magistrate, who supports and fosters the Church, can protect the state of the Church; but also in that he is a member of the Church of Christ, and it is his duty too to bring his outward power (as all members ought, each according to his measure) to the good of the Church, and to show and render himself its nurse. In sum: provided that distinction is not used to take away from the magistrate the power that the word of God gives him, I do not reject it, nor do I attribute to the magistrate more than is granted him in it. And let these things be said briefly in answer to the questions put. Now I might rightly in turn put forward various questions and demand answers to them, since those Considerations do not set out the proper opinion of their author on certain points that I am asking about; so that it might appear whether the agreement between the author of them and the remaining teachers of the Reformed Churches is in those particular points I have cited, or whether he holds peculiar opinions about that matter. For the spirits of the prophets are subject to the prophets. But I will end here, because I hope that in the matter itself we are all in agreement, and that there is only a difference in the manner of explaining it, as far as I have been able to understand so far, or I am greatly mistaken.

units.la: Deus omnium Magistratuum animos di-rigat, ut potestate suâ ita utantur, quò manifestum fiat eos quærere regnum Dei, conservationem Reformatæ Religionis, vigorem denique pietatis, ad gloriam nominis ipsius, Ecclesiæ defensionem, ac Reip. prosperitatem.
units.tr: May God direct the minds of all magistrates so that they use their power in such a way that it becomes plain that they seek the kingdom of God, the preservation of the Reformed religion, the vigour of piety in the end, to the glory of his name, the defence of the Church and the prosperity of the commonwealth.

units.la: CONCLUSIO NOSTRA In quâ hæc doctrina à calumniis Pontificiorum vindicatur.
units.tr: OUR CONCLUSION In which this doctrine is vindicated from the slanders of the Papists.

units.la: Exposuimus hactenus doctrinam Ecclesiarum Reformatarum de potestate Magistratus in rebus Ecclesia-sticis, prout eam semper, libenter ac liberè confessi & professi sunt Doctores & Pastores Ecclesiarum nostrarum, non tantum ante Synodum Dordracenam, sed etiam post eam. Inter quos quidam adhuc per Dei gratiam vivunt, qui scriptis publicis eam tuiti sunt contra Pontificios, ut patet ex praecedentibus. Nec unquam lis ulli eo nomine mota est, nec potest doctrinae ei contradici à peritis ac veris Theologis, quia non hominum, sed Dei doctrina est in verbo suo loquentis, prout pluribus adhuc à nobis ostendi potest. Nec puto quenquam repertum iri, qui doctrinam ei oppositam, hoc est, Pontificiam invehere[?] rursus in Ecclesias nostras, & sic novam doctrinam illis obtrudere conetur, nisi frontem plane perfricuerit. Non tamen desunt calumniae, quibus Pontificii, tum alii, tum Bellarm. hanc doctrinam denigrare conantur. Primò enim, neq;[?] soli injurii videantur in unctos Domini, allegant quosdam nostros Theologos, quos dicunt secum sentire. Ita Stapletonus & alii Pontificii Angli, Lutherum, Melancbtonem, Calvinum in suas partes pertrahere conantur. Sed hanc meram esse[?] calumniam, quâ in sequiorem sensum verba piorum Doctorum detorquent', dudum ostenderunt nostri Theologi & inter hos Pareus Rom. c. 13. Cl. Rivetus p. 259 260. post Reinoldum Theologum Anglum doctissimum.
units.tr: Hitherto we have set out the doctrine of the Reformed Churches concerning the power of the magistrate in ecclesiastical matters, as the teachers and ministers of our Churches have always confessed and professed it, freely and gladly, not only before the Synod of Dort but also after it. Some of them, by God's grace, are still living, and they have defended it in published writings against the Papists, as is clear from what has gone before. No dispute has ever been raised on this point, nor can this doctrine be contradicted by skilled and true theologians, since it is not the doctrine of men but of God, who speaks in his own Word; this can be shown further by us at greater length. I do not think anyone will be found who would try to bring back into our Churches the opposing doctrine, that is, the Papist one, and so try to force this new doctrine upon them, unless he has utterly brazened out his face. Nevertheless, there is no shortage of slanders by which the Papists, both others and Bellarmine, try to disparage this doctrine. First, they claim that our theologians, whom they say think as they do, are on their side, and so wrongly appeal to them. Thus Stapleton and the other English Papists try to draw Luther, Melanchthon and Calvin to their side. But our theologians, among them Pareus (on Romans 13) and the learned Rivet (pp. 259-260), after the most learned English theologian Reynolds, have long since shown that this is a sheer slander, by which they twist the words of pious teachers into a worse sense.

units.la: Secundum genus calumniarum consistit in effectis & adjunctis perniciosis scilicet, quę huic doctrinæ Bellarm. & alii Pontificii adscribunt. Quod quidem ab ipsis fieri mirum non est; Certum quippe est nullam doctrinam magis ipsorum ambitioni & contrariam & exosam esse, quàm hęc quidem est. Quæ etiam causa est, quòd, ut dudum grauissimus Theologus Pareus in Aphorismis questus est, nolunt permittere Principibus, ut intelligant, quantum potestatis in rebus Ecclesiasticis habeant. Primò ajunt confundi eâ ratione omnia, potestatem scilicet Magistratus cum ministerio Ecclesiastico. Ita olim Hardingum contra Ecclesiæ Anglicanæ Apologiam contendebat. Ita Bellarm. lib. 1. de Cleric. c. 28, Secundò dicunt hac ratione dissidia excitari inter Magistratus & mini-stros. Ita Cardinalis Perronius in oratione habitâ in conventu ordinum Galliæ 1614. Rosweydus Iesuita alicubi dicit eos, qui jus Magistratus contra usurpationes Ecclesiasticorum defendunt, novam sectam frendere & schisma facere velle. Tertiò dicunt sententiam illam adulatoriam esse & per eam Ecclesiasticos fieri mancipia Regum. Ita Bellarm. lib. 1. de Pontif. c. 7. Sed hæc omnia falsa & calumniosa esse; atque contumeliam istam recidere non tam in Ecclesiarum nostrarum Theologos, quàm in ipsum verbum Dei, à nostris non semel est ostensum. Nihil enim aliud ista doctrina adscribit Magistratibus, quàm quod Scriptura Sacra ab illis postulat iisque attribuit: dum dat Cæsari, quod Cæsaris est, & Deo, quod Dei est.
