units.tr: The second kind of slander consists in the harmful effects and consequences which Bellarmine and the other Papists attribute to this doctrine. That they do so is hardly surprising, for it is certain that no doctrine is more opposed to their ambition and more hateful to them than this one. This is also why, as the most weighty theologian Pareus complained long ago in his Aphorisms, they are unwilling to let princes understand how much power they have in ecclesiastical matters. First, they say that by this doctrine everything is confused, namely the power of the magistrate with the ecclesiastical ministry. So Harding once argued against the Apology of the English Church. So Bellarmine, On the Clergy, book 1, ch. 28. Secondly, they say that by this reasoning dissensions are stirred up between magistrates and ministers. So Cardinal Perron, in his speech delivered to the assembly of the orders of France in 1614. The Jesuit Rosweyde says somewhere that those who defend the right of the magistrate against the usurpations of churchmen wish "to rage with a new sect and make a schism." Thirdly, they say that this opinion is flattering and that through it churchmen become the slaves of kings. So Bellarmine, On the Pope, book 1, ch. 7. But our men have more than once shown that all these charges are false and slanderous, and that this insult falls not so much on the theologians of our Churches as on the Word of God itself. For this doctrine ascribes to magistrates nothing other than what Holy Scripture requires of them and assigns to them, when it gives to Caesar what is Caesar's and to God what is God's.

units.la: Et certè confusionem nullam introducei officii utriusque ex eo patet, quod secundum hanc doctrinam etsi in quibusdam conveniant circa res Ecclesiae & fidei, tamen octodecim adhuc modis circa ealdem differuut, quos commemorare instituti nostri non permittit brevitas. Quod secundo loco ajunt Pontificii contentiones & dissidia per hanc doctrinam queri inter Magistratus & Pastores: in eo vero egregie isti homines detegunt ingenium suum & ambitionem. Eo enim ipso satis minaciter indicant se nolle concorditer vivere cum Magistratu, nisi quamdiu is de jure suo discedere vult & pati ut ipsi in Ecclesia dominentur: ubi autem Magistratus jus sibi divinitus concessum & officium, quod sibi incumbit, exercere velit, se ei adversarios esse velle & dissidium excitare in Ecclesia & Repub. ac populos contra Magistratum & orthodoxae hujus doctrinae assertores concitare velle. Coeterum in eo plurimum fallunt potius quam falluntur. Neque enim vera ratio concordiæ inter Magistratum & ministros in eo consistit, ut pastores jus suum eripiant Magistratui; è contrario nullum est majus incentivum discordiæ[?], quam cùm quis Magistratum, imò quemvis minimum ex fæce[?] Romuli spoliat jure suo, & eum impedit, quo minus exercere illud possit; Societas quippe humana, ait optimè Sibbrandus p. 150. conservari nequit nisi quisque sese intra limites suæ vocationis continęat. Vera autem concordia inter Magistratum & ministerium eo fundamento nititur, ut neutra pars invadat jus alterius, sed utraque alteri, quod suum est, tribuat. Quod quidem fit per hanc doctrinam, quam consequenter pastores tenentur non tacere nedum impugnare, sed diligenter & fideliter populis proponere, & ipsi ad usum perpetuò revocare. Ita dubium non est, quin concordia inter Magistratum pium & ministerium summa sit futura. Unde etiam patet non nostram, sed contrariam doctrinam discordiae matricem inter Magistratum & ministerium esse; & causam justissimae indignationis Magistratus contra pastores, quae suo tempore in iram & & vindictam ipsi à Deo imperatam erumpit. Atque hinc perpetuo illa doctrina à nostris Theologis pro seditiosâ & contumeliosâ in Magistratus habita fuit, prout facile ostendere possem. Quod autem dicunt Pontificii, eos qui nostram hanc doctrinam profitentur Schisma moliri in Ecclesiâ, icipsum salsissimum est.
units.tr: And indeed, that there is no confusion of the two offices is clear from the fact that, according to this doctrine, although they agree on some matters concerning the affairs of the Church and the faith, they nevertheless differ on the same matters in eighteen further ways, which the brevity of my purpose does not allow me to recount. As to the second charge, which the Papists make, that this doctrine causes quarrels and dissensions between magistrates and pastors, in this these men clearly reveal their own character and ambition. For by this very fact they show, rather threateningly, that they are unwilling to live in harmony with the magistrate, unless he is willing to give up his right and allow them to lord it over the Church. But when the magistrate wishes to exercise the right divinely granted to him and the duty incumbent upon him, they want to be his adversaries, to stir up discord in Church and commonwealth, and to rouse the people against the magistrate and against the defenders of this orthodox doctrine. Moreover, in this they are much more mistaken than right. For the true basis of concord between magistrate and ministers does not consist in pastors snatching their right away from the magistrate; on the contrary, nothing is a greater incitement to discord than when someone robs the magistrate, or even the least man of the dregs of Romulus, of his right and hinders him from exercising it. For human society, as Sibrandus rightly says (p. 150), cannot be preserved unless each keeps himself within the limits of his calling. True concord between magistrate and ministry rests on this foundation: that neither party invades the right of the other, but each grants to the other what is its own. This is indeed achieved by this doctrine, which pastors are bound not only not to suppress but to set out diligently and faithfully before the people, and to keep constantly before them in use. So there is no doubt that concord between a godly magistrate and the ministry will be complete. From this it is also clear that it is not our doctrine but the contrary one that is the mother of discord between magistrate and ministry, and the cause of the magistrate's most just indignation against pastors, which in due time breaks out into the wrath and vengeance that God has commanded against them. Hence that doctrine has always been regarded by our theologians as seditious and insulting to magistrates, as I could easily show. But as to what the Papists say, that those who profess our doctrine are plotting a schism in the Church, that is utterly absurd.

units.la: E contrario doctrina adversariorum verè schismatica est, utpote quam Donatus, schismatis perniciosissimi in Ecclesiâ vetere autor, primus professus est. Quemadmodum etiam dubium non est, quin si aliquis nostris Ecclesiis contrariam doctrinam proponeret, Schisma quantum in se est efficeret, dum opiniones verbo Dei contrarias, & in Ecclesiis nostris non receptas invehere conaretur: cui machinationi, utpote perniciosissimę & quę summę utilitatis doctrinam ex Ecclesiâ profligare conaretur. à Magistratu & à veris servis Dei obviam ferìò effet eundum. Quod tertio loco dicunt hanc doctrinam adulatoriam esse, & ex Episcopis mancipia Regum seu Magistratuum efficere; id verò & ipsum calumnia est impudentissima. Quę enim est adulatio indicare ex verbo Dei quidnam Deus à Magistratu requirat, & quod illius officium & quidem laboriosissimum sit; & quorsum dignitas illius & potestas se extendat? Nec per eam Pastores mancipia Magistratus fiunt; cùm in nullâ re eos Magistratui subjiciat, nisi in quantum verbum Dei eos subjectos esse vult; nec illius libidini, sed justo & æquo imperio, quod Deo non reluctetur parere jubeat; nec denique suo jure & libertate eos privet, quæ in administratione Ecclesię divinitus ipsis est concessa. Et tantum abest, ut nostra dodoctrina[?] aduletur Magistratibus, aut illis Pastores tanquam mancipia submittat, ut potius contraria doctrina abblandiatur Papæ, & superbiæ atq; ambitioni Cleri palpum obtrudat, atque ex Magistratibus mancipia,imo lictores & carnifices ministrorum faciat. Et sic ostensum est doctrinam nostram nequaquam noxiam esse.
units.tr: On the contrary, the doctrine of our opponents is truly schismatic, since Donatus, the author of the most pernicious schism in the ancient Church, was the first to profess it. Likewise there is no doubt that if anyone were to propose a doctrine contrary to ours in our Churches, he would, as far as he is concerned, create a schism, since he would be trying to introduce opinions contrary to the Word of God and not received in our Churches. Such a scheme, which would try to banish from the Church a doctrine most pernicious to it and of the greatest use, ought to be resisted by the magistrate and by the true servants of God. As to the third charge, that this doctrine is flattering and makes bishops the slaves of kings or magistrates, that too is the most shameless slander. For what flattery is it to show from the Word of God what God requires of the magistrate, that his office is a very laborious one, and how far his dignity and power extend? Nor do pastors become slaves of the magistrate by this teaching, since it subjects them to him in nothing except in so far as the Word of God wills them to be subject; it bids them obey not his lust but his just and equitable rule, which does not resist God; and finally it does not deprive them of their own right and liberty, which has been divinely granted to them in the administration of the Church. And so far is our doctrine from flattering magistrates, or from submitting pastors to them as slaves, that rather the contrary doctrine fawns upon the Pope, offers a pat on the back to the pride and ambition of the clergy, and makes magistrates into slaves, indeed into lictors and executioners of the ministers. Thus it has been shown that our doctrine is by no means harmful.

units.la: Nunc paucis è contrario ostendemus utilitates illius: quæ novem sunt. Primus usus est conservatio veræ Religionis & puritatis illius. Si enim solis personis Ecclesiasticis cura Religionis & gubernatio Ecclesiæ relinquatur, æque imo forte magis periclitatur puritas & veritas Religionis, ac salus Ecclesiæ, quàm si soli Magistratui relinqueretur, quemadmodum ex scripturâ & experientiâ Papatus constat. Secundò necessaria est hæc doctrina, ne Papalis fastus ac Tyrannis & consequenter Idololatria Pontificia rursus introducatur. Cœpit enim revelari Antichristus per fastum ac superbiam, sub Bonifacio tertio, postea paulatim sequuta est idololatria, usque dum ad cumulum & supremum fastigium pervenit. Quare experientia nos sapientes reddere debet atq; efficere, ne per eandem viam ad eandem metam Satanā grassari patiamur. Tertiò necessaria est hæc doctrina ad conservationem pacis in Repub. & Ecclesiâ Christianâ. Nam doctrinam contrariā esse verum flabellum seditionum docet experientia Papatus. Et ratio est evidens: positâ enim illâ doctrinâ Pontificia pastores tutò populo persuadere possunt sub prætextu Religionis quicquid volunt. Magistratus autem ne hiscere quidem audet, quia statim audit ad se non pertinere res Ecclesiasticas, cum defensorem esse tantùm & executorem Ecclesiæ, contra hoc officium suum agere ipsum, dum non assentitur iis, quæ à pastoribus dicta sunt ad populum; esse hostem Ecclesiæ, excommunicationem incurrere, adeoque privationem jurisdictionis & dignitatum suarum &c. Quarto consequenter necessaria est hæc doctrina ad tuendam vitam, dignitates, bona Magistratus Christiani, imò cujuscunque Christiani, ut pręcipuè patet ex connexione inter dominium spirituale & temporale, quemadmodum Bellar. non inepte profectò, sed callidius longè, quàm plerique alii Pontificii, hoc ex illo infert. Quinto eò spectat doctrina ista, ut Magistratus Christiani intelligentes potestatem suam in rebus Ecclesiasticis adeoq; officium suum, eò magis excitimulentur, ad procurandum bonum Religionis atq; Ecclesiæ, ad extendendum Regnum Jesu Christi; quandoquidem vident ad se etiam pertinere curam religionis & Ecclesiæ iis modis, qui à nobis sunt expositi. Sextus usus est, ut Doctores & Pastores Ecclesiæ aliæque personæ Ecclesiasticæ eo melius & rectius officium suum faciant, tàm in doctrinâ, quam in vitâ, scientes se non tantùm Deum judicem supremum habere,& collegarum suorum, qui nonnunquam alii ad aliorum vitia vel ob metum, vel ob vitiorum societatem, vel ob alias causas connivere solenr)censurae obnoxios esse, sed etiam Magistratum habere inspectorem, Censorem, ac judicem tàm doctrinæ, quàm vitæ suæ. Se-ptimò hac ratione student prudentes & sapientes Ecclesiastici,qui bonum Ecclesiæ & incrementum regni Christi quærunt, piis obsequiis & secundum Deum demereri pios Magistratus suos, præcipientes hoc vel illud in rebus Ecclesiæ, quod non potest non plurimum in bonum Ecclesiæ cedere; quemadmodum contra perniciosissimum est Ecclesiæ; quando pastores existimant se potestatem architectonicam in administratione Ecclesiæ habere, Magistratum autem nihil habere potestatis in gubernatione illius, sed tantum defenfensorem esse & exequutorem sententiæ Ecclesiasticorum; adeoq; contra aut præter voluntatem Magistratus, eo ringente & indignante agunt in rebus Ecclesiæ, quæ volunt. Tunc enim irritantur Magistratus, & sæpe ea aut faciunt, aut permittunt, quæ alioquin nunquam contigissent. Octavo [?] necessaria plane hæc doctrina est studiosis Theologiæ seu illis, qui ad ministerium verbi se præparant. Maturè enim & antequam ad functionem suam exercendam veniant, debent discere, quousq; se extendant limites potestatis suæ in administratione Ecclesiæ, quid juris & potestatis habeat Magistratus in illius gubernatione, quid consequenter ipsi debeant, in quibus ei sit obediendum.
units.tr: Now, on the other hand, we will briefly show its usefulness, which is of nine kinds. (1) The first use is the preservation of true religion and its purity. For if the care of religion and the government of the Church were left to ecclesiastical persons alone, the purity and truth of religion and the welfare of the Church would be endangered just as much, or perhaps even more, than if they were left to the magistrate alone, as is clear from Scripture and from the experience of the Papacy. (2) Secondly, this doctrine is necessary so that papal arrogance and tyranny, and consequently Papist idolatry, are not introduced again. For Antichrist began to be revealed through pride and haughtiness under Boniface III; afterwards idolatry gradually followed, until it reached its height and summit. Therefore experience ought to make us wise and ensure that we do not allow Satan to advance by the same road to the same goal. (3) Thirdly, this doctrine is necessary for the preservation of peace in the commonwealth and the Christian Church. For the experience of the Papacy teaches that the contrary doctrine is a true fan for seditions. And the reason is plain: once that Papist doctrine is in place, pastors can safely persuade the people, under the pretext of religion, of whatever they wish. The magistrate, however, does not even dare to open his mouth, because he is at once told that the affairs of the Church do not concern him, that he is only the defender and executor of the Church; that to act against this duty, by not agreeing with what has been said to the people by the pastors, makes him an enemy of the Church; that he incurs excommunication and thereby the loss of his jurisdiction and dignities, and so on. (4) Fourthly, this doctrine is consequently necessary for protecting the life, dignities and goods of the Christian magistrate, indeed of any Christian, as is especially clear from the connection between spiritual and temporal lordship, from which Bellarmine infers this, not foolishly indeed, but far more cunningly than most other Papists. (5) Fifthly, this teaching aims at this: that Christian magistrates, understanding their power in ecclesiastical matters and so their duty, may be the more stirred up to promote the good of religion and the Church and to extend the kingdom of Jesus Christ, since they see that the care of religion and the Church pertains to them also, in the ways we have set out. (6) The sixth use is that teachers and pastors and other ecclesiastical persons may perform their office the better and more rightly, both in doctrine and in life, knowing that they have not only God as supreme judge, and are subject to the censure of their colleagues (some of whom, through fear, or from association with vices, or for other reasons, are wont to connive at the vices of others), but also that they have the magistrate as overseer, censor and judge of both their doctrine and their life. (7) By this reasoning, prudent and wise churchmen, who seek the good of the Church and the growth of Christ's kingdom, strive by pious obedience, and in a manner pleasing to God, to deserve well of their godly magistrates, when they advise this or that in the affairs of the Church, which cannot but contribute greatly to the good of the Church. Conversely, it is most pernicious to the Church when pastors think that they have architectonic power in the administration of the Church, and that the magistrate has no power in its government but is merely the defender and executor of the sentence of churchmen; so they act in matters of the Church against or beyond the will of the magistrate, doing what they wish while he frets and is indignant. For then the magistrates are provoked, and often they either do or permit things that would otherwise never have happened. (8) The eighth use is that this doctrine is plainly necessary for students of theology, or for those who prepare themselves for the ministry of the Word. For they must learn early, and before they come to exercise their office, how far the limits of their power in the administration of the Church extend, what right and power the magistrate has in its government, what consequently they themselves owe, and in what matters he is to be obeyed.

units.la: Quo ita φιλαρχία & φιλοτυραννία [?], hoc est, dominationis & ambitionis studio nonnihil [?] involent in officium Magistratus, eum impedire conentur eique resistant [?], quando circa res Ecclesiæ hoc vel illud ex officio facit, aut fieri vult, adeoque se & Ecclesiam, quæ ipsis committenda est olim, periculo exponant. Nonò denique necessaria est hæc doctrina ad vindicandas Ecclesias nostras à calumniis adversariorum. Remonstrantes enim hinc inde in scriptis suis præcipuè autem in Apologia acerbissimè insectantur Ecclesias nostras, quasi duas collaterales summas & architectonicas potestates statuant: Magistratum scilicet ex unâ, ministros ex altera parte; quorum ille tantum in rebus seculi; hi autem in rebus Ecclesiasticis gubernationem habeant; quâ ratione Magistratus à nobis mancipia, lictores, & carnifices (prout in Papatu sit) Ecclesiasticorum constitui dicunt, Apolog. c. 25. f. 293. 294. speciatim autem eo nomine acerbè insectantur Ecclesiam Genevensem, & Matricem, inquiunt, Ecclesiarum omnium Genevam tantùm vide ,&c. Magistratus omnia velit nolit, ex ministrorum arbitrio geri sinit: quin & auctoritatem suam iis commodat, ubi ea opus esse ministri judicant. Crimen laesae divinae Majestatis esse creditur, non parere ministrorum decretis &c. Sed hanc calumniam esse patet ex hac disputatione: quemadmodum speciatim Ecclesiae Genevensi injuriam fieri ab ipsis, ego optimus testis esse possum, qui in Ecclesia & Academia illa diu docui. Etsi enim status ibi popularis sit & quidem adeo, ut jus, pacem aut bellum decernendi; item Consules quotannis eligendi penes populum sint, etsi quoque pastores ibi ob singularem eruditionem & pietatem, quae in illis inde ab initio Reformationis ad haec usque tempora effulsit, in magna authoritate sint: tamen tantum abest, ut Magistratus ibi Mancipium ministrorum sit, & faciat, quicquid ministris lubet, ut e contrario, si minister aliquid aut dicat, ut faciat, quod ipsius Magistratus authoritati contrarium esse videatur: a Magistratu extraordinaria via, sine ulla communicatione cum consistorio coërceatur, & vel arresto publico detineatur, vel ab officio suspendatur: cujus rei ego varia exempla recentiora novi. Et tunc nos non Tyrannidis accusabamus Magistratum, nec populum concitabamus contra ipsum; sed confugiebamus ad arma nostra, hoc est, preces, quas ad Magistratum dirigebamus, quibus emollliebamus iram ejus. Idem Magistratus pro suo arbitrio, aut auger[?], aut diminuit numerum ministrorum & salaria eorum. Exigit etiam ab unoquoque ministro juramentum fidelitatis, quo ille promittit, & jurat se in officio suo religiosè ac benè versaturum & Magistratui fidelem fore: prout etiam illud ego in eâdem causâ praestiti. Nec quisquam nostrûm illud juramentum un-quam recusavit, & singuli eò me-lius sibi cavebant, ut ne praeter commune delictum etiam perjurii votam, ac poenam incurrerent. Quod quidem ideo narro tantum, ut manifestum fiat injuriam fieri Ecclesiae Genevensi ab adversariis, non autem, ut consuetudinem aut ordinem particularem ullius Ecclesiae oppugnem; aut impedire velim vel hac in parte, vel in aliis rebus, quas hactenus expoluimus quò minus Magistratus de jure suo si vult, remittat, quâ in parte quid expediat ipsius est prudenter dispicere. Atque hæc in præsentiarum sufficiant de hac materia. Pii Reges ac Magistratus facile vident se causam omnem habere, tum Deo gratias agendi, quod in libertatem suam per doctrinam Euangelii ex superbissimo jugo Cleri Romani sint vindicati; tum hanc doctrinam Ecclesiarum Reformatarum tanquam insignem gemmam diadematum ac fulcrum thronorum suorum sollicitè in Eccle-clesiâ conservandi. Ira enim &c illis jus suum illaesum servatur; & ministris Ecclesiae nec plus, nec minus quam par est tribuitur; quorum utrumque omnibus modis vitandum est. Nam ut contemptus piorum & fidelium servorum Dei contemptum Religionis secum trahit; ita etiam non nimium pastoribus est tribuendum; quemadmodum prudenter insignis servus Dei P. Martyr monet, ne superbiant ac tyrannide premant populum, & mandatis inventisque suis gloriam Dei obscurent: quae verba illius sunt, Loc. com-muni. Cl. IV. c. 1. §. 23. laudata etiam à Cl. Walaeo p. 149.
units.tr: So when those who are inflated with a love of domination and ambition [φιλαρχία, love of rule] and [φιλοτυραννία, love of tyranny] throw themselves into the office of the magistrate, they try to hinder it and resist it whenever it does or wishes to do this or that in ecclesiastical affairs in the course of its office, and so they expose both themselves and the Church, which was once entrusted to them, to danger. Ninthly, finally, this doctrine is necessary for defending our Churches against the calumnies of our adversaries. For the Remonstrants, here and there in their writings, and especially in their Apology, most bitterly attack our Churches, as if we set up two coordinate and supreme governing powers: the magistrate on the one side, and the ministers on the other, of whom the former has government only in secular matters and the latter in ecclesiastical matters. On this ground they say that among us the magistrates are made the servants, the lictors and the executioners of the ecclesiastics (as is the case under the Papacy), Apology, ch. 25, pp. 293–294. They attack in particular the Church of Geneva, and call it the mother of all Churches: Look only at Geneva, &c. The magistrate, whether it wills or not, lets everything be done at the discretion of the ministers; indeed it even lends its authority to them wherever the ministers judge it necessary. It is believed to be the crime of injured divine majesty not to obey the decrees of the ministers, &c. But that this is a calumny is clear from this disputation. Just as the wrong done to the Church of Geneva by them in particular, I can be a most reliable witness, since I taught for a long time in that Church and Academy. For although the state there is popular, and indeed to such an extent that the power to decide on law, peace or war, and likewise the choice of the consuls each year, rests with the people; and although the ministers there, on account of their outstanding learning and piety, which have shone forth in them from the beginning of the Reformation down to our own times, are held in great authority; nevertheless it is so far from the case that the magistrate there is the slave of the ministers and does whatever the ministers please, that on the contrary, if a minister says or does anything that seems contrary to the authority of the magistrate itself, he is restrained by the magistrate by an extraordinary procedure, without any consultation with the consistory, and is either held in public custody or suspended from office. I have known various recent examples of this. And yet we did not then accuse the magistrate of tyranny, nor did we stir up the people against it; instead we had recourse to our weapons, that is, prayers, which we directed to the magistrate, by which we softened its anger. The same magistrate, at its own discretion, either increases or diminishes the number of the ministers and their salaries. It also requires from each minister an oath of fidelity, by which he promises and swears that he will conduct himself in his office piously and well and will be faithful to the magistrate; just as I too took that oath in the same case. And none of us ever refused that oath, and each took greater care to avoid incurring, besides the common offence, the guilt and penalty of perjury. I mention this only so that it may be made plain that the wrong is done to the Church of Geneva by our adversaries; not that I wish to attack the custom or particular order of any Church, or to hinder the magistrate, if it wishes, from giving up its right in this or other matters which we have hitherto set forth; in which matter it is for the magistrate itself to consider prudently what is expedient. And let these things suffice for the present on this subject. Pious kings and magistrates readily see that they have every reason both to thank God that they have been freed by the doctrine of the Gospel from the most proud yoke of the Roman clergy, and to carefully preserve this doctrine of the Reformed Churches as a distinguished jewel of their crowns and a support of their thrones in the Church. For thus their right is preserved unharmed, and to the ministers of the Church is granted neither more nor less than is fitting; and each of these extremes is to be avoided by every means. For just as contempt for the pious and faithful servants of God brings with it contempt for religion, so too much is not to be granted to the ministers, as the distinguished servant of God P. Martyr wisely warns: lest they grow proud and oppress the people with tyranny, and by their own commands and inventions obscure the glory of God. These are his words, in Common Places, Book IV, ch. 1, §23, also cited by the distinguished Walaeus, p. 149.

units.la: Qui etiam p. 14. ait: quando 'exercitia ministerii cum suis dependentiis (nimirum administratio Sacramentorum, exercitium disciplinae Ecclesiasticae, cura pauperum, conservatio conventuum Ecclesiasticorum classicalium & Synodalium & reliqua, quae necessaria sunt ad conservandum bonum ordinem in cultu divino, cuibaud[?] dubiè inservit vocatio ministrorum[?] & judicatura controversiarum; quæ sæpè oriuntur in Ecclesiâ ) integra manent sine impedimento secundùm verbum Dei illis, qui ad id officium in Ecclesiâ Christi vocati sunt, & id quidem sub suprema inspectione, curâ, autoritate & imperio Magistratus secundùm verbum Dei tàm in personas, quæ administrant cultum Dei, quàm in administrationem ipsam, ministros & alios, qui Ecclesiæ præsunt non debere quicquam amplius postulare, quandoquidem nec plus nec minus ipsis à Christo est mandatum. Ita Dominus Walæus; quemadmodum etiam ejusdem judicio omnes Orthodoxi Pastores gratias agere tenentur ei, qui asserit veram potestatem, quam Magistratus secundùm verbum Dei in negociis Religionis habet. Nam experientia omnium temporum, inquit, nos docet Ecclesiam tùm demum frui verâ suâ libertate, quando sub tali Magistratu est, qui intelligit & benè novit officium, quod Deus ei supra illam commisit, ait p. 9. editionis Gallicæ Amstelodamensis per H. LaurenLaurentium, quam in hac disputatione fideliter sequuti sumus, prout etiam cæteros auctores bona fide allegavimus.
units.tr: He also says, on p. 14: when the exercises of the ministry with their dependencies (namely the administration of the Sacraments, the exercise of Church discipline, the care of the poor, the maintenance of the Church assemblies, classical and synodal, and the rest which are necessary for keeping good order in divine worship, to which the calling of ministers and the judgment of controversies, which often arise in the Church, doubtless belong) remain intact, without hindrance, according to the Word of God, for those who are called to that office in the Church of Christ; and this indeed under the supreme oversight, care, authority and command of the magistrate, according to the Word of God, both over the persons who administer the worship of God and over the administration itself, the ministers and others who preside over the Church, they ought not to demand anything more, since nothing more or less has been commanded them by Christ. Thus Lord Walaeus. In the same judgment, all orthodox ministers are bound to give thanks to him who asserts the true power which the magistrate has in matters of religion according to the Word of God. For the experience of all times, he says, teaches us that the Church then at last enjoys its true liberty, when it is under such a magistrate as understands and knows well the office which God has committed to it over the Church, says p. 9 of the French edition of Amsterdam, by H. Laurentius, whom we have faithfully followed in this disputation, just as we have cited the other authors in good faith.

units.la: Et sic quidem Magistratus potestatem in rebus Ecclesiasticis vindicavimus breviter adversum Bellarm. Proximâ disputatione ministerii Ecclesiastici naturam, dignitatem, jura contra eundem asseremus volente Domino.
units.tr: And thus we have briefly vindicated the power of the magistrate in ecclesiastical affairs against Bellarmine. In the next disputation, the Lord willing, we shall assert against the same author the nature, dignity and rights of the ecclesiastical ministry.

units.la: FINIS.
units.tr: THE END.
